GOOD OWD TIMES. Good owd times! Good owd times! Aw remember yo'
weel, When the rich mon kept th' werkin mon under his heel. Id were sixteen heawrs' werk and nod hauf an heawr's

• play, Seawr looks, scanty wages, an' two meals a day. Aw took to th' handloom afoor twelve years aw'd seen, An' aw'd getten to hate id affor avere thirteen; Aw once went for a sowjer, bud back aw soon coom, Aw're too smo to be shot, soli aw crept tack to th* loom. Good owd times! Good owd times! My owd gron- feyther's praise • Were o for the doins ov his younger days; He'd bed a herd boybood, a monhood o' strife, An' gm dornd think he'd ever a good meyl in his life; Ile allus stuck up—:in his doteagin' days— ?or th' mooast ancient o' fashions an' customs an' ways; But th' varra next minute th' truth med idsel sin, And he'd fret an' complain heaw ill favvared he'd bin. Good owd times! Good owd times! When 'twere breykin' th' law • For a poor mon to wish ony richer to row ; Ov one hauf ov his looaf he 're be taxes bereft. An' th' parson took th' haul o' wed there were left; An' when his wee morsel be good luck he'd hetten, Be 're enjoyned to be thankful for thad 'at he'd getten. Th' rich were suited, iv th' poor let their temper boil o'er, They could hang 'em, or shoot 'em, an' shut too-a-thry score. - -

Good owd times! Good owd times! My fust best wish, to day, Is for yo' to. just keep goin' farther away; >lever mind yo' them cranks as keeps flatterin' yo' so, Id's nubbut their fancy, they meon nowt at o'. Neaw a poor mon con read, vote, and mek his own laws, An' iv avoth out 's respected wherever he goes; Aw dorn'd say bud yo dud varra 'creel yo'r day, Bud yo 'n gone eawt o' date good owd times, keep away. CHARLES LANCASTER.

div.head: Varittits.
div.p: Varittits.
-- - - A fool may meet with good fortune, but the wise only

prOfit by it. It may be true that old maids look at the moon in the hope of seeing a man, but it can't be said of them that they ever go out between the acts of a play to see one. DOT'S nem. "She never gets a scolding, • She's never sent to bed, She hasn't got a napkin Put on her when she's fed; She plays with me, yet no one Tells her 'Don't make a noise.' • I sometimes wish my dolly Was me, and I was toys." An interesting budget of "Recollections of My Child- hood," by the late Miss Alcott, has just been printed. "One of my earliest memories," she says, "is of playing with books in my father's study, building towers and bridges of the biz dictionaries, looking at pictures, pre- tending to read,' and scribbling on blank pages whenever pen or pencil could be found. Many of these first attempts at authorship still exist, and I often wonder if these childish plays did not influence my after-life, since books have been my greatest comfort, castle.building a never-failing delight, and scribbling a very profitable amusement." According to Dr. Richardson. an undoubted authority on health, no point in the warfare against disease is so important as that of. getting the women of the house- hold to work heart and soul after good health. We I always (he says) look to women for the cleanliness and tidiness of home. We say a home is miserable if a good wife and mother be not at the head of it to direct the internal arrangements. A slovenly woman is a mark for discredit; but there can be no doubt that the excel- fences of tidy women in respect of order and cleanliness , have, without any distinct system or mode of scientific education, saved us from severe and fatal outbreaks of disease. SIMPLE REMRDIES.—NearIy one-half of the population are more or less afflicted with neuralgic pains. Instead of sending for the doctor, who will probably prescribe a p 1 sister and a dose of medicine, we advise the sufferer to heat a flatiron, put a double fold of flannel on the painful part, then move the iron to and fro on the flan- nel. The pain will cease almost immediately. We have seen the most painful cases of neuralgia relieved in less than ten minutes. Sprains are among_the most severe accidents to which we are liable. When a joint is sprained swelling comes on gradually. In dislocation the swelling and loss of motion of the joint happen im- mediately after the accident. A sprained limb should be kept perfectly quiet. To prevent inflammation, use poultims of wormwood, hops, or tansy. Every effort on the part of the patient to repeat in detail the cause of the accident, the sensations, experience. Etc., should be discouraged. Cheerful conversation upon other subjects and perfect rest will bring about speedy recovery, and strengthen all concerned in the belief that it is not always necessary to send for the doctor—Good Housekeeping. IN THE SURGICAL WARD.—" Chloroform or ether, doctor?"" Start him with chloroform" is the response. A handkerchief moistened with the sickening sweet fluid is placed to the patient's nostri".s. "Long breaths !" calls the surgeon, and the patient tries to answer "All right !" but his voice seems to him to step high, like the legs of a drunken man. Now he hears an elevated train coming. It is run by electricity. Its roads are of white light. Every snow and then it dashes past a station, when a bell rings. He is rushed aboard and on they go, faster and faster. The bells ring closer to- gether. "Happy ?" inquires the surgeon. "Ye-es," answers the patient, with an effort. "Happy ?" the sur- geon asks again, and there is no answer. . . . A blank, it may be of minutes, it may be of hours, then Softness, warmth, comfort! He is in the little country graveyard which he knew when a boy. He is sitting by his own body there. It is a sunny, summer afternoon. The birds are singing. And he can smell the'odour of the pines as they stir in the breeze. Is this death? Then death is a pleasant experience after all. But what is the nausea, the excruciating pain? "Spit it out !" urges someone in a friendly tone. Spit out what. death? Ah, the pain! and he is off into blankness once wore. A moment of quivering and again the balance strikes. This time he half opens his eyes. "He's playing possum,'" whispers a doctor, and the patient resents the irreverence of the remark. He is too fresh from the graveyard vision to tolerate joking familiarity, and, there! he may be dead after all! The pain again, and the blank, not so blank as before! 'there are scattering thoughts striving to assert themselves. He recognises them, slowly, as a child stammers when it reads. "Yes,—it is all right—it is all right !" he says to himself; and then, as if he saw it written in great capital letters, the thought confronts him, " 77tis must be COMING To!' "—Scribner's Magazine. Bisitor WILBERFORCE.—George Cruickshank is the authority for the following story, told to a friend by an elderly clergyman. The guests were playing at rhymes where certain words were given out to be made into couplets. The two words were cassowary and Timbuc- too. They puzzled Cruickshank, who passed them on to Wilberforce. This was his impromptu 111 were °cassowary, On the plains of Timbuctoo, I'd eat up every missionary. Black coat and hymnbook tee. Then there is the Blenheim story, about who should drive and who should walk to church. Palmerston and the host passed Wilberforce and his companions walking under their umbrella,s for it had come on to pour with rain. So the Premier put his head out of the carriage window, and said— How blest is he who ne'er consents By ill advice to walk. To which Wilberforce responded—. Nor stands in sinner's ways, nor sits Where men profanely talk. Apropos of the Psalms, the Baroness Burdett Coutts was driving him out towards Colombia Market when some- thing brought up the word drysalter. "Does your lord- ship know what a drysalter is?" said the lady. "Cer- tainly," replied Wilberforce. "Tate and Brady." By the way, he might have been excused if he had not known, for at a ball :in Manchester a yorng, lady who had been introduced to a very eligible partner engaged in that then lucrative business asked a cavalry officer with whom she was dancing. "What is a dry- , salter ?'' The soldier pulled his moustache and said, "A wholesale pickle merchant, I presume." Wilberforce was once told by his secretary, on the look-out, as is the wont of secretaries, for fees, "Mr. So-and-so must have a license for non-residence, my lord, for there is no par- sonage house." Quoth the Bishop, "He must have nothing of the kind. If there is no house, how can he want a license not to live in it ?" Fie could be good-humouredly sarcastic at times. He had been much bored by some tedious talkers at a clerical meeting. Whereupon a friend congratulated him on his patience. " Well, you >know," he replied, "one of the duties of a Bishop is to suffer fools gladly." I met him at Whitby shortly after the passage of arms between him and Lord Westbury. Some time after the two antagonists met on a not very auspicious occasion, for it was at the entrabce of the House of ,Lords, iiist after the Chancellor had given up the Great Seal. Lord Westbury remarked, "I felt in- clined to say, Bast thou found me, oh mine enemy ?' " Said Wilberforce, "1 was never so tempted in my life to finish the passage, hut I kept it down and asked, Does your lordship remember the end of the quotation ? ' " ." We lawyers," curtly responded Westbury," are not in the habit of quoting part of the sentence without know- ing the whole." "No doubt," says the Bishop, "he went home and looked it out of his family Bible, where he would see, Yea, I have found thee because thou hast sold thyself to work iniquity."—Temple Bar. HOW BOBBY LOST HIS SWEETHEART.
BY BIGIL.

Bobby Ilnker,ewho lives at Witton, is what is con- sidered a peculiar character. Bobby always contrived to make himself conspicuous even when he was a boy. If he went to an orchard for the purpose of robbing it, as is the practice amongst juveniles, he was sure to make a mess of it by either stepping into a well or midden, or something worse. If any escapade was planned by his schoolmates, and he was allowed to take part in it, he was sure to commit some fatal error, which would get the lot into trouble. But he was very good- natured, and would never split on his friends. -fie was also very innocent, but there was an amount of shrewd- ness in his character that often more than compensated for his innocence; in fact, it was frequently impossible to determine where innocence stopped and shrewdness

_ began. Bobby had a good many adventures during the years that intervened between his innocent boyhood and his attaining to the age of twenty years; but we will pass them over so as to get to his happy courting days—that period which is the most interesting and the best remem- bered of any in a person's lifetime. So well, indeed, are they remembered by most people that they are really an epoch from which they date and anti-date minor events. Now, until Bobby was turned twenty he never really fell in love in the strict sense of the word. It had somehow always happened that if ever he had taken a fancy to a girl, previous to that time, that she was sure to be keeping company with some other young man consequently Bobby had had to keep his passion in a manner bottled. But sooner or later it comes home to all of us, and Bobby was no exception to the rule. Bobby was a fair-loom weaver, and a very good I weaver too His life, at the time that lam writing of, was a pretty serene one, there being nothing to disturb his equanimity—that is, nothing out of the common. He went to the mill of a morning, did his work efficiently and satisfactorily, and spent his evenings either in reading "Bow Bells" or in having a quiet walk; then went to bed and slept the sleep of the just. But fate had something in store for him which was, for a time at ltast, to alter all this. It happened that one day a four-loom weaver, who worked at the same shed that Bobby worked at, left on account of some dispute with the cutlooker. This weaver's looms were two alleys distant from Bobby's looms—that is to say, there were two rows of looms between Bobby's and his. Now, the fact of this weaver leaving did not affect Bobby in the least, but the weaver _ . . .

that followed, and who happened to be a young woman, created such a sensation in his bosom as made him wonder himself what 'was the matter with, him. It wasn't that she said or did anything to him. No; sbe just went on with her weaving, like any sensible young woman would do, and took no notice of anybody for some time. As she told Bobby afterwards, she never saw him the first d4y at all—well, at any rate, not to notice him. But there is no doubt that Bobby was hit, and hit hard, for, as he told afterwards, "he were aboon an heawr o' gedding to sleep when he went to bed thad neet _

_ Well, to get on with the story, Bobby watched this girl so persistently, and so indefatigably, that she began to notice it, and, as a natural consequence, to feel flattered. How could she help it? for every time she looked at him she could see admiration and love fairly oozing out of his eyes. If she went for any weft Bobby was sure to follow with a weft can on his shoulder, and he always kept his " cuts " back until he saw her taking hers to the warehouse. This went on until they got on speaking terms, and then Bobby began to have errands to go of an evening, after the engine had stopped, which took him in the direction of Susie Green's home.for such was her name. This went on for some time, and then, one Saturday, he persuaded her to meet him the following afternoon, and go for a walk with him. On leaving him at tea-time that Sunday afternoon she pro- mised to meet him again the following Tuesday evening. Now Bobby was delighted at haying succeeded in gaining Susie's regard, though he had not had a chance I to properly demmstrate his affection for her, as they had only been in each other's company in the daylight and amongst people. This Tuesday evening he meant to show her that he thought the world of her. They met as agreed upon and went for a walk along the highway leading to Cherry Tree. It being a dark night they did not go far, but stopped near to the lodge gate at the entrance to Witton Park, but on the oppo- site side of the road. They begun to chat here, Bobby holding Susie's hand. By and by, as Bobby's feelings began to work upon him, he slid his arm around her waist, to which Susie made not the slightest objection. The conversation had by this time naturally drifted on to the subject of Bobby's love for her, its quality and strength. and so on. " Tha sea tha likes mo," said Susie in a doubting tone, "but it's eeasy talkin'. Heaw do aw know as tha hesn'd bawd monv a lots o' lasses t' same tale? Eh, fellas is desateful- !" "Aw've never towd nobry afoor as aw liked urn, un awm sure as aw never shall. Sitha ! iv ever aw hey aw wish aw may hey a mash i' every loom to morn!" said Bobby, and he hitched a little closer to Susie. During the disputation Bobby kept getting closer Co Susie, till at last he had got both of his arms around her waist. Susie continued to doubt his love, and it seemed as if lie would never be able to satisfy her that he was telling the truth. This had gone on for a considerable time, and Bobby had grown so earnest that he was holding Susie as if in a vice. At a certain point he seemed to make up his mind that he would clinch the matter, for, in a voice that betrayed his passion, he said—" Sitha, Susie, if awm nod tellin' tha truth--" Just then he gave Susie such a squeezing that he lifted her slightly off her feet. Susie said, "Oh, Bobby, thair killing so !' There was a crack, and Bobby felt some- thing about Susie's back give way, and his hands sunk into her back. A horrible thought struck him, and he suddenly let go of Susie, who dropped on the floor all of a heap. Bobby took to his heels and ran for his life towards home, in an agony of mind too great for words. That he had broken Susie's back he had not a doubt, and he knew that that meant certain death. When Bobby got home his face was as white as chalk, and be was out of breath. There was no one in the house but his mother. She could see at once that there was something the matter with Bobby, so she said, "Wodever's to do wi' tha, Bobby? Arta nooan so weel ?" Yigh," said Bobby, sinking into a chair, the tears welling up into his eyes at once. ' "Neaw, there's summat to do wi' tha! Wod hes ta bin dooin ?" "h. mother, this is a bonny job," said Bobby, and he roared out like a lost calf. " wey, wodever's to do, Bobby ?" "Aw've kilt Susie Green," said Bobby. " Tha's wod ?" screamed hit mother. "Oh dear! Wod mon aw do? Aw've kilt Susie Green !” " Tha's kilt Susie Green ! Wodever hes ta kilt her

for ? " "Oh, dear o' me! Aw dudn'd do id o' porpose !" " Wey, heawever dud ta kill her then ?" "w brooak her backbooan wi' squeezin' her !" wailed poor Bobby. By a little questioning Bobby's mother got all the facts out of Bobby, and then, doubting that a woman could be killed by a man squeezing her, she insisted on Bobby taking her to the spot, which he did. They found no Susie; so the mother told Bobby to say nothing to 'any- one, but to go to bed. Bobby took her advice, but he had an awful night of it. He went through the process of being hanged many a time before getting up in the morning. Bobby never expected to see Susie at her work when he went to the mill at six o'clock, but she was there be- fore him, looking as well as ever. He had only broken her stays bone. She dropped on the ground through Bobby 'letting her go so suddenlrand unawares. Bobby tried to make up to her again but she would have nothing further to do with him, and he remains a bachelor to this day, and lives in the same neighbour- hood. He has never had the courage to make up to another girl.

div.head: THg EXA
div.p: THg EXA
THE WIDNES SEWER FATALITY. THREE MEN SUFFOCATED. THE RAILWAY COMPANY CENSURED. On Tuesday afternoon Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner for South-West Lancashire, resumed and concluded

an inquiry into the circumstances attending the death of three Warrington men, servants of the London and North-Western Railway Company, which occurred under very painful circumstances on the 18th of the present month. The inquiry was held at the Police Station at Widnes, and lasted
over three hours, the jury, after hearing the evid- ence of several witnesses, deliberating on their ver-

diet in private for three-quarters of a"n hour. Mr. Preston, of Lime-st. Station, Liverpool, appeared for the railway company, and with him were Mr. Worthington, District Engineer, and Mr. Ferrand ; Dr. Affleck, Inspector under the Alkali Act, was also present. The deceased men were named John Tyrer (37), of Winwick, near IN arrington ; William Clare (n), also of Winwick ; and John Monoghan (55), Back-lane, Sankey, near Warrinaton. The cir- cumstances under which, on the day in question, they were all three

SUFFOCATED IN A SEWER have previously been stated in these columns. To put it briefly, about eight men, all servants of the Railway Compiny, were on Monday in last week employed in cleaning out a length of the sewer known as Bower's Brook, which drains several chemical works, and empties itself into the Mersey at a point near the works of Messrs. Gossage and Son. The length of sewer being operated upon commenced at the man-hole at the iron bridge, which spans the canal at the Old Marsh, and ended at a man-hole about fifty yards distant. The mode of working was as follows: A bucket of peculiar shape attached to a rope that runs through the sewer, and this rope was fixed to a winch, which, being turned, dragged the bucket along the bottom of the sewer. The sediment was thusdisturbed, and the force of the stream, or a flush of water from the canal, carried away the refuse to the river. Robert Whitworth, of Orford-street,
was

Warrington, descended in the sewer, -which is seven feet deep, and made fast the bucket to the rope. Afterwards he and William Clare followed in the path of the bucket in order to dislodge the sediment that adhered to that portion of the sewer left untouched by the bucket. At the outset the amosphere was clear ;- but, after travelling some yards, Clare said "I smell something strong." Whitworth replied "So do I; come on, let's be going along," and as the noxious vapour seemed to be travel- ling behind them, they went forward as quickly as they could. Before they had gone far, Clare fell down and cried "Oh God help us, Robert! I'm done." "I can- not help thee, Bill," replied Whitworth, "I'm done my- self." Whitworth shouted for help, and Monaghan and John Tyrer descended into the sewer to see what was the matter. The suspicions of the other men were aroused, and they followed in the wake of their com- rades, and were horrified to find all the four men lying at the bottom unconscious. With all despatch the men were brought into the open air. Whitworth showed signs of life, and ultimately recovered, but the OTHER THREE WERE DEAD. The first witness called on Tuesday wag Thomas Sankey, of Winwick, for live years a labourer in the company's employ, who had for nine months been working, on and off, at the sewer in question. He detailed how on the day in question he was present when Clare and Whit- worth went down the manhole at the Iron Bridge to tie the buckets on. He remained on the top at the "grab." The first intimation that he had that something was wrong was when he heard Whitworth shouting. Mono- ghan and Tyrer at once went down to give assistance, and witness also went down, and assisted to bring .Whit- worth, who was unconscious, to the surface. Tyrer and Monaghan, anxious to save their comrade Clare, went down again, but witness had to remain on the top in consequence of being overcome by the gas. Someone else then went down the ladder, and found all three men dead at the bottom. At the time the stench was over- powering, and witness had some difficulty in getting Whitworth out of the sewer. The foreman—John Shaw —was away at the time, and in his absence Tyrer gave orders and acted as foreman. In answer to questions put by the Coroner, Sankey said that the covers were always taken off the manholes before work was com- menced. There were four manholes, but only three ladders were provided—one at the Iron Bridge hole, one at therab hole, and a third which was sometimes placed at till third and sometimes at the second hole. On the morning when the accidenthappened the four holes were open, but there was no ladder at the Resin Works hole. He did not know whether life might have been saved had there been one. There was no difficulty in getting out of the holes. If he encountered a stench in a sewer that he thought was dangerous he should come out. He did not think it. would be possible to clean the sewer without men having to go down, and he thought it would be better if there were ladders at every hole, but he did not see how they were to be fixed. In answer to Mr. Pres- ton witness said that he never before knew the smell to be so strong. "He never felt the like of it before." The

div.head: WATER WAS BLACK_ AS INK,
div.p: WATER WAS BLACK_ AS INK,

and blacker than ever he saw it before. The work was carried on in the ttsual way. Answering jurors, witness said that he did not know how he got down the hole and up again with Whitworth. He thought that the hole was about eighteen inches hi width, but was not prepared to say that it was not over fifteen, as he had never seen it measured. James Bate, who is also in the employ of the company, was the next witness who gave evidence, and he explained that it was his business to shovel the refuse out of the sewer. When on the occasion under considera- tion he went into the sewer he felt a queer sensation, and turned back. He became sick, and vomited. He was not until afterwards aware of the deceased having been suffocated. He could not say whether a ladder placed at each hole would better tend to the preservation of life, but in such a case the men would not have as far to go. If the manholes were larger the men might get away quicker, and the stench also might get away quicker. In answer to questions, witness said that he had never before known the stench to be 'so bad. It had, however, Made him sick before, and six weeks ago Clare was over- come by it, and witness carried him out. The smell had been the worst during the last three months. It was not a fapt that he himself had to be assisted out of the sewer some weeks ago. The water from the copper works passed where he was working, and the Widnes Alkali Works were close to. This completed the evidence called by the police, but Dr. Affieck made an interesting state- ment to the jury. He said that previous to the accident he was not aware that it was the custom to employ men to go down the sewer, or he should have felt it his duty to warn them of the extreme danger that they incurred. He did not think, considering the nature of the ground at Widnes, that there was any sewer or culvert in the town that it was safe to enter regularly. No doubt, at times the sewers might be free from gases, but at other times they were almost certain to have such quantities ef gas in them as would be dangerous and, in fact, fatal to life. The sewers could never be properly clear of gas. The sewer in ques- tion ran past many deposits of alkali water, which were an active source of nuisance, and there would no doubt be percolations of acid into the sewer. They were aware that there was sulphuretted hydrogen in the drain, as in other drains, but there had not hitherto been such a quantity as to constitute a nuisance to the neighbour- hood, and bring the matter under the provisions of the Alkali Act. But while there was not sufficient gas to , cause a nuisance, it was a different thing to go into the culverted portion of a sewer, as the gas became stirred up and was very injurious. snowing the character of the drainage, it did not to him seem right to send men into the sewer at all. A toothed rake, properly construc- ted to fit the sewer, would disturb the sediment suffi- ciently to get it cleared away. No man should go down a sewer at Widnes unless he had some respiratory appar- atus with him, and means were constantly at hand to bring the person so engaged hack at once. Some sug- gestions had been mooted previously, which he thought should be carried out. In answer to Mr. Preston the doctor said that he was not aware that in 1883 the Lon- don and North-Western Railway Co. themselves complained to the Local Government Board about the discharges from the chemical works into the brook. Mr. Preston informed the court that the recommendations now made by the alkali inspector were made by the company in 1883, but had never been acted upon. The company were not legally bound to clean nut the sewer. The , Coroner said that the company must either let the sedi- ment remain in or clean it out, and they seemed to have adopted the second alternative. Whether legally bound to clean out the sewer or not, if the com- pany did so they were bound to take all possible precautions for the saving of life. (Mr. Pres 7 ton : The creatioh of the gas is originally an unlawful act). For the purposes of the inquiry he would grant that ; still the company knew such unlawful act might arise. This remark Mr. Preston disputed, saying that such a thing had not happened before, and there was no- thing to show that the culvert was dangerous to life, and the Coroner pointed out that what had happened six weeks before was a warning. Dr. Affieck, in answer to Mr. Preston, said that he should think the extraordinary discolouration of the water was due to some extra quan- tity of alkali or sulphur drainage getting into it. It might have come from any of the works, or from some of the waste deposits near the brook, If any works knowingly discharged acid inta the brook it would be considered an infraction of the Act, but at the same time accidents would occur at the works, and acids might thus get into the brook. Mr. Preston p 'tinted out that it was provided that works in which acids are produced should be carried on in such a manner that the acid should not come in contact with alkali waste, or with drain- age, so as to cause a nuisance, but that a channel should be provided to carry it into the sea or the river. After further discussion, the foreman Shaw, who volunteered to give evidence, said that he told Tyrer the sewer wanted cleaning out, but the men were) not to go down if there was a bad smell. In summing up, the Coroner said the Company had taken upon themselves the obligation of cleaning out the sewer' and were bound to protect with all possible safeguards the lives of the men employed. Dr. Affieck had said that it was unsafe for men to go down any sewer in Widnes, and the ques- tion arose—did they think the company would have such knowledge? Taking it for granted that the company considered their method the proper one, had they taken sufficient precautions to protect life? Me thought that the manholes should be as wide and large as possible,

and that there should be a ladder at each. They could either exonerate or censure Shaw, as they thought fit, and if they considered the coippany to be at fault they could make a presentment to that effect. After retiring the jury
INER, SATURDAY, JUNE 30, 1888.

div.head: TTNANdMOTISLY.AGREED
div.p: TTNANdMOTISLY.AGREED

on a verdict to the effect that the deceased came to their death by accident, due to the culpable negligence of the London and North-Western Railway or Canal Company by not providing reasonable or proper exits, er by en- forcing certain safeguards such as ropes or respirators. The jury were, moreover, of opinion that it was abso- lutely unsafe, on scientific evidence, to allow men to go down this sewer without better approaches, ventilation, and wearing and breathing apparatus. The inquiry then , terminated.

of the Channel Tunnel Bill on Wednesday afternoon. The majority against the scheme was excessive; it was, in fact, 143—a majority of nearly two to one, the votes for the bill being no more than 165. The Liberal leader's action has been 'made the subject of some ungenerous detraction. I can only say thit it was perfectly notorious four years ago that Mr. Gladstone was in favour of the Channel Tunnel. His speech, however, did not set him right with the in- dignant Conservatives. Re based the defence of his consistency not upon the known fact that he had been overruled in his own cabinet, but Upon the not so relevant proposition that while Mr. Chamberlain had opposed the Channel Tunnel in the name of the Liberal Government, he had not opposed it upon its merits. Mr. Gladstone made it a charge aflamst the present Government that it was opposing it upon its merits. Of course this brought up Lord Randolph Churchill; but Lord Ran- dolph's own foresight on this matter has not been conspicuous, seeing that be turns out to be a share- holder in the very company whose scheme he op- posed. In the division, 'several Radicals voted against the scheme and one or two Conservatives in its favour; and the end is that our military strength is judged to be insufficient to present an enemy from coming through an opening in the earth some 30 yards in diameter.

div.head: POLICE COURT INCIDENT.
div.p: A POLICE COURT INCIDENT.

An amusing scene was witnessed at the Warring- ton Borough Police Court on Monday morning. A number of Irish people named Michael Costello, Ann Costello, his mother, Margaret Costello, his Sister, John Rooney, an old man, Catherine Rooney, his wife, Bridget Rooney and Mary Rooney, his daugh- ters, Michael Devitt, a powerfully-built navvy, and Mary Davitt, his wife, were all summoned to an- swer charges of creating breaches of the peace by fighting in Ship-yard, off Bridge-st., where they all. reside. The defendants, each in it very excited state, were ranged in a long row along the dock, and on hearing a constable state that he saw the defendants fighting on Sunday, the 17th inst, each individual insisted on telling his or her tale, at the same time, appealing to witnesses in the body of the court to corroborate their statements. The Chairman (Alderman Davies) remarked that "it was worse than an Irish Parliament."—The Chief Constable (to defendants) : Be quiet, will you?— Bridget Rooney (submissively) : "Yes, lovey.' Quiet having been restored, the constable, in reply to Alderman Davies, said that Margaiet Costello, Mary Rooney, and Mary Devitt were the most peaceably inclined of the, defendants at the time of the row.—John Rooney: I was in bed when the row commenced.—Alderman Davies: You should have stayed there.—Michael Costello wished to know why he had been summoned, as he was entirely in-' nocent of creating any disturbance. His remarks were interrupted by the Rooneys, who made a statement to the effect that Mary Rooney had asked the consent of Michael Costello's parents to their marriage, and had received instead a black eye from his mother. Her people had resented this, and other persons joining in, a row had commenced, in the thick of which the officer came up and took the names of the combatants.' Each party protested their own innocence, and denounced the others.— The Bench dismissed the charges against Mary Rooney, Mary Davitt, and Margaret Costello, and ordered each of the others to find one surety of £5 for their good behaviour for six months, or to go to prison for seven days.—The sureties were found.

RHYMES IN TILE DIALECT. TH' LAST FAREWELL. Eh, Joan! heaw ill th'art leokin' ! Thi hands are long un thin; Thi figure, onct.so comely, It's nowt bud booan un skin. It's hard to see thee lvin' • So poorly theer on t' bed, An yet aw cornd help tbinkin' O'er t' pleasures as we've hed. We went to skoo together, An' booath lived ia t' same fowd ; That's five an' forty year sin', An' yet th'art true as gowd. Thro' pleasure an' thro' trubhle, sunleet, snow, or gloom, , Tha's proved thisel' true hearted Thro' every change as coom. An' neaw th'art lyin' helpless, An' worn, an' weary theer ; • Mi voice—God knows id,—trembles, Mi heart's weighed deswn wi' fear, For summat thi strangeness Brings t' tear-drops to mi een ; While thine look up so kindly— So trustful an' serene. Tha towd me when we mated As childer hi th' skoo' wo', As aw wur th' chum tha trusted Un cherished t' mooast ov o. We stood, wi' hands gript firmly, An' vowed wi' blended breoth, As we'd ston to one another An' be true mates till deoth. Joan, lad, mi heart's near brokken, Ther's few sitch mates as thee; Aw cried when t' doctor met me An towd me as tha'd dee. It's Sorrow's only comfort, To know, if t' wost befell, As we'st nod be long asunder, Aw'm off deawn t' broo misel'. Thi breath, it's geddin' shorter— Ther's sweot drops o' thi broo ; Aw do hope God 'll gi'e thee Strength as 'll ged thee thro'. Iv aw wur th' heir to millions, Aw'd sacrifice o t' wealth To see thee, good owd Joanie, Restooared to hearty health. Let's clasp eawr hands together; Heaw strange thine feels to mine. Aw'll kiss thee, for aw like thee, Skoo-mate ov owd lang syne. Thi hond it's geddin' cowder, Tha'll meet yo'r Matty soon; It's five year, come this winter, Sin hoo wur co'd aboon. Aw'll do o as tha's axed me; An' when aw'm left alooan, Aw'll think o' thee, an' treasure Thi memory when tha'rt gooan. Aw know tha rt reight for leovin' This world o' woe an' sin; For th' angels sing i' heaven When souls like thine goo in. JACK 0' ANN'S.
THE BLOOD PURIFIER. J. Spring medicine! Spring medicine! Spring medicine !
AMEEF

div.head: FRON LONDON LETTERS,
div.p: FRON LONDON LETTERS,

The hurried visit of the Princess of Wales to Dessau last week is reported at Berlin to be con- nected with a project of marriage between Princess Victoria of Wales and the Hereditary Prince of Anhalt-Dessau, who was born in August, 1856. "We are a doomed party," said one of the Dissen- tient Liberals on Thursday. His view is that by- elections have shown, and are displaying, that there is no permanent place tor a fourth party. For hiin- self, this gentleman appears inclined to give up the notion that Liberals are separatists ; but at any rate he is convinced that separation is the destiny of the Dissentient Liberals. The times are moving. It is just twenty-six years since the bishops and clergy took united action against Sunday "desecration." The form which their action took was a protest against Sun- day excursion trains. Nowadays a united protest by the bishops against Sunday trains would be a miracle. The form of Sunday misuse which they do condemn—and they condemned it lately in Con- vocation—was the selfish enjoyment of Sunday by the rich. I learn that the Church Association propose " sending rounding the hat" in connection with the suit they have instituted against the Bishop of Lincoln. It seems strange that the society should prosecute Dr. King for acting up to his interpreta- tion of the Ornaments Rubric when they them- selves in their official publications speak of the Irubric as ambiguous, and as not bearing its meaning on its face, and further, that "until it is made clear the controversy will not cease." A census has recently been taken of the public- houses and beerhouses in the Parliamentary borough of Buniley. The result is most remarkable and in- structive. There are, it appears, in Burnley 177 houses of this description, and of these 132 are the property of brewers, 33 are leased to brewers,whilst only 12 are free. In other words, out of 177 licensed premises 165 are what are called "tied houses," the publicans being to all intents and purposes the brewers' slaves. There is reason to believe the reports of a matri- monial engagement between a daughter of the late German Emperor and the Crown Prince of Greece- is correct. The Greek Constitution would not oblige the Princess to join the National Church, but the children of the marriage must be educated in that faith. King George, like the Princessids a Lutheran Protestant. The associated report that the Princess Victoria of Prussia will be married in England to Prince Alexander of Battenberg is regarded as less probable. Nothing has occurred to change the German Chancellor's view of this alliance. The authority of the Emperor as to marriages in his family is final, and would undoubtedly be obeyed in this case; and the performance of the ceremony in England—which means probably the Isle of Wight—implies a visit of the widowed Empress, which it is said on good authority is not yet atraeged. Mr. T. P. O'Connor gave a reception on Wednesday night for the fitst time at his new newspaper offices. Mr. John Morley and at least,...e. hundred Liberal members of Parliament were present. Miss Fortes- cue, Mr. Edmund Yates, and a large number of other eelebrities were also present, and altogether there was a crush which deserves to be remembered as the first great function of the only euccessful evening paper which London has seen for a number of years. Mr. Morley remained for about half an hour, but the rest of the company continued some time longer to enjoy the hospitality of Mr. ana Mrs. T. P. O'Connor. It was probably the first time in the history of the press that it had been found possible to combine the amenities of a private house with the hard work-a-day realities of a prin- ting office. Since his feturn from America, Mr. Chamberlain has resumed that course of hospitality at Prince's- gardens which has for some years been a feature in the Parliamentary season. His dinner parties are, by reason of the careful selection of guests, drawn from a far-reaching circle of the most eminent men of the day, about the most interesting reunions of the season. Mr. Chamberlain rarely limits his guests to the London circle. Whatever eminent men chance to be passing through London are sure to be met in turn at his table. Still, the aristocracy of birth predominates at his residence, now known as "The Dukeries," Whenever there is a seat to spare, there is one ef the titled gentlemen of England to fill it. A commoner who was recently privileged to sit at the table tells me how secretly gratified he was by the attention of the waiter. "Hock, my lord ?" said the man, drawing a bow at a venture. He could not conceive anyone at the table under the status of a baron. The last of the Jubilees—that of Her Majesty's Coronation—did, beyond official recognition, not attract much attention on Thursday. Those who are old enough to remember 50 years ago recall the gay processions in many towns of the kingdom, and proceedings. not very unlike those of the Jubilee of last year, upon the auspicious day when the Queen was crowned at Westminster. Her Majesty's happy reign was not of many years when Cardinal Wise- man, thinking of this ceremony,vvrete of the pre-Re- formation period that "time was when it needed not a coronation to fill the aisles of Westminster but since he ruled where Cardinal Manning now holds authority there has been so great a revi- val in the Church of England that to see those aisles crowded has been in recent years no uncommon sight. Her Majesty, I learn from a sure authority, 1 is really in excellent health—very strong, and never more comfortable in regard to the duties of State; but she is unable, owing to neuralgic pains which have their origin in the circulation, to take much walking exercise, and from .the same cause finds difficulty in standing for any prolonged time. It is said that the Queen has followed with particular interest and satisfaction the proclamations of the new Emperor, her grandson. If ladies of title have not yet stormed the stage, they have at all events determined to make them- selves heard in the concert room. On Thursday week a musical entertainment in aid of the fund for distressed Irish ladies is to be given in St. James's Hall. On that occasion the distinguished ladies who are generally found in their fauteuil in front will occupy the orchestra. The chorus is to be Adaniless. At its head, the leader of the attack, will be the Duchess of Sutherland. Two Countesses Gleichen are members of it. The Marchioness of Blandford, five countesses (including their lady- ships of North esk, Cowper, and Clarendon) a viscoun- tess, and 14 Ladies (including Lady Arthur Hill, Lady Albertha Edgcumbe, Lady Curzon, Lady Hast- ings, Lady Churchill, and Lady Aveland), and six- teen honourable% besides some forty other untitled ladies, all in society, will be under the bdton of Viscountess Folkestone. At the organ, it is true, Dr. Bridge will preside, and Mr. Henchell is per- mitted to sing a song; but, with these exceptions, all the pieces, the solos, the choruses, and the orches- tral compositions will be rendered by ladies. The Queen is the chief patron of the entertainment, and after her comes the Princess of Wales. England is safe again. Its invasion by France through a hole beneath the water has been made impossible for another year by the ' rejection

Some men sell the vacant thrones of angels reserved for themselves for short and turbulent pleasures. An editor, in reply to a young writer who wished to know which magazine would give him the highest posi- tion quickest, advised "a powder magazine, especially if you contribute a fiery article." , "Sancho," said a dying planter to his slave, "for your faithful services I mean now to do you an honour, and I leave it in my will that you shall be buried in our family ground." "Au. mass," replied Sancho, "Sancho no good to be buried; Sancho rather have de money or de freedom; I besides, if de devil come in de dark to look for massa, lie mistake and take de poor nigger man." "I could gaze at the moon for hours, Mr. Sampson," she said, in a voice full of sweetness and pneumonia; "I never tire of it." " Ah," he responded, "would that I were the man in it ! " " Yes,",she assented, softly. "And I why, Miss Clara? he asked, getting ready to take her hand. "Because, Mr. Sampson," she said, shyly veiling 'her eyes with her long lashes, "you would be 4,000,000 miles away I" Dressmakers can buy no better sewing cotton than Bagley and Wright's, which for strength is unequalled.—Adve.

must have her y ; yoq have appealed to me. I'll set 7ou and the whole concern straight in next to no time.' Tom Chilton's exuberant delight was very pain. ful to Phyllis, and seemed to chill her. She did not answer him, so he ran on—" "You shall suggest all the improvements, Phyllis, and I'll carry them ,out. My money and yours, eh The combined sums will make a business, won't they ?" "I suppose so." "You don't seem sanguine ; well, I suppose you are well-nigh worn out with the worry of this place; it is too much for a woman." "Too much fer a woman; yea," echoed Phyllis wearily. "Poor darling !" And he drew nearer to her and laid his hand on her arm, he would have taken her altogether in his had he dared. She instinctively stepped back, then suddenly re- rPembering that she-was not acting her allotted part, she said, with so much feeling,. "Thank you, thank ki you, Tom, you are always so nd and good to me," that Tom Chilton felt himself encouraged, and after looking at her in surprise for a second, he asked— "ls there any chance at the end of the two years of my being anything more than a partner, Phyllis ? " 'That depends on yourself,"she replied, striving to smile. "On myself—if it depended on myself I'd take you to church to-morrow ! ' "But that is impossible.' "Worse luck to it. Only if you would give mesome hope,—say that at the end oi two years you will be my wife, I'd be a happier man." 0111 say it, Tom; be faithful to me, and trust me in everything, and I will be your wife in two years." She was in his arms now and he was smothering her neck and face with kisses. Needless to say, she struggled to be free, and all on a sudden he let her go as though something had stung him. It was the recollection of "that other fellow," as he con- temptuously called Geoffrey Stanhope. 4' Has he dropped you, Phyllis, that you are so genial-like to me ?' he asked, with a coarsene.ss that was part of his nature. " don't know what you mean—dropped me ? " "Geoffrey Stanhope as has been philandering after you for so long.' "Tom, I told you just now that I would only promise to be your wife on condition that you trusted me fully. It is scarcely trusting me to ask me such a question as this." Tom scratched his head and looked perplexed. "But I can't have a swell betwixt you and me, Phyllis; that wouldn't suit an honest man, and I've always tried to keep myself an honest man." ' "Do you think, Tom, that I am less honest than you, that I should consent to be your wife; if—" "No more; don't say any more, Phyllis. I'll trust you, and take your word for it, that Geoffrey Stanhope has never been, and won't ever be, anything to you.." "Stop, Tom, I don't wish you to sail under any false colours. I will not go so far as to say Mr. Geoffrey has never, been anything to me, but I will promise that in future he shall be as dead and out of my life ; and that come weal, come woe, when once I am your wife, no man, be he gentle or humble, shall come between us to destroy our pea Ce." "Thank you, my girl, you've a 'brave heart and a noble one. I won't ask any more questions—only be thankful. I know what you think is right, is right, and I give you my word I will always be satisfied with it. Give us a kiss of your own free will to seal the bargain." She raised her head to his and gave the asked for kiss. Perhaps it was a cold one, but it satisfied Tom, and maybe warmer ones would come with time. "And now tell the men you are master here," she said. "I must go and see the mother, I've left her o'er long." Having got rid of him, she did not immediately go to her mother, but ran upstairs and locked herself in her room. She must be alone—alone with her own Feelings for a brief space, or they would prove too strong for her, and she would not be able to master them. Not long, however, could she pass in her solitude, or she would be missed, so once inore resuming the outer semblance of content, she went down to the parlour. Airs. said— " I have a bit of news for you, mother, that wi I make you very happy. lam engaged to be married to Tom Chilton." Mrs. Knight fairly started from her chair. "That I have come to my senses, mother, and know now that Simen Knight's daughter is no fit wife for Mr. Stanhope's son; like should male with like if the world is to go • even." HOUSE OF LORDS.-MOXDAY.
'rho LORD STEWARD (Earl of Mount Edgecumbe) hrought up the Queen's reply to their lordships address of condolence on the death of the Emperor Frederick.

Other business was gone through, and the House ad- journed. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY. The Speaker took the chair at 3 5 p.m. Lord Arthur Hill, Controller of the Household, ap- peared at the bar and brought up a message from `Ma Crown, thanking the House for its resolution of tem- Oolence with her Majesty on the occasion of the death of tb.3 late Emperor of Germany.

div.head: QUESTIONS.
div.p: QUESTIONS.

Answering Mr. Kilb—ride, Mr. BALFOUR said it Was true that the Athy Board of Guardians had Yeen dissolved by aled order of the Local Government Board, the reason bsing that the Board had deliberately made excessive ar.d illegal payments out of The funds of the Union. Mr. OtansrowE asked the Chief Secretary whether the Government would lay on the table of the House a copy of the record, and the derositions in the court of firsi instance, and on appeal, in the case of Mr. John Dillon. --Mr. BALFOUR, ardid derisive cheers from the Irish benches, said that the course suggested was unusual, ;.nd in view of the faCtlhat there watmothing special it, this particular case, he did not think 'it WO:.Ild be expe- dient to grant the'return. On the motion df Mr. CAINE, a return was ordere,i showing the revenue derived from licenses for the sale of intoxicating liquora and from the inhabited how; • duty respectively for each county of England and lA'at(\i forthe last financial year.

div.head: MR.. MORLEY'S MOTION.
div.p: MR.. MORLEY'S MOTION.

Mr. Join; MORLEY rose, amidst Opposition cheers, to move that in the opinion of that House, the operation .of the Crimes Act, and the manner of its administration, undermined respect for law, estranged the minds of the ~people of Ireland. and were deeply injurious to the in- terests of the United Kingdom. He said one of the three kingdoms had been for a year placed under exceptional and repressive legislation. Seventeen or more members of the House of Commons had been impiisoned in con- sequence, and in one gaol alone there were forty prisoners under the Act. Collisions be- tween the people and the police had been of almost unexampled frequency since the Act was passed, and the High Court of Justice in Ireland the other day pronounced a judgment which had in effect discredited the most important part of the machinery by which the Act was carried out. The Opposition chal- lenged the polity the Government were pursuing throughout; its justice, expediency, and wisdom, and they challenged even the allegations of the Government of the transient and temporary success of the Act. The .alministration of the Coercion Act up to this time had 11 been nothing more nor less than a scandal, and it fully justified the statement of himself and his friends at the outset that neither the law nor the cotnmon sense not the equity of tte resident magistrates were on sucha level as to make them safe substitutes for a jury. The-State of Ireland was becoming worse .from day to day, and by all that came from Ireland they would see before many months were past the necessity for doing away with a system that deepened confusion and tar- nished the honour, the credit, and the renown of the Parliament and people of this country. Mr. Goscmix, who followed, repudiated the idea that the Governmentwas putting political opponents in prison.The-Government were applying to Ireland the principles that had made Eng- land what it was. It was the introduction of a new standard of law, and a new interpretation of the duties of citizens that had made Ireland what it was now. He claimed that success was attending the policy of the Go- vernment, who knew that their progress could only be slow. They would find it difficult to win the affections of the Irish people, but they would not try to do that by the sacrifice of all their previous principles. (Cheers.) Mr. R. REID, the Solicitor-Generalfor Ireland, Mr. &n- -orm, and others, continued the debate.
The debate was acijournpd WI the motion of MR. O'BRIEN.
The Reformatory Schools Act. (1866) Amendment Bill was read a third time. The House adjourned at 12 20 a.m. HOUSE OF LORDS.--Tunsosr.

The Lord Chancellor took his seat. at 4 15 p.m. 'BILLS ADVINCRD.—The Factory and Workshops Act (1878) Amendment (Scotland) Bill passed Committee.— The North Sea Fisheries Bill passed the third reading. SFCOOND RFADINGS.—The Suffragans Nomination Bill passed the second reading.—The Earl of ROSETIRRY moved the second reading of the Companies Clauses Consolidation Act (1845) Amendment. Bill. The measure. he explained, was to enable provident and industrial societies having investments in companies, to he renre- sented on the boards by ono of their members, who was not an ordinary shareholder. The bill passed the second reading.—Upon the motion of Lord Ilsascnnx, the Distress for Rent (Dublin) Bill was read a second time. The House adlourned at 5 15 p.m.

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TcrasuAT.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TcrasuAT.

The Speaker took the chair at 3 p.m. Among the notices of motion was one given by Mr. Swrow Balm who intimated that he would, when oppor- turtity.olfered. move a resolution declaring the opinion of the /louse that the rapid increase in the popu- lation of the United Kingdom. the permanently depressed condition of agriculture, the poverty, over- crowding, and lack of employment in many parts of the United Kingdom, now render the consideration and development and, if possible, the carrying, out by the Government of some scheme of State colonisation, a national necessity.

div.head: QUESTIONS.
div.p: QUESTIONS.

Mr. Balfour was no—t in hit; accustomed seat during question time; and the queries addressed to him were answered by the Irish Solicitor-General (Mr. Madden), who was cross-examined at considerable length as to the reason why the Government had refused to lay upon the table a copy of the judament of the Court of Exchequer in the Killengh habeas corpu.t cases, seeing that a copy of the Chief Baron's address to the jury, in the case of Blunt V. Balfour. bad been laid upon the table.— Mr. MADhEN, amid loud cheers from the Irish members, replied that all the judmnents of the courts could not be laid on the table. It was necessary that some dis- cretion should be exercised as to the Judgments lished- _ _

..„ Mr. W. H. SMITH" made a reply which indicated that in the future he will ask the House to give un Wednesdays TO the Government. as well as the present days placed at the service of private members. Mr. RITCHIE said, in reply, that the total amount of van and wheel tax in England and Wales was estimated at £168,000, and from the house tax at £51.0.000. making a total of £700,000. No actual account could be given of the yield of the taxes in Lancashire, or any other county by itself. THE VOTE OF CENSURE.

At half-past four, Mr. W. O'BRIEN resumed the debate on the motion of censure, which was on Monday night submitted to the House by Mr. John Morley. When Mr. O'Brien rose he was •received with tre- mendous cheers from the Opposition benches; and he spoke in an exceedingly full House, considerably over 500 members being present. The strangers' galleries were densely crowded while some 30 noble lords were in the seats set aside for peers. Mr. O'BRIEN, who spoke with great emotion and im- mense oratorical force, commenced by some words of criticism on the speech delivered by Mr. T. W. Russell, who, said he, was in a large measure responsible for the institution of the plan of campaign, because of his opposition to legislation on ehalf of the Irish tenants. The hon. gentleman next tannted the Govern- ment with inability to produce any Irish horrors with which to terrify the English public, except the murder of Fitzmaurice in county Kerry. which. as • fact, was the only county in which the Man of Campaign had no hold on the people. While he listened to the references to Fitzinaurice and his daughter, he could not help thinking of the thousands of Norah Fitzmaurices who had been thrown out on to the road side to die, or had been driven from home to meet a worse fate in the streets of New York. (Loud Opposition cheers. Mr. O'Brien averred that the "brave work" of the Chief Secretary consisted in endeavouring to crush a parcel of poor Irish tenants, because they were more than a naatch for him, but lie had failed, and he would continue to fail, not- withstanding, that his Government had skulked over to , Borne, and invoked the aid of the Holy Inquisition to strengthen the arm oflmperialEngland. (Great Oppo- sition cheering.) This disgusting claptrap about crime in Ireland was what was known in America as "the policy of the bloody shirt." It was a policy of war and hatred between peoples who desired to live together at peace, and, thank God, the policy both here and in America was seen through, discredited, and played out. (Cheers.) The hon. gentleman proceeded to defend the Plan of Campaign, and defied the Chief Secretary to show that it, was being used to extort fresh concessions. The hon. gentleman 11 ealt with the particulars of the ease of I ;he tenants of Lord Massetene, and in conclusion said the Irish people had confidence in God and in the great human heart of the British masses, and believed they had only to know the working of coercion to loathe it and discard it for ever. (Loud Opposition cheers.) Mr. CTIAPLIN, who commenced his speech amid cries of " Balfour," expressed his sunrise that Mr. O'Brien had not attempted to redly to the charges made on the pre- vious night by Cal. Saundersan. He proceeded to denounce the Plan of Campaign and the conduct of the National League, saying that their real object was to prevent the payment of rent even by those who were well able to do so. He quoted from Mr. Gladstone's speeches to show that he had contradicted himself in regard to what was the policy of the present Government, sa7,-ine that he laid the blame for these con- tradictions on Mr. Gladstone's memory, which seemed to be failing latterly, (Cheers and hisses.) Mr. GLADSTONE, who was received with great cheering from the Opposition benches, said he did not feel his temper to be severely tried by the rather violent attacks of Kr. Chaplin. While he was sensible that the lapse of I

div.head: THE
div.p: THE

time was uteleubtedl•,• ex• remely tormetanie. and tee • ffecte important to him ea fliers than one particular; • et he hoped for a lit tie while, at any rate—(loud anti orolenged cheers)—he might remain not wholly unable I to gene with antagonists of the ealihre of the right hon. eretternan opposite (Mr. Chaplin). (Loud cheers and Ineglitere MT. Gladstone having justified the speech to which reference had been made by Mr. Chaplin, and ex- eressed regret tirat the Government had felt it their duty to confine this important debate to two nights, said he was compelled, first, to reiterate a complaint of the member for Neweestle (Mr. John Morley; that informa- tion had been withheld from the House which ought to eave been given. He charged the Government, in fact, that they had endeavoured to oust the Heine of Come aions from proper jurisdiction in watching the operation of an exceptional law, and in making provision, wher- ever circumstances seemed to require it, for the main- tenance of the sanctity of private rights. (Cheers.) They were refused any information as to the depositions erninected with the imprisonment of Mr. Dillon, and as o the,eases of conspiracy, and also in regard to derelict !and. A graver matter still as the refusal of information with regard to the deplorable and disgrace- ful transactions at Mitchelstown. The Chancellor of the Fesdhequer had spoken of two cases of murder in whioh Its Crimes Act had been instrumental in bringing the murderers to justice. He rejoiced at this result; but aid Mr. Goschen think that these were the main matters ier which the Act was passed? (Cheers.) They had always been willing to consider the provisions of the Act for the bond fide operation of the criminal law, but their contention from the first was that this was an Act framed, not for the purpose of putting down crime, but directed really against combination. With regard to the Planet Campaign, Mr. Gladstone said he understooe that the contention was this, that the Plan was framee when Parliament had refused to make any legislative provisions for the necessities of the tenantry in the year 1886—(hear, hear),—and that it met the case by making demands upon the land- lords equal or interior to those which under the Act ef 1887 the Land Commissioners had acknowledged te le just. (Loud Opposition cheers.) It was idle to ad- vance against the contention the naked doctrine that the taw was the law, and should be obeyed. (Ministefial cries of "Oh.") There might be many in the House to whom it seemed a cardinal principle of duty to make no investigation of Irish history.. (Ministerial cries of "Oh.") tee it was not so in Ireland. The recollections and traditious of Irish history was burnt into the very souls of the people. ("Oh.") They knew what were the horrors and the almost incredible atrocities that had been done in the name of the law—(loud Opposition theers)—and the murders and crimes of every description which, when they had not been done in the name of the law, had been covered by subsequent acts of indemnity. (Renewed cheers.) Yet. the Government supposed that a people whose whole souls were full of these painful and grievous eecollectiens could come to the considera- tion of the law in the same mind and spirit as a judge sitting upon the bench. (Opposition cheers.) In this they showed their ignorance of human nature, and their incapacity for 'statesmanship. (" Oh.") The principles upon which they acted had never guided wise legislative assemblies. (Cheers.) They had always made allow- ance in these cases for the circumstances that deter- mined the character of national emotions and recollec- tions, and had been aware that there were, in the midst of humae affairs, cases tint unfrequently wherein law had been on the one side and justice on the other. (Loud Opposition cheers and some interruption.) The Go- vernment had never considered how far that might have been the case with Mr. Dillon. (Cheers.) Mr. Gladstone went on to examine Mr. 'Dillon's case, saying that Loud I was subjected to the indignity of being proclaimed under the Crimea Act solely in order that Mr. Dillon might not have the benefit of a jury—(loud cheers)—a proceeding which was mean, as well as harsh and cruel. It was, in his opinion. Mr. Billon. who, by his great influence, prevented the terrible accumulation ot the Michelstown disaster. And that useful influ- ence ought to have been taken into considera- tion by the judge when lie inflicted upon the hon. gentlemen the maximum term of imprisonment. The present state of things ought to 'bring about much re- flection, and it was a state of things which could not be disposed of by the 'majority of the House of Commons that night, especielly after the daring statements made by the Chief Secretary and the Irish Solicitor-General, in reference to the Killeogh case. It had been stated that they were found guilty of conspiracy at common law. By whom'? Mr. MADDTN (Irith Soliaitor-General) said he did not state that the persons were ound guilty of a conspiracy at common law, but that the judges said there was be- fore them evidence upon which a jury might have found them guilty of conspiracy. (Ministerial cheers.) Mr. GLADSTONE was glad to hear this explanation, and withdrew what he intended to say upon the subject, although if the hon. gentleman would refer to The 7imeA he would End he had been seriously misrepresented. (Laughter:) The right 'hon. gentleman went on to examine the judgment of the Chief Baron in the Tulleagh case, and in great detail pointed out the erroneous view of the law taken by the resident magis- trates. As to the statistics showing a diminution of boycotting, he declined to accept them 80 long as he had no power of testing their accuracy. Probably is diminu• tion in the number of agrarian crimes was meant : hut he did not believe that such diminution was caused by the operation of the Crimes Act. Lord Spencer's triumph over agrarian offences was tenfold what had been now achieved. (Cheers and dissent.) Ent he did not con- clude from the reduction in the number that he was making any step towards solving the Irish question. Mr. Gladstone commented at some length upon the conduct of the Irish econstabillary, remarking that he thought the position of that force seemed to show that the progress, of which Mr. Goschen had spoken, was a progress, not forward. hut backward in the solution of the Irish question. (Laughter and cheenel continuing. he said the. nen of Campaign was still holding its ground, and the Government had been distinctly challenged that night. to say whether they could point out a single instance in which the opposite power of the Government and the landlords had triumphed over it. The Chancellor of the Exchequer had challenged the words of the motion, hut did he think that respect for law had increased among the people of Ireland generally since the enactment. or the Crimes Act, or that the minds of the people of the country had not been estranged from the system of Government in force among them. The right hon. gentleman did not seem ready to accept these challenges. Mr. GOSCHEN : I will interrupt the right hon. gentle- man if he wishes me. The statement in the resolution is that we are "undermining respect forthe law," which did not exist in his time—(Ministerial cheers)—and also that we are estranging affection, Which also in his time we did not possess. (Renewed Ministerial cheers.) •

Mr. GLADSTONE said that the Chancellor of the Ea• chequer had not touched either of his challenges. In reply to another observation from 'Mr. Goschen. the right hon. gentleman said that of all the practices of n Government in difficulties there was none so shabby as throwing upon the Opposition the responsibilities for the state of public affairs. Against Mr. fieschen'a assertion of success, he (Mr. Gladstone) had given proofs of failure. In so far as estrangement was concerned, there had been brought into play another •force against that which was, used by the Government, 'namely, the force of the affection which was springing up in the minds of the English people for Ireland. What they on that si& of the Rouse thought was this—for there never wag a period where the Opposition was so sharply manifesteq. between what was known as Dublin Castle and the people of Ireland—on the one side, they saw the Govern- tnent and its powerful agencies, political, judicial, and social.; on the other side, they saw the masses of the population and their representatives In the House, from whom rose a unanimous chorus of protestation against. the system by which the government was now carried on in Ireland. In conclusion, the right hon. geneleman said that in meeting this 'motion they paid a debt of honour to the Government. He admitted,it was fair that they should in that House make known the substance of the accusations which they made against the Government, and which they in- tended to make against them in the country. They dealt now not only with the House, but with a nation They had an appeal which the Chief Secretary and hi. colleagues •could not take away from them. Tn tribunal they 'Would go—(Opposition eheersl—and the verdict of that tribunal they could foresee, and thev were satisfied with .and rejoiced in the sentence which, they knew that it would, and could not but pronounce (Loud Opposition,cheers.) Mr. Gladstone spoke for an hour and forty minutes. and during the whole time the Rouse was densely crowded. 'When he sat down, there were loud cries oF "Balfour," but the Chief Secretary did not rite. Mr. S. GEDOE caught the Speaker's eye, and made short speech in defence of the Government. —Mr. Joux Etrts continued the debate on behalf of the Oppo- sition.

Mr. Baryons, who was greeted with loud cheers, said. in reference to the complaint that no information wa.. given to the House. that win:xi the Government did their best in that direction they got no gratitude. hut only the suggestion that they were either too stupid or too idle to prepare the return in a form with which it could be of use to the House. (Laughter.) Sir War. HARCOURT.: Hear, he.

Mr. BALFOUR said it was well fox the right hon. gentle- man to ,say "Hear, heat," but the return had been pre- pared in the best possible way. Ile was prepared to go a long way for the sake of lion. gentlemen opposite, and to give them almost everything they wanted. Mr. TIVOLI' : Yes, and put 19 of us in gaol. Mr. BALFOUR went on to say that in regard to tiirse returns it was not his function to supply lion, gentle- men opposite with either industry or intelligence. The right hon. gentleman then proceeded to discuss the operation of the first section of the Crimes Act, which deals with secret inquiries, saving that the clause was taken from Mr. Gladstone's own bill. Mr. Gladstone had' said that nobody objected to the clause. Mr. GLADSTOXE: I did not say that; I said the prin- ciple of a secret inquiry was not subjected to serious debate.
Mr. BALsorrn said the C1a11136 was incomparably milder than that of Mr. Gladatone's bill. tie went on to say that he did notice the force of the argument that the

(Ministerial cheers.) lie 'elitist not see why Mr. Dillon should have different treat- !Tient merely because be was Mr. Dillon. Mr. T. HEALY : That is not (Shouts of "Name The SPEAKF.R : The debate cannot be conducted with these constant running comments by hen. members. Mr. BAT.FOCrE ;wanted to know when the principle came into operation that the cloth coat should have one kind of treatment and the frieze coat another. The right bon. gentleman bad gone into an elaborate discus- ohm npnn the matter of the treatment of priests in prim, and said they were not treated as laymen. MT. GLADSTONE: I said you were afraid to do so. 'Loud Opposition cheers.) Mr. BALFOUR was surprised that any allegation of timidity should be made against him. (Ministerial cheers.) Priests were not treated as first-class mis- demeanants, hut in the ordinary way. Mr. PARNELL: And compelled to pick oakum. Mr. Rai Foca rejoined that so far as he was concerned they had been compelled to conform to all the regula- tions, excepting the wearing of prison clothes. It was very difficult to strip a Catholic priest of the garb which he was compelled to wear by canonical law. and he decided on the eid e of mercy. ("Oh, oh.") The right hon. gentleman then went on to discuss the matter of the Killeogh conspiracy. They had been told that the conspiracy was analogous to the rase of work- men in this country, who struck against a certain employer— Sir W. FIARCOURT : Why not? Mr. Beasoue. : Because the combination in Ireland is directed to the starving of the police. The epeakerwent on to defend the resident coanated with the Killeogh case, and the technical &talk of the matter. He believed that the persons implicated were proud of theoffence, and would have been indignant had they not been found guilty. It wiis childish tie say that the Act was administered harshly, and that those people did not deserve any punishment. He had newer beard ot hon. gentlemen below the gansrway using their in- fluence to alleviate the misery of those unhappy victims of boycotting who had been senteneed, for some imaginary offence, by the National League. What the Opposition had done was to use their whole political influence, in the House and in the country, to de- nounce the policeman, the magistrate, and the Govern- ment, who were attempting to put an esi to the tyranny of the National League. (Ministerial cheers.) It was said that the offences of Mr. Dillon and of others were political offences, and that, therefore, they should be treated differently from offenders against the ordinary law. Mr. Balfour was pursuing his argument on this subject when he was several times interrupted by hon. members opposite, and the Speaker had fre- quently to call for order. The right hon. gentleman directed his arguments to demonstrating the justice of the sentence passed upon Mr. Dillon and the proper ap- plication of the Act to his case. As to the Plan ot Cam- paign, he attacked the morality of that institution. His complaint against the Plan of Campaign was briefly stated. In the first place be said that it absolutely pre- vented 01 settlements between landlord and tenant, or made them extremely difficult. Almost all settle- ments were in the nature of compromise, and the Plan almost absolutely excluded compromises. (Cries of "No, no," from the Irish benches.) Mr. Wm. O'BRIEN explained that the right hon. gentle- man WES wrong. Mr. BALFOUR said that at all events the com- promise was not such a compromise as his party was chiefly interested in. (Laughter and cheers.) It was decided with the leaders of the plan, not between landlords and tenants. His next complaint against the plan was that it inflicted infinite sufferings to the tenants. It also compelled tenants moderately rented not to pay their rents, even when they were in a position to do so. People who could and would not pay their rents were called patriots in Ire- land, but in England mean swindlers. (Ministerial cheers,) The Plan involved outrage in its very essence, compulsion, tyranny, and boycotting. (Ministerial cheers.) The repression of crime in Ireland depended not a little on coercion. The various Crimes Acts had repressed it, and if the present Act were re- pealed, crime would rise again. At this moment derelict farms were again being occupied. Rents were being largely paid, and social disorders were dis- appearing, except where the Plan of Campaign existed. The Government. therefore, had not worked in vita in Ireland—(lood Ministerial cheers) —and there were many hearts in that country rejoicing that there was a Unionist Government in power--ederisive cheers)— showing a desire and resolution to break and divide the tyranny under which they were suffering. In conclu- sion, Mr. Balfour said : We hope to see Ireland absorbed and amalgamated with the other con- stituent parts of the British Empire, sharing our institutions, fostered by our wealth, and with some of he wrong that we inflicted on Irish industry in the last eentury redressed, we hope to !see eery Irishman gladly .einicing in community of sentiment with every Eng- 17shrnan. every alcotehman, and every Welshman, shar- ing the fortunes of the British Empire, and sharing the traditions on which those fortunes are rested. (Loud Ministerial cheers.) Mr. SEXTON next spoke. Delivering an eloquent speech, he accused the Chief Secretary of slandering a man whom he had put into prison for political purposes. During the progress of Mr. Sexton's speech a long in- terview took place between Mr. Gladstone, Mr. Morley, Lnrd Dertington, Mr. Smith, and Mr. Balfour, evidently with the view of shortening the debate, and as a result it was decided that the division should be taken imme- diately after the hon. member for West Belfast had re- enmed his seats . _

... Mr Sexton havina spoken for over an hour, concluded et 19 50. when the liouge divided— For Mr. Morley's resolution 273 Against: Onvernment majority The House adjourned at 1 40. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—Wanrresnar.
The Speaker took the chair at twenty minutes after twelve o'clock. The East and West Yorkshire Union Railways Bill (which has come down from the House of Lords) was read a second time.
