ME LICENSING CLAUSES. Moving the ommission of the next clause— clause 9 which empowered the County Council to close public-houses on Sundays and on special days, Mr. Iltrainz made reference to the Government surrender of the licensing clauses, commenting on the strong feeling they had aroused in the country, and re- marking that both in point of time and the efficiency of the County Council they felt it extremely desirable the clauses should not be proceeded with. Certain members still thought they might have dealt with the particular question of Sunday closing, nor indeed had they shrunk from the position they had taken up, for they had always contended that this question was one that might be dealt with locally in a satisfactory manner. But the considerations which prompted the Government to abandon the licensing clauses applied also to this particu- lar clause, and it was not worth while to complicate the elections by the introduction of the solitary question of Sunday closing. In abandoning the clause he believed the Government were not going against the temperance party.—Sir W. HARCOURT said, amid cheers, that if the County Council was to be a living body capable of doing something for the good of the community. the Govern- ment must not be so timid about introducing questions that would create difference of opinion. These bodies ought to be the guardians of that which affec- ted the health and the morals of the com- munity over which they were placed, and this question of Sunday closing was one that should undoubtedly be placed in their hands. Was he to understand that the Government opposed their own clause? He showed, amid considerable amusement. ' what an extraordinary attitude they had assumed on this question, and, after subjecting Mr. Caine to scath- ing criticism, said they ought to have a downright tem- perance vote on the clause, which he hoped the Com- mittee would retain. Mr. CAINE urged temperance re- formers to let the clause go, and, incensed at Sir William Ilarcourt's satire, described the right hon. gentleman as Uncle Pumblechook, the noted character in Dickens's "Great Expectations." Sir Wilfrid LAWSON Slip- ported the clause, saying he was willing to take what he could get, and in this matter was like the Scotchman who went to be married, and when asked if he would have the woman to be his wife, replied, "Yea, I am willing; but I would rather have her sister."—The debate, in which many other members took part; was both exciting and amusing. The Committee divided, and there were for the retention of the clause, 213; against, 275; majority against, 62. The clause was con- sequently struck out.—Clause 10, transferring the licen- sing powers to the County Council, was struck out, the voting being for the clause, 175; against, 252; majority against, 77.—The other licensing clauses were also struck out, and the House adjourned at ten minutes past twelve o'clock.

div.head: CHANNEL TUNNEL SCHEME.
div.p: THE CHANNEL TUNNEL SCHEME.

_ Sir EDWARD WATICrN moved the second reading of the Channel Tunnel Bill, explaining that it only gave power to continue the experiments, leaving the Government of the day to decide whether the experimental works should be widened and the tunnel completed. The works on both sides the Channel were now two and a half miles in length, or one-tenth of the entire distance; and they wished„to prove by making a driftway that the tunnel could be successfully constructed. He contended that the underground way would be of the greatest value to British trade, and that it would not weaken out military position in the least. Should this country ever be menaced by France the tunnel could be closed in three minutes by flooding, or by touching a button any- where in England the entrance might be blown up.— Sir Michael Hicks-Beach moved that the bill be read a second time that day six months, denying that the leadbr of the House had consented to the principle of the bill, and asserting that such a tunnel would open the door to attack, and they had no right to look at the ques- tion without reference to the possibility of war with France. Mr. Gladstone strongly supported the bill, say- ing that the arguments of the President of the Board of Trade were mere bugbears. The course taken with re- gard to the scheme when he himself was in power was taken not in antagonism to the principle of the bill, but simply to save the time of Parliament. The tunnel would, he maintained, be of great advantage to our com- merce, and knit closer the friendship between the two nations.' The other end of the tunnel, he said, amid some amusement, caused no anxiety at all; and he failed to see, with the -mighty power we possessed to repel invasion, that there was much cause for alarm. Mr. SLAG° supported the motion, maintaining that the ready means of communication would greatly increase commerce between England and France and the whole of Europe, enormously stimulating trade in light articles, into the manufacture of which taste and skill, scientific and artistic, entered very largely indeed. The tunnel would also be of immense importance as a link to direct communication between this country, the Continent, and India; and he ventured to think the old-world notions ' of hostility to France would rapidly disappear under the benign influence of this.new method of communication, which would greatly.increase the country's prosperity. As to the fear of invasion the exploits of the" Pirates of Penzance" were hard matters of fact compared to the conquest of' England through this tunnel. Lord RAN- DOLPH CHURCHILL was decidedly opposed to the project on the ground of economy. After further debate the House divided, and there were for the second reading 165; against, 307; majority against, 143. The House adjourned at a quarter to six o'clock. -
HOUSE OF LORDS.—TIMRSDAY. Their Lordships met at Tour o'clock. . . . .

The Royal Assent was given by commission to several public bills. After a discussion about bogus companies the bill to check their practices was read a second time, and so was the Limited Partnerships Bill. Some con- versation as to the defence of our naval quarters in the Pacific followed. Their Lordships adjourned at 20 minutes to seven o'clock.

HOUSE OF COMMONS, THURSDAY. The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. The questions included such widely different topics as Mr. Dillon's imprisonment, the troubles in Zululand, the defective war stores, the charter to the Royal College of Surgeons, official secrets, literary pensions, and the dis- turbance at Dundalk. A new writ was issued for South Sligo to fill the vacancy caused by Mr. Kennedy's resig- nation. Report of Supply was agreed to; so was the report of Ways and Means.

div.head: LOCAL GOVERNMENT BILL.
div.p: THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT BILL.

The House resumed committee on the Local Govern- ment Bill on clause 8, providing for the transfer to the County Council of the powers of certain Government departments and other authorities.—On the motion that the clause a.st now stood should be part of the bill, Sir W. HARCOURT pointed out that powers vested in the Home Office relating to the inspection of factories and nines might well be left to the local authorities.—Mr. HITCRIX said it would be found when the provisional

Severe weather was reported from various parts of the country on Monday. At Oxford a terrific thunderstorm. accompanied by heavy rain and hail. broke•nver the city early in the morning. The streets were: flooded, and the hail greatly damaged the crops. At Aldershot, in the afternoon. a storm of unprecedented severity was experienced. Rain fed in torrents, flooding the cellars of houses and some of the side streets. A second storm passed over Aldershot. in the evening, accompanied by floods of rain and heavy showers of hail. At Dorking, when the storm was at its height, three bullocks grazing in Betchworth Park were struck by lightning and killed. The animals, which were very valuable ones, belonged to Lord Francis Hope. At Buckingham the storm broke at about half-past two in the afternoon. Very large hailstones fell, and hundreds of panes of glass were broken. In the village of Thornborough. near Bucking- ham, the windows of the parish church were almost totally destroyed. The crops have suffered severely. At Einsworth (Hants) rain fell in floods. The roads in many places were speedily rendered impassable, and groat damage is reported from the outlying district.. At the National Schoolrooms the windows were struck by lightning and broken; whilst in the shop of Mr. J. Mos- dell a shelf of fancy goods was struck and shattered.

_ A heavy thunderstorm broke over the Merthyr hills is the afternoon, accompanied by smart showers of rain. Hailstones of unusual size fell in the Lower Bre- conshire During a heavy thunderstorm which broke over the ;iistrict south of Chichester in the morning a youtm Inan standing in a meadow was struck by lightning and killed. A terrific thunderstorm visited Colchester and neigh. bourhood •during the early hours of Tm!sday, ac eompanied by a deluge of rain. Houses were struck by lightning at Stanway, Fingringhoe, and Creffield-road. setting a barn on fire at one place. No fatalities arc reported. Further reports were received on Tuesday of damage by thunderstorms. On Monday, Mrs. Ellen Stockholm, wife of a tax collector at Mitcheltroy. near Monmouth. was struck dead as she was working In the bakehouse. Floods caused landslips on the Wye Valley Railway. The daughter of Mark Rose, farmer, at Dorking, and a child attending the Betchworth School near there, were both struck and temporarily rendered unconscious. Three valuable beasts and nearly 30 sheep were killed at Betch- worth and Headley. • TERRIBLE SCENE IN I CHURCH.

VIENNA, MONDAY.—Advices from Brezezie, in the Bochnia district of Galicia, state that during divige service in the Parish Church there the building was struck by lightning. Three persons were killed and 30 slightly injured, while 240 others received slight contu- sions from the falling masonry. The Bishop of Cracow. who was conducting the service, appealed to the con- gregation to remain calm, his advice being the means r f preventing a still greater disaster, which a rush for the doors would probably have occasioned.
THE DROWNING SEASON.-LOSS OF
SEVENTEEN LIVES.

Six persons, five of whom were women, have been drowned by the capsizing of a pleasure boat in New Bay, Now York. Whilst bathing in,the Shannon at Limerick. on Mon- day, Private Ledger, Ist Batt. Derbyshire Regiment, was drowned. The body was recovered soon afterwards. Two boys, named Fortune and Jackson, were found drowned in a reservoir at Laisterdyke, near Bradford, on Monday. It is supposed that one fell in'wlaile play- ing, and that the other tried to rescue him.

Two boys, named Win. White and John Conolly, started for a sail on Carlingford Lough, on Thursday, and have not been heard of sim.e. The boat was after- wards found bottom upwards, and it is feared the boys are drowned.

A sad boating fatality occurred, on Sunday, near Bognor. Four young men, named James Barnes, Wm. Rogers, Stephen Hewitt, and John Hewitt, left Bognor in a small pleasure boat, to row across the bay to Selsey Bill, about six miles, the sea being calm. Early this morning the boat was found capsized on the sands, with the bodies of two men lying near The other bodies have not been recovered. All the deceased were prac- tical boatmen.

At the inquest held upon the bodies of Win. Smith and Annie K Knowles, drowned whilst boating on the river Derwent, the evidenctrihowed that the conduct of the people on the land, and also that of those in boats at the time of the fatal disaster, was most cowardly.—Alfred Powell said that no rescue was attempted from the shore, where a crowd assembled immediately after the calamity.—The proprietor of the Boathouse Hotel stated that env one could have waded to the rescue, and he added in his evidence that when he and another gentle- man took a boat with drags no one told them where the accident occurred, although they shouted for informa- tion, and the search had to be conducted indiscrimi- nately.—Verdict, "Accidental death." Several juron added that lifebuoys and other precautions ought to be taken for such cases of emergency.

FATAL CoLLISIOI. IN THE CHANNEL.—The steamer .E,gean, of Leith, 750 tons, and the German ship Northampton, of Bostock, 1,173 tons, collided 55 miles N.N.E. of the Longships at 1 a.m. on Saturda7. Both vessels sank within 25 minutes of the collision. The survivors of their crews were landed at Plymouth, Sunday. The Northampton left Cardiff on the 22nd met., with conis for Monte Video; the .rEgean left Bilbao on the 20th, with iron ore for Glasgow. At the time of the collision the wind was light from E.N.E., and the weather was clear. The Northampton was running to the westward with nll sails set, when, it is alleged, the hlg,ean ran into her on the fore part of her starboard miten rigging, cutting her down betfity the water's edge and carrying away her after-rigging aud spars. The captain of the Northampton, finding his vessel was sink- ing, rapidly lowered a boat, and left her with eight of his creVsand his wife. The Xzean had her bows crushed in. She was fitted with a et-Ilisinn bulkhead, but it did not reach up to her main deck. The captain of the dEgean lowered his lifeboat and jolly boat, and saved all his crew, as well as seven of the German vessel's crew. Two of the crew of the Northampton were Inst. It is believed they were crushed by falling spars.

Lord Tollemache has sold two of his pictures by Sir Joshua Reynolds for £15,000 each, and one by Gains- norough for £14,000. - -
The Countess of Rosebery ig stated to be suffering From congestion of the lungs, following upon an attack 9f measles caught while nursing her children.

&TOOLING FATALITY AT BOLTON.—A grinder named Griffia was killed at Messrs. Dobson and Barlow's works, Bolton, on Tuesday, by the bursting of a grindstone, f rag- ,ments -of which shattered him to pieces. At the inquest on Dr. Zukertort, the famous chest player, held in London on Saturday, medical evidence was given that deceased died of cerebral hemorrhage, and the jury returned a verdict or "Death from natural causes." .

-- FATAL ACCIDENT TO A LADV.—A coroner's juiy Eeightieigh, Surrey, on Tuesday returned a verdict ot accidental death in the case of Lady Giffard, wife of Admiral. Sir George Gifford, [C.C.S., who was killed by i ailing downstairs.

At Marlborough-street Police Court, on Saturday, Julia Mogson, 28., cook, in service at Mount-street, Grosvenor- square, was remanded, charged with causing the death of her infant on the 3rd inst. The infant was found charred in the kitchen range. A dinner in honour of the Marquis of Lansdowne was given on Saturday at Baßiotllvge on his appointment as Viceroy of India. There was a large and distin- guished company, including Lord Northbrook, Lord Ripon, and Lord Justice Bowen. _ _

In consequence of the Liberal victory in the Rene municipal elections, several of the cardinals are urging the Pope to adopt a more conciliatory attitude towards the Italian Government, and to give authority to Catho- lic voters to take part in politital elections. REM.

THE BIRMINGHAM TRAGEOL—The young man Jones, who, in a frenzy brought on by jealousy, made a furious attack on a family named Harris, at Aston, last week, will now have to take. his trial on the capital charge, one of the injured children having died from the revolver wounds inflicted upon her. SENTENCE OF DEATH FOR WIFE MURDER. At the Oxfordshire Assize on Tuesday, before Mr. Juatic€ Denman, Robert Upton, 61, a labourer, was indicted for the wilful murder of hie wife, at Milton-under-Wych- wood, on the 23rd of May. As a result of a quarrel, the prisoner knocked his wife down, and then struck her with en iron bar. A verdict of "Guilty" was returned, and sentence of death passed.

SAD DROWNING FATALITY.—A sad accident occurred on the river Derwent, at Matlock Bridge, on Saturday night. At dusk a boat, in which were seated a youth earned William Smith, of Matlock Bank, and Annie Knowles, a pupil teacher, of Tansley, struck the railway °ridge. Thereupon Smith rose to his feet, and the result was that the boat capsized, and he and Miss Knowles were drowned. Both bodies were recovered. On Saturday, an engine driver, named H. B. Jones. of Aston, was committed, on the coroner's warrant, the Warwickshire Assizes, charged with the wilful intur- der. of Florence Mabel Harris, whose mother he had re- cently been cohabiting with. In a fit of jealousy, the accused shot the deceased and Mrs. Harris, and beat an infant unmercifully about the head. The two latter lie hi a critical condition. A LOCAL PREACHER CHARGED WITH THEFT.—At Devon. port, on Monday morning, James A. Pearce, clerk, was remanded on a charge of being in possession of a marked half sovereign, stolen on Saturday night from the Post-office. The prisoner, who is a local preacher and superintendent, of the Bible Christian Sunday Schocls, has been in Government employ for 20 years. In consequence of repeated robberies a trap was laid for him, with this result.

SUSPICIOUS DmaTn.—At noon, on Monday,Captain Cook. labourer, Church•street, Halifax, died at the lockup. Sowerby Bridge. He was found in a field close to the highway, near Allangate, unconscious, and was removed to the police station, on Sunday evening. It has since transpired that the deceased had an altercation in the toad near to where he was found with a tramp, named Thomas Lee, and his wife, and they have been taken into custody pending the inquest. An alarming accident occurred on the Midland Rail- way, at Plumtree, a small station on the Nottingham and Milton Line, on Saturday. A ballast train was being shunted to allow a fast train to pass when the brske and two waggons left the metals. Several men were in the brake, two of whom, Geo. Clements and Jarvis Kay sustained injuries which necessitated their removal home to Leicester, after being surgically at. tended. The line was blocked for a considerable time.

WARNING TO PARRNTS.—At Platts Common, Barnsley, on Monday, Mr. D. Wightman, coroner, held an inquest on Gwen&line Mabel Daykin, aged 4, daughter of a miner. The evidence showed that the mother, suspect- ing the child was affected with worms, got two powders from Mr. Matthews, chemist, Hoyland Common. The .child died soon after their administration, and presented symptoms of narcotic poisoriing. The chemist declared that the powders only contained jalap and calomel. Died From narcotic poisoning was the verdict.

RETURN OF THE PRINCE AND PRINCESS OF WALES,— The Prince and Princess of Wales, Prince Albert Victor, and suite, arrived at Dover from Calais at half-past five on Monday, and proceeded by special train for London. Their Royal Highnesses were received at Dover by Major-General Montgomery Moore. commanding the South-Eastern District, and a guard of honour was drawn up on the pier. A Royal salute was fired from the bAtteries on the heights. There was a very large assemblage on the pier to witness the arrival,of their Royal Highnesses. DARING ESCAPE FROM WALTON Geol.—an extraordin- ary escape was made from Walton Gaol, Liverpool, on Monday, possessing some features in common with that of Jackson, the Strangeways Gaol murderer. The hero at Liverpool was James Lynch. a sailor, who was sen- tenced at the last Liverpool assizes, for robbery, to 18 months' imprisonment Yesterday Lynch was set to do some work in an outhouse, wherein he was locked, and after making a hole in the roof, obtained two ladders. which he lashed together, and so gained the top of the outer wall. He then made off. So far no clue has been obtained of his whereabouts. THE HANDEL FESTIVAL—The Handel Festival COM- meueed at the Crystal Palace, London, on Monday, with every prospect of a most suceAssful anniversary. The principal soloists engaged for the rendering of "The Messiah" were Madame- Albani, Madame Patey, Mr. Santley. and Mr. Edward Lloyd. each of whom executed their respective parts to the satisfaction of an enormous audience, numbering about 24,000. The orchestra and the choir had been materially strengthened for the occa- sion. The performance was preceded by the Dead March from "Saul," in memory of the Emperor Frederick of Germany, and it was noted that the principal singers %CUM dressed in mourning.

KAM ENGINES TO BE SOPERSEDED.-Mr. Fletcher, chief inspector of alkali works, in his annual report, issued on Monday, deals with a number of subjects of 2rest interest to manufacturers. His remarks upon Mr. Flargreaves's hot-air engine, or theremo mow, are pciallv important. He says that it will not only effect the prevention of black smoke, but promises to revolu- •oionise our methods of producing power. It has been found that an energy of 40-horse power can be main- tained with the expenditure of two gallons of coal tar, or 451 b. of coal, per hour. Either liquid fuel or coal can be used. This is a result three times more favourable than that realised by the best and five or six times more than by ordinary steam engines, and it is probable that these results will be increased.

THE RAILWAY AND CANAL TRAFFIC FIL!.---TI If Grand Committee on Trade met on Monday, and further considered the Railway and Canal Traffic Bill.— Sir B. Samuelson moved an amendment to the effect that in determining the cla.ssification of the traffic, and the inaximum rates, the Board of Trade have due Fe- yard to the rights and interests of the public, of traders, ;;T-Id of railway companies.—The President of the Board of Trade hoped the Committee would tell the Board dis- tinctly on which principle they were to approach this ssork. After further discussion, Mr. Chamberlain said lr thought they should confine themselves to the direc- tion that the rates should he just and reasonable. They should take a vote first as to whether the committee was or opinion it was advisable to leave an unfettered discre- te the Board of Trade. On a division 35 voted for giving discretionary power, and 20 against.

TRIC HERRING FISHING IN THE SOLWAY.--The herring fishing in the Solway is at present very brisk, the waters off Allonby and Maryport swarming w!th fish which Kaye migrated from ..t.he Irish Sea. There have been several very large takes of herring, and the catches of fishermen are limited only by the carrying capacity of thoir boats. An old fisherman named Ilavery, Maryport, I,,aded his boat the other night until she was in danger of sinking, whilst he left several of his nets full, which disappeared on his return to the place after discharging. tie fishermen belonging to the Isle of Man and Mor- ,..acnhe are, in consequence of the scarcity of fish in these ',Arts. enjoying the harvest in the Solway, but the great- ,•At ,Inculty is experienced in ohtaininz a market for ;he herring at from 2s. to 3s. 6d. per 124, the hawkers laving formed ring." The Maryport fishermen had o. unusual experience on Sunday, finding an immense shoal of celebrated Solway herrings in the Solway Firth. t. few boats only were out, hut, they in a very short time landed 100,000.

£5OO DAMAVES IN A DIVORCE NCIT.—In the Divorce Division, on Saturday. Mr. Justice Butt and a common jury had before them the case of Skinner v. Skinner and llodgson.—The petition was that of the husband. a breaker-up of ships, for a divorce, by reason of his wife's adultery with the co-respondent, Mr. Joseph Rev Hodgson, who was formerly in his employ. There was a claim for damages. There was no defence.—Mr. Tatlock appeared for the petitioner, who married the respondent in 1875 at the Parish Church of Southwark, and they afterwards lived at 14, East India-road, she being a widow with one chad. In the course of his business he bought a stranded ship at Honfleur, for the purpose of breaking up, and employed the co-respondent to manage his business. After a time the respondent came to Flonfleur for the benefit of her health. Subse- quently the petitioner had to leave for London, after which the co-respondent became unduly intimate wits her, it being alleged that he drugged her in the first instance.—The jury found for the petitioner, and assessed the damages at £5OO.—A decree ni3i with costs was granted.

THE THANET ELECTION.-LETTER FROM MIL GLADSTONE.

Mr. Lowther addre;sea-a-M-eeting of electors at West- gate on Saturday night Referring to the temperance question, he said that he was in favour of temperance. divorced from robbery and spoilat ion. As to the state- tnent that lie was in favour of a fixed duty on corn, he said this was one thing above all others that he had de- nommed. Be considered that our present fiscal system required serious modification, and the reform which ha had consistently advocated was some plan by which they could ensure a free and regular supply of cheap food from the colonies. and a free market for British produce throughout the Colonial Empire. The members of the Church of r.rigland Temperance Society in Thruiet have decided to support Mr. Lowther. Mr. Stanley Hawkins, of Margate. who wrote calling "dr. Gladstone's attention to Lord Brabourne's letter .m is son's candidature for Thane, has received the fol- lowing reply from the ex-Premier :—" I need not trouble I think, with any notice of the utterly groundless accusations against nip, which are contained in the letter you enclose ; but I assure you at once of lucy' cordial interest in the election for the Isle of Thanei. you have, on one side. the Tory cause represented by a gentleman strange to the country, but well-known for his fervent desires to re-impose a duty on foreign corn, which now feeds more than half the people. On the other aide, lam happy to think, the Liberal cause is in the hands of Mr. Enatchbull-Ilugessen, who bears one of th,• best known names in Kent, and who adorns that name by his attachment to the urinciples of liberty and justice. We now see the tyrannical and reckless policy of the Government, which, if it. stood alone, would leave , ;ci the Irish people no remedy but violence, partially, but nappily, counteracted by popular verdicts such as those from Southampton rind Ayr, which have convinced the Irish nation that the British people are on their ,ide, and intend to have a true union of the two coun- tries, founded, not as heretofore on force, but on ion. It is now for the constituency of the Isle of fh.inet Codetermine whether they will add their voice, io the voices which have so lately echoed through the land, and thereby strengthen the cause of law and good government in Ireland, or whether they will hav# her still continue to be the only portion of the empire governed by coercive laws, it, di-ec`. opposition to the- constitutionally-expressed co. icti is of her people, and five-sixths of her represent at iv. a." The Isle of Thanet is the smahest county constituency in the south of England. The average width is about four miles, and the extreme length, running, from CISt to west, is eleven miles. The population of Thanet is a little over 50,000, of which 40.000 are centred in Rams- gate and Margate. In the summer season it is estimated that the influx of visitors trebles the population. For, electoral purposes the island is divided into six poll- ing districts, viz.. Ramsgate, with 3,497 voters; Mar- gate. 12,703 ; Broadstairs, 772 ; Birchington, 465 Sandwich, 414; and Minster, 377.

div.head: EXTRAORDINARY DISTURBANCE IN CHESHIRE.,
div.p: EXTRAORDINARY DISTURBANCE IN CHESHIRE.,

At Altrincham Police Court, on Thursday, James Simon and George Buckland, navvies employed on the Ship Canal works; John Moore, labourer; and 11 Henry Cheetharn, fustian cutler; allot Lymm, were I charged with unlawfully wounding, with intent to do grievous bodily harm, one Michael Donnellan, a 1 labourer in the employ of Mr. Winstanley, farmer. Mr. Humphries, of Runcorn, who appeared for the prosecution, said that some three or fobr weeks ago there was a disturbance between navvies connected with th e Ship Canal and some Irish labourers who had I come over for the h arvest. As a res ul t. one Irish man had been committed to take his trial, and ever since there had been a great deal of ill-feeling, and the Irishmen had been subjected to threats, abuse, and violence. At many farms there was an establishment known as the " Paddy house," in which the Irish took up their quarters, and. tins was the scene of the assault in question. About 1i o'clock on Sunday night, Mr. Winstanley was aroused by hearing a number of men making a great noise in the yard. He got up and ordered them away, and one cal- led out to him to go to bed. The nien went to the Paddy house, and called for the Irish to come out, and as they declined they got a wooden prop, with which they eventually broke open the door. After a desperate resis- tance on the part of those inside, the assailants rushed in. Simon seizing Michael Donnellan, got his head under his arm, struck him on the head and face, jumped on hirn with his knees, and banged his head against the floor. Meantims, Moore struck a light, in order that Simon might have a better opportunity of seeing what he was doing, and said kick or kill the —, the others looking on. Dr. Williamson was sent for, and found the prose- cutor suffering from various wounds, one of which, on the hip, from the abrasion of the skis, he was able to say was the result of a kick. The man was in danger until Monday evening.—Mr. J. S. Coppock, of Manchester, submitted that there was no evidence against Buckland and Cheetham, who were there merely as spectators while the defence so fir as the others were concerned would be that it was a free fight.—The Bench held that the evidence implicated all the prisoners, and, as the case was a serious one, they committed all the prisoners for trial. As the prisoners were residents, bail would be grant,ed.

It has gone to the hearts of Englishmen that Mr• JonN DILLori. has been sent to gaol for six months • for making such a speech as is made every night in this country; and it has not lessened the feeling dn. the matter to know that, to make sure that their victim should not have the benefit of trial by jury, County Louth was proclaimed after the aPeech was made. When Mr. BALFOUR is re- elinded of this, he turns pertly round, and says it la all in accordance with the law of the land—as if the fact that such things can be dime in the name Of the law has not made the Crimes Act hateful 'B4A hideous in the eyes of his countrymen. Mr. ?LkusroNE might well say :—" These things are 'coown and felt. The Irish people are aware what 'are the horrors, what are the atrocities,. almost in- eredible, that have been done in Ireland under the name of law—the tortures, the murders, the erimes of every description which when they have not been done under the name of law have been eovered by subsequent acts of indemnity." It is a reproach to a nation when "law is on one side and illsti3e on the other ; " this has often been the case in Ireland; it is so to-day; and it is because the People of this country have at last realised the fact, that they will not rest until this great wrong la Sighted. Public attention is centred just now ePon Mr. DILLON, but it is with a full knowledge !hat there are scores of other men of lesser note 'Prig in gaol for offences which are no offences before the higher law of the conscience. Speech from the throne of the Emperor 11, on the opening of the German Parlia- has been looked forward to with great Crest, and now that it has been delivered it everywhere given satisfaction. It was known IL.4t the heir to the German throne was of warlike Positioli, and there was reason to fear that his I,Zeasion would mark a departure from the path 'eh was trodden by his father • and his grand- he r . But power brings a sense of responsibility th kings, as to meaner men; and it may be that t 4 Young Emperor has already felt that it is one to speak as an irresponsible young man, and • te another to deliver himself as the head of a Zeat nation. It is tolerably certain, at any rate, 1114) so long as he keeps in the mood indicated by • aPeech of Monday, his policy will be one of „efence not defiance." We as foreigners are •joaturally interested in what he has to say as to b,reign relations, particularly as it is felt that Ger- tZnY holds the key of the situation as to European to;ities. In this respect his language leaves nothing 4°e desired. "In foreign politics," he says, "I I_lll resolved to maintain peace with every one, so 17 as lies in my power. My love for the German ii7kY and my position in regard to it, will never !upt me to jeopardise for the country the benefits 11;Peace, unless the necessity of war is forced upon 1)1' an attack on the Empire or its allies." This clear and emphatic language, and must be as an intimation that so far as the new u- is concerned he will not become a dis- if he is not disturbed. He is attached to army; but to use its strength for aggressive is far, he adds, from his heart. But mere intention is not sufficient; and, to the end Germany may be in a position to hold her the alliance with Austria and Italy is to be - Still, the Emperor says : " Our agreements with Austria-Hungary and Permit me to my satisfaction to cultivate oftlilly my personal friendship for the Emperor • 11/48ia and the peaceful relations which have ted for the pastehrindred years with the neigh- Russian Empire, and which correspond tkr_ bay own feelings and with the interests of tll4'4t allY." Russia may not be pleased to find there is no hope of snapping the chain which B,Germany and Austria and Italy together; kra,Fille. cannot find cause of offence in the tem- tett l'e) if guarded, way in which she is herself re- cite. The language is the language of the tliPerer, but it is the language, too, of Prince thrc,l4,, rtea. He has been the powcr behind the for many years, and it would seem that, if • eB, he will exercise that power for many years to tistv • This cordiality of relationship between the guarZaperor and the old Chancellor is the best fp arltee for continuity of policy, and, therefore, r Preservation of peace. It is impossible to Of Prince BISMARCK changing his policy he change of Ruler; but it would be possible 'anperor to dispense with the services of • .it Chancellor, "and then who could say what kay 8 aPPen ? in the sense of that declaration shall continue striving to make Imperial legislation continue in the future to afford to the working population the protection which it can extend in conformity with the principles of Christian morality to the weak and distressed in the struggle for existence.' There are some statesmen in the country who look upon it as a weak point in the character of Prince Ms- MARC% that he supports State assurance for the benefit and protection of working-men. They re- gard it as a feeble attempt to stem the tide of Socialism ; and predict its failure. But what if it I should succeed? Germany will then be in a better position than England, where little or nothing is being done to grapple with the terrible evils which are growing in our growing cities. The experi- mentis well worth trying in this country. Ger- many, it is true, has her own special trouble in the need, as she believes, which lies upon her, of main- taming a huge standing .army. Meantime it is something to have the assurance that there is no immediate prospect of that army being set in motion. The now Emperor has spoken, and his words are words of peace.

THE gas question still occupies the minds of the ratepayers of Warrington. On Monday evening there will be a Public Meeting in the Market Shed, Market-street, to consider tho proposals of the Gas Committee consequent upon the retire- ment of Mr. PATERSON as manager of the Gas- works; and on Tuesday evening the Town Council will, it is understood, come to some decision on the question. The MAYOR was requisitioned to call a Town's Meeting, and why he declined to do so has not been made intelligible. To decline to convene the meeting because the gas question is still pending, cannot be said to be rational; for that is precisely why it is deemed desirable to obtain the views of the ° ratepayers. His Worship does not seem to be aware that the burgesses are as much a part of the Corporation as the Mayor and Aldermen; and that constitutional usage pre- scribes that, when the burgesses formulate a desire to be called together to express an opinion on any question, it is the duty of the Chief Magistrate to call them together. However, the meeting will be held, and it is to be hoped that the ratepayers will attend in such numbers as to make it clear that the issues raised are of no small interest to them. If we are not very much mistaken, there is a strong feeling against the proposal to give Mr. PATERSON a retaining fee of £lOO a year as consulting engineer to the Gas Committee. It is felt that the new manager—if he is competent—should have a free hand; or that a better man should be appointed to the post, if there are doubts as to his com- petency. Then there is the point raised by Councillor PLATT as to whether the Gas Com- mittee might not encourage the use of gas by dealing less stringently with cottage occupiers in the matter of deposits. If the statement is correct that gas is not used in the majority of the houses in Warrington, it is a matter which demands the instant attention of the Committee ; it means that they are on a bad system, and should set to work to devise a better. But the most serious question for consideration is thal of the leakage. There is something wrong, either in the official figures, the management, or the mains, when we find it on record that between one year and another that leakage has risen from four to four- teen per cent. For the year ending March, 1880, the loss, or leakage, is given as 7,510,000 cubic feet, or something like four per cent. of the total amount of gas manufactured. For the next year— the last year for which an official return has been issued—the leakage is found to be no less than 28,000,000 cubic feet, or fourteen per cent. It is past comprehension, and, indeed, almost beyond belief, that a leakage which has been reduced—to give the money value—to £1,126 should, in twelve months, rise to a loss equivalent to £3,087. If such a thing Irls happened, and if there be no adequate explanation, the matter is one which should be referred to the investigation of an in- dependent gas engineer. An extra loss of over £3,000 a year is too important to be lightly treated ; and we trust that this, and other matters at issue, will be fully and carefully considered at the public meeting, and at the meeting of the Town Council.

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."

A London correspondent says :—" The Arch- bishop of Canterbury has this season developed a taste for horse riding, and may be frequently seen in the Row before dinner." Oh,the times and the manners! The meek and lowly one whom the archbishop professes to follow was content to ride upon an ass; but then He hadn't a salary of £lO,OOO a year.

The "Times" has been severely taken to task for its report of the proceedings of the so-called private meeting last week of the Conservative party. Mr. Bartley protests against the inaccur- acy of the report of his speech; and Mr. Curzon goes the length of saying that the account which is given of what he said is "not even a caracature ; it is a concoction." This is pretty much like thundering into the ear of the Thun- dertr.

The "Times," by way of reply, protests against a great party meeting being treated as private, and with this we can agree; but it is hardly sufficient to tell those who complain of grossly inaccurate reports that they have their leaders to blame. Surely the " Times " is also to blame? If a journal has imposed upon it reports which are "concoctions," the least it ought to do, whilst re- ferring to the difficulty of getting a reliable report, should be to frankly apologise for its misrepresen- tations. But, then, the "Times" is always be- hind the times as to manners and morals—not to say a word as to politics.

What about the fishing in Walton Reservoir? Sir Gilbert Greenall promised that permission to fish should be given to the public, but that there should be a small fee—the proceeds of which should go to the Infirmary. But the promise seems to have been of the pie-crust order—made to be broken.

• The latest rumour is that the member for War- rington has let the fishing at the reservoir for four years to a party of fifteen, and at the rate of los 6d a year, per man. This, of course, should mean £7 17s 6d a year, for four years, to the War- rington Infirmary; and we hope to see the sum in the next list of contributions. But does this quite end the matter? Is it of no moment that Sir Gilbert Greenall has not kept his word with the public?

There was a time when the right to fish in Wal- ton Reservoir belonged to the Warrington Water- works Company, and there was no difficulty then about the public obtaining permission to fish. The Reservoir still belongs to the Company; but Sir Gilbert holds the fishing right. It was soon seen why ho got possession of the title' for as soon as he secured it the "hold fisherman" was given the cold shoulder. But an election came; a conditional promise was made; and that promise is not redeemed; for a favour to fifteen only cannot be said to extend to the public. We leave the inhabitants of War- rington to say what they think of Sir Gilbert Greenall. Already the fishermen of the town have made remarks ,which, like red herring, are full flavoured, and very strong.

CADBURY Boos, caution the public again st those Dutch Cocoas and their English imitations, sold as pure Cocoa, to which about 4 per cent. of Alkali and other agents are added, tor give appa- rent strength to the liquor, by making it a dart coiour. This addition may be detected by the scent when a tin is freshly opened. No Cocoa can be stronger than Cadbury's, which is guaranteed ABSOLUTELY PURE.—Advt. A meeting of cotton weavers was held on Wednesday night at Blackburn to protest against the infusion of steam into weaving sheds. The system was condemned as life destroying. Another remand for a week was granted on Wednes- day, by the Liverpool county Magistrates in the case of Nicholas R. Hesketh, charged with stealing various sums of money belonging to the Garston Local Board, in whose employment he was until recently as sur- veyor. PRIZE FIGHT IN SUSSEX.—EarIy on Wednesday morn- ing a number of men proceeded from Brighton to Rot- ting,de.an, three miles away, and formed a ring, in which a prize fight was commenced between a London and a Birmingham man, whose names did not transpire. The men fought half-an-hour, the Birmingham man breaking an arm, when the parties decamped on the appearance of strangers. RIOT AT HOLYHEAD.—Late on Wednesday night a serious fight took place at Holyhead between a number of bluejackets who had broken leave from Her Majesty's ship Neptune and the members of the Holyhead police force, in charge of Sergeant Foxhall. Large crowds con- gregated in the streets to witness the encounter. The police were so severely injured that medical aid had to be summoned, and the riot was only stopped by armed pickets from the man-of-war. • ifousE FURNISHING.—Messrs. Urquhart and Adamson, the well-known designers and manufacturers of art fur- niture, Bold-st., Liverpool, aro sending out some novel and striking advertisements of their goods in the shape of small photographs of various articles attached to their business card, stating price and particulars. The obvious advantage of this method is that intending pur- chasers are enabled practically to see and judge of the design and general appearance, and even form some idea of the quality and durability of the goods, for which this firm has acquired so well-merited a reputation.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 30, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 30, 1888.

Two publicans were fined at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, for breaking the law; but in neither instance was the license endorsed. In the first case, the offence proved was that of supplying beer to two constables whilst on duty. The Bench stated that the offence was a "very _serious ono ; " but, with curious inconsistency, they imposed a fine of is and costs only. The publican would not ' think that "very serious." It was not, to say the least of it, in the direction—to 'quote the "Mikado"—of mai;ing "the punishment fit the crime."

The inquest on the bodies of the three men who lost their lives in the Widnes sewer has ended, as we supposed it would, in the jury declaring that there has been culpable negligence on the part either of the Railway Company or the Canal Company. This means., that the relatives will have a claim for compensation. It is a poor consolation, but it is bettei than nothing. The sewer has proved to be a terrible.deA) trap, and for the future no workman ought to he permitted to enter it until every means are taken to ensure that there will be no fnrlEir.l.iss of life.

A London correspondent says:—" The Clerk of the Peace for the West Riding of Yorkshire has received a list of fifty-eight gentlemen who have been added to the Commission of the Peace for the Riding. A year ago about the same number were added to the bench. It is needless to say what is the political complexion of all these J.P.'s- Mr. Beamont, of Warrington, is credited with the say- ing that in Cheshire there are as many Leghs as fleas. Applied to the West Riding of the great county, the phrase would require altering to—a swarm of fleas and as many J.P.'s.

The Welsh took the lead in promoting- mea- sute for securing rights of way; Englani fol- lowed; and now we have a Scottish Rights of Way Bill. Ireland, as yet, is not in it ; she is seek- ing a right to deal with these rights. It is hardly likely that any of the bills will pass this year ; and, meanwhile, the land-grabbers will be at work as usual. If we had Home Rule all round, there would be no delay in such a matter; for bills would not be, as they are now, in each other's way. But patience, patience ; all things come round to those who can wait. ,

In the House of Lords, on Thursday, Viscount Cross took occasion to say that the accounts which had appeared in the papers of the Report of the Royal Commission on Education were un- authorised and inaccurate. It will be several weeks yet, it seems, before the official Report is issued. There can be no question, however, that the accounts in cirqgilation are substantially cor- rect, and they clearly reveal a reactionary tendency in the direction of sectarian education. Liberal educationists must be on the alert; it must not be forgotten that there is a Tory Government in office.

Referring to the fact that guarantors have been called on to make good deficits as to the exhibi- tions at Liverpool and at Folkestone, " Truth " says : "The result at Liverpool was astonishingly bad, considering the size of the city, its close proximity to so many industrial centres and the elaborate fuss that was raised about the under- taking." In this instance, " Truth " does not ap- pear to have got at the truth. Seeing that Man- chester had an unrivalled exhibition, and that Liverpool was holding a second exhibition in two years, it would have been astonishing if the result haa been other than bad. It was the expected that happened in this case.

The squabble in the German papers as to whether Sir Morrell Mackenzie was playing a political part in declining to recognise cancer as the disease from which the late Emperor suffered is anything but agreeable. The point is that, if it had been stated that the Crown Prince was suffering from an incurable disease, he could not have ascended the throne. So long as there really was a doubt, Sir Morrell was, of course. justified in withholding final judgment. There is one /side of the case that is at any rate satisfactory ; and that is that if the late Emperor had been told, whilst Crown Prince, that the disease was cancer, he would not, throne or no throne, have been for a moment party to any misrepresentation on the subject.

The "World," although a Tory organ, says: "It is a great misfortune that there is no statesman in the House of Commons who can kindle and rally the national feeling of the country, the sense of Imperial greatness, and the resolution to maintain the unity of the Empire." We may admit the ab- sence of the " statesman " without acknowledging the "misfortune." The country cannot rally to a cry which has nothing behind it. Both parties can shout "Unity of the Empire," because both parties are anxious to maintain it. What the " World " wants is a statesman to "grapple with things im- possible and get the better of them " ; but such a prodigy does not live in 1888.

Mr. Dillon wears the prison suit, for it is Mr. BaHour's boast that he treats all criminals alike. And yet not all; he has been beaten by the priests who have refused to don the prison garb. On this point, Mr. Gladstone hit the Irish Secretary hard, and yet not too hard, when he said : "And why did the right hon. gentleman, who is troubled with a stiff, unbending conscience, bend that conscience in the case of the priest (Cheers.) If the prison dress be the same thing for Mr. Dillon and the freize coat, it is the same thing for Mr. Dillon and the priest. But the right hon. gentleman has not dared to put the prison dress upon the priest. He receded from it, not because he was merciful, but because he was afraid. (Loud cheers.)" Yes, Balfour can bluster, but he has his times of terror.

The Government, on Thursday evening, were in the unhappy plight of having to vote against their own proposal to confer on County Councils the power to close public-houses on Sunday, Good, Friday, or Christmas Day. As they cannot en- dow the brewers, they avenge themselves by crippling the new Councils. And Mr. Caine voted with them! He professes to believe that Mr. Stevenson's Sunday Closing Bill will be helped by the Government and will become law this session. We should be glad to find that his anticipation is correct ,• but suspect that tho Ministry are making a 'show of patronage of the bill which will end in nothing being done. If they are really in earnest about Sunday closing, why not have left the issue to the decisions of the County Councils.?
