div.p: LOCAL NEWS.

MOST PEOPLE ARE IGNORANT Of the value of eyesight. In many instances, when they first find their eyesight failing, they purchaSe all kinds of in- ferior taanufactured speceacles, which in the end cause their eyes to burn and ache. To remedy this defect, A. Franks, of 95 and 97, Deansgate, and 44, Market-st., Manchester, 143, Lord-st., Southport, and 60, Whitefriargate, Hull, has invented his "Per- fection" Spectacles, which he adapts at either of the above addresses at 7s 6d per pair. lie will guarantee that they are not to be equalled in the coun- try for clearness, coolness, and rest they impart to the eyes. Pamphlet "how to preserve the sight" free on application.—Advt RUNCORN Realm. BOARD.—The annual meeting for the election of three members to the above Board was held on Thursday evening. Mr W. Handley occupied the chair, and observed that probably this was the last time the ratepayers would be called together for such a pur- pose, as it was proposed by the Local Government Bill to absorb the Burial Boards into the District Councils. The retiring menibers—Messrs W. Whittaker, W. Mellor, and E. Imison—were unanimously re-elected. THE REY. Ram CONNELL, MA., Trinity College, Dub- lin, has been appointed by the Vicar Designate, the Rev. George Henry St. Patrick Garrett, to the stipendiary curacy of St. Mary's, Widnes, in succession to the Rev. A. P. Hamilton Wilson, now curate of Glossop Parish Church. At his ordination by the Archbishop of Dublin, in 1885, Mr. Connell was licensed to the curacy of St. George's Church, Dublin under the Rev. T. Lucas Scott, late chaplain to the Lord-Lieutenant of Ireland. CONGREGATIONALISM AT WIDNES. The following in- formation with reference to the Widnes Congregational Church, is taken fro ri the Lancashire Congregational Calendar just published :—This church, on January Ist, 1837, had on the church- roll 59 members. During the year 3 died, 3 were transfOrred, and 3 withdrew. Nine- teen members were added to the roll, leaving on January Ist, 1888, 69 members. The attendance ae church has also steadily increased during the year. The average at- tendance has been—morning, 42; evening, 96. The sit- tings show a steady increase for the year, viz., sittings let, January Ist, 1887, 60; ditto, January Ist, 1888, 87. The Sunday School is also increasing. Total on books, 1886, 120 ; ditto, 1887, 174. The place is most incon- venient in many ways, besides our having to pay rent for the same. The church is now seriously considering the advisibility of building schools. We have a plot of land belonging to and adjoining the chapel, which is well adapted for the purpose, and we have £6O towards the building fund, which we propose increasing if the Union grant us £5O. The strain on the church during the last two or three years has been severe, having to hold sales of work each year to meet their deficiencies, but a bazaar in aid of new schools would be a stimulant to our band of workers, and would receive the hearty support of the Widnes people. CrOSSAGES EXCURSION FROM WIDNES,—The workpeople of Messrs. Gossage and Son, soap manufacturers, Wid- nes. had their 30th annual excursion on Saturday. The firm treated the men in the liberal manner that has al- ways been a distinguishing and pleasant feature, and a most enjoyable day was spent at the popular seaside re- sort of Blackpool, which place had been chosen by an overwhelming majority over the other places proposed. Each man received two tickets, one being for his wife or his sweetheart, and Is 6d is also allowed for dinner. The youths are given one ticket and a shilling. No less than thirteen hundred tickets were issued, and two trains of eighteen coaches each departed from Widnes about seven o'clock ; and safely arrived at Blackpool with their living freight about ten o'clock.. The whole of the arrange- ments and the comfort of the passengers were admirably attended to by a committee consisting of Messrs. A. Thorpe, R. Corke, W. Hartland, Wm. Jackson, John Rogers, J. Briggs, T. Whitley, C. Jones, J. Jackson' J. Povah, I. Turton J. Hulme, W. Hag,ner, J. Williams, J. Davies, J. Hardes, McConnell, and G. Proctor. The trippers were favoured with most beautiful weather, and enjoyed to the full the many amusements that are pro- vided at the "Brighton of the-North." They were ad- mitted at a reduced rate into the Winter Gardens. the Royal Palace Gardens, and the Aquarium. In the even- ing the excursionists had a splendid run home, the second train arriving in Widnes at a quarter past nine. DEATH AND FUNERAL OF MRS. S. B. CHADWICK, OF RUN- cons.—The people of Runcorn will regret to hear of the death of Mrs. Chadwick, wife of Mr. S. B. Chadwick, J.P., of Crofton Lodge, Run- corn. For some time past the deceased lady has been in feeble health, and she had lately resided at Llan- dudno, in the hope that the bracing air of that locality would restore her wonted vitality. On Friday last, how- ever, her condition became so critical that Ms. Chadwick and Dr. McDougall were telegraphed for. Death. oc- curred on Saturday morning. The remains of the de- ceased, who had attained the age of 68 years, were interred in the family vault at Daresbury parish Church on Wednesday. The funeral cortege started from Runcorn at eleven o'clock, and consisted of the following : Doctor's carriage, Dr. McDougall, Mr. J. Shaw Green. The hearse. Ist coach, S. B. Chadwick, Esq., Rev. Mr. Hughes. 2nd, Rev. W. C. Safford, Rev. W. F. Atten- borough, J. Read, Esq. 3rd, Major Hazlehurst, G. Li Wigg, Esq., V. Rayner, Esq. 4th, John Brundrit, Esq., J.P., R. Davies, Esq., Thos. Bankes, Esq. sth, Rev. W. Chambers, Rev. J. J. Bryant. 6th, Mr. Taylor,•Mr. Matthew Rathborne, Mr. J. Ball. The service in the church was conducted by the Rev. W. F. Attenborough, and at the grave side by the Rev. W. C. Safford. The arrangements were carried out by Mr. W. H. Rogerson, and 'Mr. S. Yarwood supplied the hearse. Weaths and crosses adorned the coffin, the following having sontributed floral offerings : S. B. Chadwick, Esq., Mrs. Spencer Silvir, Mrs. Chas. Hazlehurst, Mrs. Safford, Att,enborough (the Rev. W. F. and Mrs.), Miss Read, C. W. Hazlehurst (Major and Mrs) Mr. and the Misses Read, Mrs. G. L. Wigg, Mrs. Rayner, Miss Hazlehurst, Mr. and Mrs. J. W. Shaw, John Brun- drit, Esq., J.P., Mr. and Mrs. White, Mrs. Chorlton, Mrs. Barclay, Miss. A. Rougier, Misses Joy and Maggie Chorl- ton, Mr. and Mrs. Bryant, Mr. and Mrs. Hunter, Mr. J. Shaw Green, Miss M. Challoner, Mr. and Mrs. Sutton and Mrs. Ormes, and Sarah Longford, Alice Pritchard, and Annie Houghton (servants.) PRESENTATION TO A RUNCORN MINISTER.—There was a large gathering of members and friends at the Primi- tive Methodist Sunday School, Regent-st., Runcorn, to bid farewell to the Rev. J. Causland, the pastor, prior to his removal to the St. Helens circuit, and also to tes- tify to their continued esteem and respect. The pro- ceedings commenced with a tea, and afterwards Mr. W. H. Gyton' of Warrington, Was requested to take the chair.—Mr. Peacock explained that there had been no difficulty in obtaining subscriptions to the testimonial, and many persons had felt grieved because they were not appealed to. Mr. Causland had refused to accept a money gift. Alluding to the reports that had been cir- culated stating that the revd. gentleman. had received from £7OO to £2,000 from the London and North-Wes- tern Railway Company as compensation for serious in- juries received in a collision on their line some months since, Mr. Peacock said there was no truth whatever in these reports.—Mr. Roberts, of Liverpool, a mom ber of the Church of England, who labours amongst all sections of the Christian Church, then presented Mr. Causland with a capital por- trait of himself, set in a handsome gilt frame. The in- scription read as follows :—" Presented to the Rev. J. Causland as an expression of the high appreciation of his services as a Christian minister during the three years of his superintendency of this, the Preston Brook Circuit by a number of friends and well wishers. June, 1888." In accepting the gift, the rev, gentleman ad- verted to his unfortunate accident on the railway, and stated that that day he had received a kind and con- siderate letter from the company. and throughout the whole of his painful affliction they had manifested much , sympathy. They had stated that if his health was so broken down that he would be obliged to retire and throw himself on the connexional superannuation fund, they would grant him such compensation as would be equivalent to his salary. In concluding a sympathetic speech, Mr. Causland cordially thanked the friends 'for their kindness.—The Chairman, on behalf of the sub- scribers, then presented Mrs. Causland with a portrait of herself, as a companion to that of her husband. She was also presented with a miniature chest of drawers by Mr. 6 J. Reyes, and other tokens of affection 6,nn Mr. C. Hill and Mrs. Hoxworth. The meeting was closed in the cus- tomary manner.

MARRIAGE OF A RUNCORN BREWER. On Thursday morning the marriage of Mr. Thomas Jones, brewer, of the South Bang Hotel, Runcorn' and MN Ada Rhodes, youngest daughter of the late Mr. George Rhodes, of Leinster-gardens, was solemnized at the Parish Church, Runcorn. The service was performed by the vicar (the Rev. A. Maitland Wood, MA.) Mr. Walter Jones offi- ciated as best man, and Miss Ringland as bridesmaid, whilst the bride was given away by her brother, Mr. W. A. Rhodes. After the wedding the happy couple left Runcorn for North vales to spend the honeymoon. The presents were num6rous and valuable. PLOWER SERVICE AT RUNCORN. The annual flower service in connection with Bethesda Congregational Chapel, Runcorn, was held in that sacred eilifice on Sun- day evening. The decorations were on a very modest scale A stage erected within the communion rails wan filled with foliage plants and plants in bloom. Many members of the congregation, however, had brought bouquets of beautiful flowers, and these were afterwards collected, and on Monday were distributed amongst the , sick persons in the town. Hymns appropriate to the oc- casion were sung, and the Rev. J. D. Thomas, the pastor, preached a suitable sermon. There was a large congre- gation, and a collection was taken iu aid of funds of the chapel. BURGLARY FROM A WIDNES PUBLIC Horse.—At Widnes Police Court, on Tuesday, Anthony O'Brien and Mark O'Brien, brothers, were charged on remand with having between Sunday night, the 17th, and Monday morning, the 18th inst., burglariously entered the Ship Inn; Vic- toria-st., Widnes, and stolen therefrom a silver watch and gold guard, and a cash box containing £4 in money, belonging to Jos. Passey, a lodger, and also a quantity of tobacco, lemonade, bottled porter, &c., the property of the landlord, William Jones. The circumstances have been previously reported. Anthony pleaded not guilty. Mark said he committed the robbery alone, but was wearing his brothers cap at the time. Both prisoners were committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial. WIDNES LIBERALS AND THE COERCION ACT.—At a meeting of the members of the Simm's Cross District of the Whines Division Liberal Association, on Thursday night, the following resolution was unanimously passed: "That in the opinion of this meeting the manner in which the Coercion Act is being administered in Ireland tends to bring English law and justice into contempt, and to perpetuate hatred instead of promoting union between England and Ireland ; is contrary to the pledges given by the Government when the Act was passed, and that the recent sentences upon Mr. John Dillon, the member for Mayo, and upon others of our fellow sub- jects, are flagrant instances of the said maladministra- tion." A similar resolution was also passed at the meeting of the Liberals of Aigburth district last night. WOUNDED BY A Borne AT WIDNES.—On Monday, at Widnes Police Court, Catherine Fallen, a married woman, of 10, Cromwell-st., was charged with causing grievous bodily harm to a man named Peter Molloy. It appeared that on Saturday Molloy was standing at the back door of a labourer named Thomas Molloy, in Crom- well-st., and they were drinking whisky from a bottle. After having consumed the whole of the spirit Molloy handed the empty bottle to the woman to, have a drink. Molloy seized hold of her by the wrist, and she, snatch- ing the bottle from his hand, struck him on the face with it. The bottle was broken, and Molloy was seriously cut about the lips. He was unable to appear.—Mr. Knowles, who appeared for the defendant, said the woman was frightened at the man holding her, and she struck him in self-defence.—The prisoner was remanded, but bail was allowed. ROBBED BY A SISTER AT WIDNES.—JuIia O'Brien, a woman having no fixed abode, was brought before the Widnes magistrates on Monday. charged with stealing from the person of her sister, Mary Broadhurst, a purse containing 19s sd. The prosecutrix said she was the wife of Thomas Broadhurst, 15. Caroline-st. About two o'clock on Saturday afternoon, the 18th inst., the pri- soner entered the house and refused to leave when re- quested. Whilst she was employed cutting some bread the prisoner extracted her purse from her pocket, and at once took her departure. An hour afterwards a }a- ung girl named Dwyer brought back the purse, from which es fld had been taken. Mary Wilson deposed to seeing the robbery committed, and Mary Tarpey- stated that she saw the prisoner put something in her breast and then throw the purse in the street. The prisoner, who had only just been released from gaol, was now committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial. FALL FROM A TRAIN AT Ruecom—lmmediately after the departure of the 6-4 p.m. train from Runcorn to Liverpool, on' Thursday evening, Mr. Ward, acting stationmaster at Runcorn, discovered a man lying across the metals on the up line, on the arches over top locks. The man was quite conscious, but complained of a very serious pain in the head, and Dr. McDougall was sent for. That gentleman's assistant quickly arrived, and he stated that the symptoms might develops into concus- sion of the brain, and ordered his removal to Liverpool, whither he was conveyed by the next train. The man stated that his name was John Payne, and was a mem- ber of the Derby Police Force. After spending his holi- days he was on his way home from Cork to Derby via Liverpool. He explained the circumstances in which he was found by stating that after the train had passed Runcorn he was looking through the carriage window on the off side, when the door flew open, and he fell to the ground. The doctor's prognostications proved true, and the man is now suffering from concussion of the brain. THE HONEST RUNCORN CONSTABLE: SCENE IN COURT. —At Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, before Mr. C. Reynold and Major Hazlehurst, Samuel Jones and John Slater, navvies, were charged with having drunk and disorderly in Bridge-st. on the 23rd instant. Inspector O'Donnell and P.C. 77 gave evidence that the men were drunk and fighting,—P.C. Gibson then got ipto the wit- ness box, and stated positively that the mbn were not drunk.—Superintendent Hollingworth : There is a report pending against you? Witness: There is, which will come on afterwards.—How mine yod to get into that box without beingasked ? I have come to see Justice done to the prisoners. There is no doubt there will be about 20 witnesses amongst the audience to show that these men were given into custody wrongfully. I attend here as an honest constable.—Why were you removed from Hyde to here, sir ? That has nothing to do with it.— Mr. Reynolds: He has a right to come here and give any evidence he may like.—Superintendent Hollingworth said to test the constable's honesty he asked why he was removed from Hyde, but P.C. Gibson refused to answer the question.—T. Bell, butcher, Bridge-st., also deposed that Slater was sober.--P.C. Sutherland said both pri- soners were drunk when brought to the police station.— While the Bench were considering the ease, P.C. Gibson again entered the witness box, and said; Your worships, I should just like to ask the seperintendent a question.— Mr. Reynolds: Just stand down.—The constable at once obeyed the order.—The Bench did not think the evidence such as would' warrant them in convicting, and dis- charged the prisoners. A WIDNES FURNACE:NAN AND HIS CREDITORS: THE EFFECT OF BRINK.—At Widnes County Court, yester- day, before His Honour Judge, T. P. E. Thompson, Peter Blong, of 58, Cromwell-st., applied, for an administra- tion order. Mr. Knowles appeared for the debtor, and Mr. Peters represented three of the creditors. Mr. Knowles said that Blong was employed as a furnaceman at the works of Messrs Hall Brothers and Shaw, and when in full work earned about £2 per week, but fre- quently when the furnace was out be had to go into the yard as a labourer at 3s per day. The amount of his debts was £33 lOs 4d. He suffered much from ill- health, and was not able to pay more than is per week. —Dr. Hutchinson was called, and stated that Blong was not a strong Man, and was not suited to work at a furnace. He had recommended have to get a light job.—By Mr. Peters : The men who worked at the furnace and drank much were apt to he pale. (Blong had a very emaciated appearance and a very pale face.)—Judge Thompson: For the benefit of working men, Doctor, may I ask, can they work better if they drink or if they don't ?—Doctor Flutchinson : They can work better if they don't. Two glasses of beer may do a man good, but anything beyond that is not good.— Mr. Knowles said the men who worked at the chemical furnaces were nearly roasted alive, and they were bound to have beer.—Mr. Peters alleged that after the debtor had appeared at court a month ago he was led ;home drunk, and he argued for an order of lOs per month. At the rate proposed by Mr. Knowles the man would be two years in paying the court, expenses.—Walter Murray, baker, assistant to Mr. Joshua Midwood, gave evidence as to the drunkenness.—His Honour made an order of 8s per month. SAD EPISODE IN A MARRIED LIFE AT WlDNES.—Before Mr. H. Wade Deacon and Mr. G. Pilkington, at Widnes Police Court, on Thursday, John Hunt. a bricksetter, of Gossage-st., was summoned under the Wife's Mainten- ance Act to show cause why he should not contribute to- wards the support of his wife Mary Hunt. Mr. W. T. Husband appeared for the complainant, and Mr. Knowles for the defendant.—Mr. Knowles said the defendant wished his wife to return to htm. He was vary fond of her and was willing to promise the Bench that he would be kind and 'good to her if she would return.—Mrs Hunt said she had tried him so many times ; she dare not go back.—The case was then proceeded with.—Mr. Hus- band said'the parties had been married for 27 years, and there had been eight children of the union, the youngest child being six years of age. Although they had been living in the same house he understood that they had not cohabited together for the last six years. The evi- dence of desertion was not very strong, and had he been consulted before the summons was taken out, he would have had the case taken under the Aggravated Assaults Act. It had been held, however, that where the hus- band drove his wife from home with violence, and re- fused to take her in that was desertion.—On Friday night the 25th May, the defendant took up a knife from the table and threatened to strike his wife with it, but she left the house. On the following day he came home in a ' state of intoxication, bolted the door, and drove her up stairs. She locked herself in her bedroom, but he broke open the door and "hammered and beat" her with his fists until she was black and blue. He threatened to end her existence by making her jump through the window. The neighbours gathered round the house and the wo- man made her escape, and she had since lived at 9, Bold- st. She had been three times to see him, 'but on one oc- casion he abused her and threatened to have her locked up.—Mrs Hunt having given evidence the Bench did not' consider the desertion proved, and Mr. Husband with- drew the summons, and remarked that proceedings would probably be taken under another act.

ANNIVERSARY SERVICES AT RIINCORN.—The anniver- sary of the opening of the church-of St. Michael and All Angels was celebrated on Sunday. when the Rev. W. 11. Binney, M.A., vicar of Northwich, preached to large congrzgations at both the morning and evening services. The collections were in aid of the choir fund.—At Holy Trinity Church the animal sermons on behalf of the day and Sunday schools were preached by the Rev. Dr. Bartle, of Southport. There were large congregations at each service.

CRUELTY TO A HORSE AT WIDNES. Patrick Ryan, a young man of Mill-st., was brought before Mr. Deacon and Mr. Pilkington at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Whurs- day, charged with cruelly ill-treating a horse.—Mr. Jas. Griffin, Inspector of the Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, said on Tuesday, the 19th inst., he saw the defendant in charge of a horse drawing a cart laden with four sets of potatoes. Noticing the animal flinch, he examined it, and found three large wounds on the back and shoulders. The wounds were discharging blood and matter, and the horse was in very poor condi- tion, and was suffering very great pain.—The defendant pleaded guilty, and was fined 40s and costs, or a month's hard labour. THE RENOWNED RUNCORN RELISH is prepared from the choicest herbs, roots, and spices, which render it of most valuable assistance in the digestion of food.--Prepared and sold wholesale by Isaac Stubbs. Lowlands-road. Runcorn.— ,Adrt.

WILFUL DAMAGE AT WIDNES.—On Thursday, at Wid- nes Petty Sessions, Patrick Riley, a youth, whose home is at 21, Davis-st., was summoned for wilfully damaging a plate glass window, of ' the shop of Mr. J. B. Imison, pawnbroker, Waterloo-road.—Arthur Oswald Imison and John Williamson deposed to seeing the prisoner throw a large stone at the window and smash it. The sum of £4 8s had been expended in replacing the window.--P.C. Murray said the prisoner was under the influence of liquor at the time, and he said he could not help it.—The prisoner pleaded guilty and was fined 40s and costs, to- gether with the amount of the damage. In default, the prisoner was sent to gaol for a month. RUNCORN SAVINGS' BANK.—The half-yearly meeting of this bank was held at the offices, High-street, on Thurs- day. Mr J. Brundrit occupied the chair, and there were present Messrs W. F. Salkeld, J. Simpson, James • Pritchard, T. Handley-, W. Littler, Dr. McDougall, and other managers, together with the actuary, Mr W. Handley. The actuary produced a certificate from the auditors, who stated that they had examined the ac- counts for the past six months, and found them correct. The next business was to appoint trustees in the place of Messrs. Charles Reynolds,Williarn Hayes, S. B. Chad- wick, and the late Sir R. Brooke, Bart. It was decided not to fill the vacancies, but to await the result of the Royal Commission which was at present /inquiring into thew:l-king of Trustees Savings Banks. WIDNES BOWLERS AT HUNTS CROSS.—A handicap at bowls, confined to Widnes players, took place on Thurs. day- upon the green attached to Hunts Cross Hotel. The conditions were: Entrance fee, one shilling; first prize, a guinea; game 15 up, limit 7; all competitors, excepting those thrown out in the first round, to obtain a prize, which consisted of the entrance fees and 103 , added by the proprietor. Fifty-seven entered the corn- , hpetition, and, notwithstanding the inclement state of the weather, a very large gathering took place. The first and 'second prizes were divided between Mr Andrew Carragher and Mr George Windsor, and amongst other , prize winners were Messrs W. Melvin. W. Upward, C. Broom 'P. Davies, J. Whitfield, Talton, Bell, Porter, ' Hulme, Radley, Fitzpatrick, Bray, Ashton, Stone,' Hud- son, Wade, Whittaker, Southwell, Woolley, Lecom her, ,Dixon, and Steinthardt. Tea was provided in Mr. Hilditch's very best style, and about 40 sat down to the repast. SHOCKING ASSAULT CASE ON A GIRL AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday. before Mr H. Wade Deacon, a married woman named Elizabeth Broxton, who lives in Arthur-st., was charged with having on .the 26th instant inflicted grievous bodily harm upon Mary Schumann, aged 13 years, the daughter of William Schumann, labourer, of 54, Kent-st. From a statement made by Superindent Johnstone, it appeared that on the :evening of the date mentioned a n unbar of children were playing in front of the prisoner's house.. As her husband was ill in bed, the noise very much annoyed him, and the prisoner ran the children away. The girl was carrying a stool, and one of her companions was carrying a brush. The prisoner said, "Get out of here you young devils, or I'll knock you down," and then, snatching the brush from the girl's hand, she struck the girl Schumann on the head with it, knocking her to the grouad. The girl was taken to the police station and examined by Dr. O'Keeffe, who found her suffering from a dangerous wound on the head. She is now in a critical state, and the prisoner was remanded for a week.

ROWDYISM AT WIDNES.-At Widnes Petty Sessions on Tharsday, Thomas Heaton, flatman, of Birkenhead, was charged with assaulting Robert H. Wilkinson, draper, Victoria-road.—lt was alleged that on Sunday evening Mr. Wilkinson and his brother were taking a walk along Moor-lane, when a gang of young men amongst whom were the defendant, threw stones at them until they arrived within a few yards of each other. The prisoner then attacked the complainant, and struck him in the ribs and altogether treated him very severely. He was also strnck on the head with a stone, and his brother was also similarly treated by some of the other men.—The prisoner called a man named Alf. Greenhalgh, who said the complainant and his brother were the persons who threw stones and that the complainant used his stick.— The complainant said he used the stick in self defence.— Inspector Keighley said he saw the young gentlemen shortly after the occurrence, and they appeared to have been roughly used. Greenhalgh then said he saw the ill- treatment to which they had been subjected.—A fine of 20s and costs, 9s 6d, was imposed, or in default, a month's imprisonment,

ALLEGED DISEASED MEAT AT WIDNES.—George Maddi- son, a butcher, occupying a shop in, Widnes Market Hall, was brought before Mr. IT. Wade Deacon and Mr. G. Pilkington, at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, charged with having exposed for sale diseased meat that was intended for human food.—Mr. Mearns, of St. Helens, defended.—Mr. Dickson,-the nuisance inspector to the Widnes Local Board, staed that on the first day of May he saw part of the carcase of a cow,exposed for sale at the defendant's shop. He examined the beef, and concluded that it was unsound and not 'fit for human food. It was afterwards examined by three veterinary surgeons, and was ordered to be destroyed by a magis- trate.—ln cross-examination witness admitted that the meat was hung outside the shop, which was locked up, and that Mr. Maddison was not present.—Mr. Shepherd, market inspector, and Mr. Taylor, veterinary surgeon, corroborated.—For the defence Mr. Mearns stated (and evidence in confirmation was called) that the beef was part of the carcase of a poor cow, and had been bought from Mr. Walker, a butcher, with an extensive business at the Liverpool Abbatoir, and had been passed by the officers of the Liverpool Corporation. It was what was called steak beef .—The Bench considered there was a doubt in the case, and dismissed it.

STUERS' FITTINTTURE CREAM.—For giving a brilliant gloss to all kinds of mahogany and Frenbh polished furniture with half the usual labour, use Stubbs' Furniture Cream. Sold in bottles, id., 2d., and 3d.—lsaac Stubbs, Lowlands-road, Run- corn.—Advt. COLLIERY FATALITY.— On Wednesday, - 4ohn Jarvis, 39 years of age, of Park-road, St. Helens, and employed in the Legh, Pit, Haydoek, belonging Messrs. Richard Evans &, Co., was inStantly killed. He was engaged tunnelling, when a piece of rock fell from the roof, and on his body being found he was quite dead. The body was reraovad • home to await an inquest. A BLOCK ON THE LINE.—On Saturday night some delay was caused to passenger traffic on the Cheshire Lines Railway, between Liverpool and Warrington, by a block on the line, which is said to have been the cause of an error. The trains which left Liver- pool at 10-45 p.m., 11 p.m., and 11-15 p.m. were all hindered, the first not arriving at Warrington until 1-30 a.m. on Sunday. Even by that time the line had not been cleared, for to enable the trains to con- tinue their journeys they were shunted on to the down line, and run off again at Warrington. Ting HOME IRON TRADE.—There is greater steadi- ness in the English iron market, our advices agree- ing that trade is improring, although the signs in- dicating that change tue as yet not very pronoun- ced. It remains to be seen whether the better ten- dency observable is the fereginner of a permanent improvement, long hoped for,br whether it is again only a temporary flicker. Pig-iron, although quiet, is firm in the north of England, and tending up- wards. Scotch makers' iron, on the contrary, is still very changeable. Bessemer iron, whilst its quotation in the north-west is 6d. a ton lower, is reported ' very steady. In both these cases the heavy stocks operate against any substantial im- provement. A little more firmness is perceptible in Lancashire. Shipments of pig-iron are above the monthly average. The better tone in the manufac- tured iron market is maintained, the demand being well sustained.—lron. SCOTTISH STEAMSHIP IN COLLISION WITH A RUN- CORN VESSEL.—On Thursday, in the Court of Ad- miralty, London, before Sir James Hannen, assisted by Trinity Masters, the owners and master and crew of the brigantine Diadem, of the port of Run- corn, sought to recover damages from the owners of the steamship Cyrus,.pf the port of Grangemouth, for the sinking of their vessel, with her cargo and the effects of the crew, in a collision which took place in the river Tyne on the 17th of April last. The Diadem was on a voyage from Runcorn to Heb- burn-on-Tyne with a cargo of rock salt, while the Cyrus was on a voyage from South Shields to Bilbao with a cargo of coke. The collision took place about half-past two o'clock in the morning. The Diadem was sunk as a result of the collision. The defendants counter-claimed for the damage. sus- tained by the Cyrus, alleging that the occurrence was brought about by the improper navigation of the brigantine. Mr. Barnes, Q.C., and Mr. Pyke were council for the plaintiffs, and Sir W. Philli- more and Mr. Holman appeared for the defend- ants. The case was not concluded when the court rose.
LANCASHIRE GENERAL SassroM,---At the annual ' general session of Lancashire county magistrates, held at Preston on Thursday, the chairman, Mr. J.

, T. Hibbert, expressed regret that the Government had, since the introduction of the Local Govern- ment Bill, been gradually going down an inclined plane, having first made a concession that boroughs of 100,000 inhabitants should be made counties, and then reduced the limit to 50,000. Mr. Hibbert pointed out the financial difficulties which would be entailed, and it was resolved that acommittee be appointed to consider the best means of carrying the bill into effect.

div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN. By "ARIEL."

That people have for years been patiently wait- ing to learn the plan of the Runcorn Commissioners for the improvement of Waterloo Bridge. That the bridge is a disgrace to the town, and that the manner in which the subject has been shelved from time to time is not creditable to business men. That the meetings of the Waterloo Bridge Com- mittee are few and far between, or else your repor- ter, sir, does not notice them. That it is time the Committee was thoroughly awakened from its lethargy. That there was a gathering of literary, political, and social notables la the " Star " Office in London, on Wednesday night and that Mr. and Mrs. Brim- ner, and Mr. T. E. Ellis were present. That Inspector O'Donnell, who boldly announces himself as a teetotaller, has cone amongst the pub- licans like a bombshell, and that the twelve boni- faces upon whom he made a call the other Satur- day night did not altogether regard the visit 88 complimentary. That it ought to be recognised that the Inspector is doing what the law and his duty demands, and that to avoid unpleasant consequences the publi- cans will have to pay more strict attention to the requirements of the Act of Parliament in conduct,. ing what is no doubt a difficult business. That he who is in the right need have no fear. _ . .
That Dr. Steele and Mri. Lloyd Wigg have been placed on the Commission of the Peace for Chester, and will be sworn in at Knutsford Quarter Sessions, on Monday.

div.head: PROSECUTIONS AGAINST_ PUBLICANS AT RUN-
div.p: PROSECUTIONS AGAINST_ PUBLICANS AT RUN-
CORN.

At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Mr. C. Reynolds and Major Hazlehurst, Sinclair Armstrong, landlord of the Bull's Head Inn, Halton- rcad, was charged with having on the 16th instant supplied beer to two constables, named Edward Brew and John Gibson, while on duty. Mr. A. Fletcher, of North wich, appeared for the defendant, who pleaded not guilty. Inspector O'Donnell said that at five minutes past nine on the evening of the date in question he saw the constables enter the Bull's Head Inn. They-were both in uniform and on duty. After waiting a minute or two he followed them in the house, and met them at the parlour door. He asked them what they were doing there, and not being satisfied with their explanation, he called the landlord and asked him if he had supplied them with beer. He replied "No," but afterwards, when a pint was pointed out to him, he ad- mitted that he had served them with a pint each, and added, "I didn't charge them, I returned them their money."—Cross-examined by Mr. Fletcher:. He (wit- ness) did not take beer. The two constables were not off duty until twelve o'clock that night ;. on other nights they would have been off duty at nine o'clock. There was no badge worn by which a publican could tell when a policeman was on or off duty, but a policeman was al- ways on duty when in uniform.—By the Superintendent: It was patt of the regulations of that force to prevent people from knowing when a constable was off duty.— P.C. Brew said he went into the inn with P.C. Gibson, who called for two pints of beer. The landlord supplied them, and witness gave him a shilling. The landlord pulled a handful of change out of his pocket and then put the shilling back on the table. They saw the inspec- tor pass the window, and witness put his beer under the seat, and Gibson placed his on the table. At first the defendant denied to the in- spector that he had served any liquor to them.—By Mr. Fletcher: He lived about two hun- dred yards away from the Bull's Head, and he had frequently called for a drink on his way home from the office when he had been off duty, but had his uniform on. I.le knew that he was considered to be on duty when he had his uniform on. He did not think the landlord knew they were on duty that night.—Sergeant Woolley having given evidence Mr. Fletcher addressed the Bench for the defence. He said if there was to be a change in the administration of the Licensing Act in Runcorn, let the licensed Victuallers know it at once. He challenged Superintendent Hollingworth to state that he had ever given an order upon a publican to supply a constable with beer, and common sense would tell them that the constable had never asked for the orders. Yet if the constables had gone into any house in the town on a warm summers evening and asked for a glass of beer, they had had it. He ventured topubmit that that was sanctioned by old usage; if there was tope a new order of things, let the licensed victuallers know it, but do not make the defendant in this case the scape-goat. It had never yet been defined in the county that an officer in uniform was always on duty and he thought that in fairness to the licensed victuallers there should be some definite rule laid down for their guidance.—The defen- dant was called, and said during the five years he had kept the inn there had not been any complaints against him, and he had never been warned not to supply the police whilst in uniform. In other towns constables on duty wore armlets. The two constables walked straight into his parlour, sat down, and called for two drinks, and he had no hesitation in supplying them . as he thought they were off duty. He had never denied to the Inspector that he had served the beer.—By Super- intendent Hollingsworth: He knew the law that he' ought not to supply policemen on duty.—Mr. Reynolds said as this was the first offence a nominal penalty of only is and costs, 12s 6d, would be imposed. They would not endorse the license, but the offence was a very seri- ous one all the same.—A charge of bribing the constable by giving them the beer was withdrawn. Joseph Grundy, landlord of the Masonic Hotel, Devon- shire-place, was charged with having, on the 16th June, unlawfully sold intoxicating liquor to two drunken men named Thomas Warne and Joseph Wood. There was a further charge of permitting drunkenness on licensed premises.—Mr. C. H. Lewis, of Widnes, defended.—The charge of selling was first taken.—lnspector O'Donnell deposed that he visited the Masonic Hotel at a quarter to eleven on the night in question in company with Ser- geant Woolley, and at the bar they, found Warne and Wood who were drunk, with two pint glasses half filled, before them. The landlord denied that he had served the men, and said he did not know who had served them. Warne said he had no place of residence' and Wood said he belonged to the flat H.H. West. He had since ascer- tained that one of the names was not correct. —By Mr. Lewin: One of the men might have asked him to have a drink, but he was not at all disgusted with that because he was a teetotaller. He did not go into the house with the idea of catching a publican, but to do his duty. There was no noise in the house. He visited perphaps a dozen public-houses that night. He was in plain clothes. P.S. Woolley gave corroborative evidence, and 'Constable Dale and Sergeant Gosling were also called.—For the defence, Mr. Lewin pointed out that it was the rule of the firm that no drunken men must be served, and the person who broke that rule was instantly dismissed. He called the defen- dant, who said he had kept the Masonic Hotel for three years, and there had been no complaint against him. It was about half-past ten when the Inspector and Sergeant visited the home. He was at the wholesale window at the time. Until the officers drew his attention to the men he had not seen them, and had certainly not served them with beer. He told the Inspector he could not ac- count for the men having beer, but some people ordered beer and then gave it to others. The inen were not drunk. They were as steady as a die, and could talk plainly. Warne asked the Inspector to have a drink, and he (witness) told him, "Don't be so cheeky; that's the Inspector." The men walked out of the house right enough, and he went with them to the surgery, but the doctor was not in.—William Johnson and Hugh Troncy, barmen, denied having served the men with drink.— Frank Dixon, who had never been in a police court in his life, said the men were not drunk. There were a lot of men in the bar, but there was no noise.—Themas Parkes, a flatman, said he knew both men, and they had given their proper names. The men were not drunk. A third man said he had paid for the beer.—The Bench said they thought the case proved.—lnspecter Honing- worth said the defendant was a respectable man, and tried to conduct his house properly. He had seen the rules referred to, and it must have been an oversight as the servants of the firm were liable to instant dismissal for serving a drunken man.—Mr. Reynolds said the magistrates were aware of the great diftculty there was in conducting licensed houses. It was not a question of harassing the trade at ; but there was ho doubt in this case and they had no hesitation in inflicting a fine of 1.3., and costs 16 6d. The license would not be endorse& —Superintendent Hollingworth asked whether under the- circumstances he might not withdraw the second case.— Mr. Lewin said if the firm decided to appeal he supposed he could give notice to the clerk in the ordinary course. —Superintendent Hollingworth then withdrew hie. ap- plication and said he would go on with the second, case. —Mr. Lewin contended that he had already withdrawn it, but the magistrates upheld thesuperintendent.—Ulti- mately it was decided to adjourn the second ease for a fortnight.—Mr. Lewitt: If we don't appeal I unde- stand we have heard the last of it.—Mr. Ashton (magis- trates' clerk) : No, no.—Mr. Reynolds said the license would not be endorsed.

div.head: "FROM CABIN BOY TO CAPTAIN."
div.p: "FROM CABIN BOY TO CAPTAIN."

"If I had paid ten pounds a bottle for Warner's SAYE Cure it would have been cheap, as to it I owe my life," exclaimed Captain Paige, of 5, Southwell Grove Road, Leytonstone, Essex, who has recently been completely restored to health, after years of sickness, by the use of this medicine. The cap- tain's story is an interesting one, and we give it in his own words: "Ever since a child I have lived upon the water, rising from cabin-boy to captain. I visited nearly every part of the globe, having no ill-health for more than twenty years; but whon trouble came it attacked me in the shape of sharp, acute, knife-like pains in the right side. Th.se at times were so severe that I would involuntarily fall on the deck, and was obliged to be carried below. At last I was obliged to leave my ship and return home. The doctor,' said I had muscular rheumatism. They did no good, and I slowly grew worse. Finally I consulted the physicians at the hospital, who, on making an examination of my water, said my case was hopeless, and that they could do me no good. My own medical man informed my family that I might last a month, but there was no hope of recovery. While in this deplorable condition my son procured me a bottle of Warner's SAFE Cure. I took the medicine faithfully, and at the end of ten days was very much better, and by a month able to walk some distance. After taking it contimsously for a few months my health was com- pletely restored. I eat and sleep well, have not a pain nor ache, and have dumb-founded my friends by my re- covery and cure. I recommend the medicine far and near, and take pleasure at all times in letting people know of its wonderful virtues."

WARRINGTON V. STOI-KPO aT (2ND ELEVENS).—PIayed at Stockport on Saturday, and resulted in an easy win for Warrington, owing to the fine batting of Warburton and the excellent bowling of Russell and Unsworth. Warrington, having won the toss, commenced disas- trously, Adamson being well caught at short slip off the first delivery, and four wickets were down for 27 runs. On Spinks joining Warburton a good stand was made, the latter being in good hitting form. The scoring was very fast, 76 runs being scored before the fifth wicket fell, Spinks having played well for 23. The remaining batsmen materially helped to raise the score, the ninth wicket falling at 166, after having put on 36 runs. War- burton made 88 by some really good hitting. Thompson played good cricket for his 16, but was unfortunately run out, the innings closing for 170, a very good total considering the bad start of the innings. Unsworth bowled the first over for the visitors, and after being hit for four, had his revenge, Bailey beim,' finely caught by Voisey at cover point. The home team wickets fell quickly, the second and third being down for 12, the bowling being rather too good for the hatSmen ; six wickets for 34 looked well for a win for Warrington, and in one hour the home team were all out for 48; the top scorer being J. Burrows, 13 not out, but he was missed at the boundary early in his innings. The bowling analysis read as follows :—Unsworth, 9 overs, 4 wickets, 27 runs; Russell, 82 overs, 3 maidens, 6 wickets, 15 runs. The victory of Warrington was rather unexpected although well deserved, as the team showed to much greater advantage at all points of the game,and for once the fielding of the visitors was excellent. -Score :—War' • rington, 170; Stockport, 48. WARRINGTON V. STOCK PC/RT.—Played at Warrington, on Saturday, and resulted in a victory for the visitors by 15 runs. An ea: ly start was made, the haime team bat- ting. Crosfield and Clarke were soon dismissed, the latter playing -a ball on. Tinsley (32) and Ford (26) hit merrily, eight fours and a six being quickly scored, and Ford was bowled. Tie iley stayed to 71, and was then out from a mis-hit. rodinore, Fleetwood, and Yonge hit freely.. The last-named was out through a misunder- standing. A. Brown was most successful with the ball for Stockport. The visitor, had two out for twenty, and then a long stand was made. At 50 Clarke smartly fielded the ball at cover and returned to Tinsley. Over anxiety by the wicket-keeper saved Hollins his wicket when it appeared impossible for him to get home. Cros- field went on at 78, and wickets fell quickly. Fleetwood was bowling well at this time, sending down five maidens in succession. MoLa,chlan was run out to a hit from Hollins which touched the bowler's hand and knocked down the wicket. Rollins was caught, and Brown saw the winning hit made. The innings closed for 125. Crosfield was very successful, five wicke s for 28 runs, and had he gone on sooner a different result might have been seen. Score:—

NOTES BY THE WAY.

Four county cricket matches were brought to a con- clusion on W,-(lnesday. At Nottingham Kent defeated Notts by six wicki.Ls. The other matches—The Austra- lians v. Yorkshire, Surrey v. Oxford University, and Marylebone Club and Ground v. Cambridge University —were drawn. On Saturday Prescot had to lower their flag to Stoney- croft, who scored 187, while the Prescot players were all dismissed for 91, the individual scoring being small. Huyton opposed Sefton, and, ping in first, hit up 172, of which H. Eccles scored 53. The game ended in a draw. Fleetwood, who is ;laving his first season as second pro- fessional of the Warrington Club, is making a reputation as being a" puzzler" with the ball. When he has a suitable wicket he is exceedingly difficult to play. On Saturday he fairly non-plussed the Stockport batters. , E. Ford, on of the best and most stylish batters of the Warrington Club, and who has just returned from the West Indies, has already shown that he has not lost any of his skill while away in the land of hot air and iced • water, for he knocked up 100 last week for his club in a match against Sixteen of Oxford and District without giving a chance. Ford is always willing to assist any club in Sal- Irday afternoon matches.—" Athletic News." The Warrington Cycling Club is prospering. It num- bers about forty irk. ushers, and when the weather per- mits there are enjoyable runs on Wednesdays and Satur- day. Warrington cyclists have been very much in evidence at the sports which have been held so far in the locality ; this season. In Hollins Allen it is quite clear the "good I old town" has a representative rider of the first rank. At Widnes festival Allen carried off with considerable ease the first prizes in both of the events which he con- tested, and last Saturday he again secured the premier places in the two bicycle races at St. Helens Junction sports. Not ordy that, but the only riders who could be said to have made good seconds were Garnett at Widnes, and Webster at St. Helens ,Junction both of these being Warrington cyclist,. It is tbe 0., noted, too, that Garnett won a first prize in a three mile race at Widnes in an easy fashion.

A meeting of Liv, ,pool magistrates was held on Wed- nesday, when a committee of five was Appointed to inquire into the state of the law affecting disorderly houses in the city and the best mode of putting them in _force.

div.head: RETURN OF THE VOLUNTEERS.
div.p: RETURN OF THE VOLUNTEERS.

The Warrington Volunteers returned from South- port on Saturday afternoon, after spending a week under canvas at that pleasant s-aside resort. On the night of the last day of their stay in camp, the Commanding Officor played tlae men a nice little trick in order to test their alertness in case of an emergency. After they had all turned in for the night, and the lights had been extinguished, they I were suddenly startled by the bugle sounding the "assembly." Dressing as they went, the men hur- ried on to the parade ground, where the battalion was formed in line. Colonel Greenall then compli- mented the battalion on the alacrity that had been displayed in response to the summons, which, he added, was only given to see how the men would act in case of a night attack. They then returned to their tents, and resumed their disturbed slum- bers. The arrival of the battalion at the Central Station shortly after five o'clock was witnessed by a considerable nunaber of people, who had assembled in Horsemarket and Winwick-streets, and when the "citizen soldiers" marehed through the town to headquarters there was quite a rush of people to see them. Before being dismissed the men, who looked ' all the better for their camp experience, were ad- dressed by _ _ .

Colonel GREENALL, who expressed his gratification and pleasure at their behaviour during the week's encamp- ment. They would remember that he told them their object in going into camp was to learn duty and discip- line, and he had been very gratified to find that they had all, from the highest officer to the lowest man in the ranks, most willingly and, he might say, ably done their duty. He understood that the work some of them were called upon to do was somewhat severe, but it was neces- sary if they wished to have a proper knowledge of their duties. They had one and all worked, and worked with , a will; and he thanked them most sincerely for the sup- port they had rendered him. He took it that they had all enjoyed their outing, and would like to go into camp another year, all being well. It would, however, depend upon them whether they did or not. If they earned the capitation money for the corps they would be in a posi- tion to go to Strensall, or some other place. Arrange- ments had been made with the Widnes corps to allow the Warrington volunteers the use of their range, and he sincerely hoped that they would all take advantage of the opportunity which would be afforded them for prac- tice. Whilst in camp he had not had to inflict any severe punishment upon any of the men for misconduct. There had not been a single case of drunkenness brought under his notice, and the offences which had been brought forward were—although, of course, offences—of a trivial character. They should be very proud of such a fact, as, he could assure them, he was. (Cheers.) It only remained for him once more to thank them—from the Adjutant downwards. To Captain Adam he felt that much of the credit which was showered upon them by the Inspecting Officer on Friday was due—(cheers)— also to the energetic sergeant-major—(cheers)—the officers, staff officers, and the non-commissioned officers, as well as to the quarter-master for his excellent arrange- ments. (Cheers.) He thanked them earnestly for their personal kindness to him, and for their consideration; but above all, and chiefly, for the way in which they had carried out their soldiers' duties during their absence from Warrington. (Cheers.) r The men then dispersed,

div.head: WARRINGTON TRAINING COLLEGE.
div.p: WARRINGTON TRAINING COLLEGE.

The triennial re-union of past and present stu- dents of this college was held on Saturday, when there were about 400 students present, in addition to a number of clergymen. The proceedings of the day were commenced by a service that was held in the Parish Church. It was conducted by the Rev. Morley Stevenson, Principal of the College, who was accompanied by the Rector of Warrington (Rev. F. W. Willis), the Rev. J. A. Drummond, curate-in- charge of St. Elphin's ; the Rev. 0. P. Whalley, curate of St. James', Latchford ; and the Rev. Canon Gore, vicar of Bowdon and archdeacon of Maccles- field, by whom the sermon was preached. The prayers were read by the Rev. M. Stevenson, the first lesson by the Rev. 0. P. Whalley, and the second by the Rev. J. A. Drummond. An an- them by Mendelssolin was sung, the solos being taken by two of the students of the College. J. L. Hopkins' festal " Te Deum" was also sung, Mr. W. S. Woods presiding at the organ. The preacher ; selected as the subject of his discourse the words, , "That your faith should not stand in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God "-1 Cor. ii. 5. In the course of an interesting sermon Canon Gore said that he did not undervalue the high standing intel- lectually to which the students of the college at- tained, nor would he make light of the immense responsibility which was laid upon them in respect to the intellectual training of the young. They would not, however, be able to do much sure and abiding work without spiritual aid. The Church had built her training colleges because she desired that her children should be trained up in the know- ledge of religion. If it was important to teach the children, it was still more important to teach the teachers, in order that they might go to their work good women, grounded in the faith, intelligent in apprehending it, and diligent in practising it. The importance of this careful training was greater than ever to-clay, for the reason that they did not always find themselves placed in schools where the full, and definite, and dogmatic teaching of the faith was permitted. It might be that they were only allowed to give a Bible lesson, perhaps only to read the Bible. He was glad that such positions should be occupied by devout daughters of the Church, for in such cases everything depended upon the personal character of the teacher and the tone of her teach- ing. She would not seek to make proselytes, that would be dishonourable, but she could not fail to impress children with the supreme importance and attractiveness of the word of God.

Afterwards luncheon was served in the Practising SchooLs, Hamilton-st. The Dean of Chester occupied the chair, and amongst those who had accepted invitations to be present were :—Archdeacons Anson and Gore. the Rev. Canons Warr, Tonge, Dodd, Stowell, Maclure, the Rev. F. W. and Mrs. Willis, the Rev. M. and Mrs. Stevenson, the Rev. J. J. and Mrs. Langharn, the Rev. T. A. Rushton, the Rev J. J. Scott (Manchester), the Rev. J. A. Drummond, the Rev. B. B. Prescott,,the Rev. A. P. Holme, the Rev. I. Phillips, the Rev. S. and Mrs. Wilkinson, the Rev. 0. P. Whalley, the Rev. L. J. T. Darwall, Mr. John Tinsley, Dr. and Mrs. Sherratt, Dr. and Mrs. Adams, Dr. and Mrs. McFall, Mr. H. G. Crews, Miss Crews, Mr. G. Harwood, Major Linton, Zr., Mrs., and Miss Buckton, Miss Bell, Dr. and Mrs. Witkins, Mr. C. Twiss, Councillor R. W. Francomb, Councillor J. E. Wright, Mr. and Mrs. Pearse, Mr. and Mrs. Cawley, and Mr. Scott Coward. The caterer was Mr. T. 0. Speak- man, of the Saracen's Head Hotel. Wilderspool.—After the health of "The Queen" had been honoured, Mr. BucaTom proposed the health of " The preacher of the day." In responding Archdeacon Goan wished long life and prosperity to the institution that had that day gathered together her past and present student.—The CHAIRMAN proposed "Pros- perity to the Training College." In doing so he said that he was well aware that their college, graced as it was now by its own private chapel, with the regular call to daily worship, was laying a foundation which would stand every student in good stead during her after life. He wished to assure the teachers that the clergy followed them with sympathy and goodwill into theirwork where- ever they w,ould take it up—work for God and for their country—not an empty sympathy, but a real sympathy, watching their progress with interest and prayerfulness, doing what in them lay in their various stations that the influences around them might at least soften the difficul- ties ot their lot, and enable them to maintain with cheer- fulness the somewhat monotonous requirements of the code. But let them fot a moment forget codes, and merge themselves entirely in the thought of the great- ness, the dignity, the nobility, and the reward that awaited their work, for it was quite right that those who were labouring for the young should have their full and competent reward here. But they would allow him to repeat that the great reward was that which was yet to come, when every faithful service would be recognised by Him who alone could judge of what service was. Whatever gifts they might have, they had not the gift of balancing difficulties ; they had not the gift of exactly appraising all the adverse circumstances under which work was done. He was sure that those who had returned to Warrington that day to enjoy the friendships which had been knit in the Training College at Warrington would readily join heartily and with one voice in wishing' con- tinued prosperity to an institution to which they were conscious they owed much. In respond- ing to the toast, the Rev. M. STEVENSON re- ferred to the loyalty of the students, who did not forget the college where they had received their training. He was glad to see the Dean of Chester present; for the col- lege had no truer friend than he. He was also glad to welcome the new rector of Warrington, and he hoped that in the future they would always have the constant support and ready sympathy of Mr. Willis. (Applause.) Two important events had happened since they met three years ago one was the building of the chapel, and the other the building of the practising school. He supposed that if there was a cloud upon the educational world at present it was that they seemed to be rapidly approaching the time when the supply of teachers was perhaps exceeding the demand. If there had been any difficulty in the way of the prosperity of the college it had arisen from that. Not that they had very much to complain of, but still there was a certain difficulty in finding suitable positions for those who left the college, and some had to wait a while before they got places. Past students might give valuable assis- tance in this respect by notifying him of any vacancies that came under their notice. Mr. COWARD, in the course of a short address, said that the

judgment he had formed of the work done by the stu- dents of the College was very favourable, and it had grown year by year. The College was exercising a moral influence throughout the country in the character, demeanour, and devotion to duty of the students; in fact, he did not think any man could bear a higher moral testimony than he was ready to bear in the face of the world. The College was also doing a good work for edu- cation. They must not allow petty jealousies of other schools, especially Board schools, to mar their peace and harmony in the work in which they were engaged. (Hear, hear.) Whether they admitted it or not, the School Board system was a powerful factor in the edu- cational system, and, furthermore, it was slowly, but surely, making ground. He advised them to do away with petty jealousies, and wished to see the schools made—rather more than they were now—great mind- moulding places—Canon MACLURE proposed the health of "The visitors," coupling with the toast the name of the Rev. F. W. Willis, the new Rector of Warrington. He predicted that the College, if conducted on sound prin- ciples and judiciously managed, would have a long and prosperous career. The RECTOR, in reply, after thanking those present for the welcome they had accorded to him, spoke of the close connection between religion and edu- cation.—The Rev. J. J. SCOTT proposed the health of "The Chairman," who briefly acknowledged the com- pliment. . . _

A return was then made to the College, where Mr. Birtles, photographer, of Sankey-st., took photographs in groups of all present, then of the past students, and then of the present students. Tea was then dispensed, a,14:1 a concert followed. Mr. W. S. Woods was the ac- companist. - The room was afterwards cleared for dan- cing.

div.head: EXAMINVIt, SATITRD.AY, JUNE 30, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINVIt, SATITRD.AY, JUNE 30, 1888.
THE SHIP CANAL WORKS AND HOW THEY WILL AFFECT WARRINGTON AND THE DISTRICT.
NO. 24.-FROII THE WEAVER TO EASTHAM.

From the point where the canal strikes Prod- sham Score at the mouth of the Weaver, it will run its course westward through Frodsham Lordship and across the channel of the stream known as Holpool Gutter. The waters of the "Gutter" will be impounded in the canal, and at this point an embankment will be formed on the northern side of the canal. This embankment will be only a short one—some two and a half chains In length. Its western end will be placed at the east corner of the most northerly of the two powder magazines situate near the junction of the Holpool Gutter with the estuary of the Mersey. Some distance westwards the canal will encroach upon one of the numerous indentations of the Mersey estuary, and here another embankment will be necessary on the northern side. This embankment will be some five furlongs and nine chains in length, and its western termination will be a little over three furlongs to the east of the Ferry House at Ince. Past this ferry, and until it reaches Ince Lighthouse, the canal will run through the mainland, after which the natural and artificial waterways will again for over a mile be separated by an embankment stretching from near Ince Lighthouse to the base of the triangular piece of land known as Stanlow Point, on the apex of which are the remains of an ancient abbey. .

div.head: STANLOW ABBEY.
div.p: STANLOW ABBEY.

Of this Abbey we are told that it was "Founded by John, Constable of Chester, on the eve of his pilgrimage to the Holy Land, in 1178. It was of the Cistercian order, its site being near the confluence of the Gowy and the Mersey, in one of the most miserable and sterile parts of Ches- hire. For nearly half a century after its founda- tion nothing is recorded of the progress of the monastery, but later on we hear that it grew rich at the expense of the De Lacies, and other wealthy families, who added to the original endowment. The advowsons of the churches of Rochdale, Blackburn, Eccles, and Whalley, with extensive lands in the two counties of Cheshire and Lancashire, in time became annexed to their possessions. The monks were be- ginning to grow rich, and at the same time dissatis- fied with their dreary abode at Stanlaw, and they longed for a translation to a more congenial site. Moreover, in 1279 the sea broke in upon them, did great damage to the abbey, and washed away the bridge leading from Stanlaw to Chester, thereby in- terrupting their communication. 1287 the great tower of the chyrch was blown down, and two years la,ter both lire and flood nearly destroyed the edi- fice. All these misfortunes tended ta add to the disgust of the monks, and they determined to peti- tion the Pope for permission to remove to Whalley. He acceded to their request, and in 1289 a bull was issued authorising their translation, and empower- them to appropriate the revenues of Whalley Church and its dependencies, on the condition of endowing a sufficient vicarage whenever the opportunity should be afforded by the resignation or death of the then incumbent.'

Near Stanlow Point the canal rill intersect the bed of the river Gowy, and an embankment will be made to stretch from one bank of the Gowy to the other. Still going westward, the canal will run through the townships of Great Stanney and Whitby, this latter township affording the basis for the eastern end of an embankment which stretches westward past Ellesmere Port, and has its other end in the township of Nethe,rpool. Opposite Elles- mere, locks will be made through this embankment to permit of a passage between the canal and the Mersey. The last embankment, it we trace the canal from Manchester westward, or the first, if we start at Eastham and go inland, will have one of its ends at Eastham, where the canal itself be- gins, and the other end in the township of Nether- pool. This embankment will be raised upon the foreshore or bed of the Mersey, and will be about two and a half miles in length. THE INCE HALL ESTATES. _

For the protection of Ince Hall Estates, it is laid down that the owner shall be entitled at all times to use the canal between the Holpool Gutter and the river Gowy, and also between Holpool Gutter and the nearest lock or entrance from the canal into the Mersey estuary, situate west of the "Gut- ter," free of toll for the carriage or conveyance of agricultural produce from the estates, or of build- ing materials to be used upon the estates, in any barge not exceeding one hundred tons belonging to or hired by the owner. The Canal Company are under an obligation to construct and maintain a wharf or landing place on the south. side of the canal for the use of, free of wharfage dues, the owner of the Ince estates, and his tenants and workmen. The use of this wharfiwill, however, be subject to any reasonable bye-laws made by the Company and approved by the Board of Trade. In order to provide an access from the south to Ince ferry, the Company will maintain, near the place where the canal intersects the present road leading •to the ferry, a boat of sufficient capacity to convey carriages, carts, horses, and passengers across the canal. The Company will provide the necessary ' labour for working this boat by night or by day, and free of toll and charges so far, at all events, as the owner and tenants of the Ince Hall estates are concerned. To this ferry suitable approaches. having "reasonable gradients," will be made by the Canal Company on each side of the canal, and dur- ing the progress of the works some temporary means of crossing the canal will have to be devised by the Company if they are requested to do so by the owner of the estates. THE DEAN AND CHAPTER OF CHESTER. The rights of the Dean and Chapter of Chester, who own lands in the townships of Great Stanney, Little Stanney, Stoke, and Stanlow, are variously provided for. Subject to reasonable bye-laws, made by the Company, the Dean and Chapter and their tenants and agents are to be entitled, free from all dues and charges, to abstract and use for manufac- turing or agricultural purposes, the water in the canal, and to empty surface drains and waste water therein. The estate of the Dean and Chapter is, like the Ince Hall estate, to be provided with a wharf for the landing, free of charge, of manure and other materials to be used in the cultivation of the land. No land purchased by the company on this estate is to be used for any trade or business which will be injurious or prejudicial to the remainder of the estate, and the Dean and Chapter have the right of pre-emption over all lands purchased from them which may not be required by the company for the purposes of the canal or its incidental works, ex- cepting such as lies to the north of the canal, or that on the south of the canal, which has been parcliased by the company, at the request of the Dean and Chapter, under a particular section of the

EASTHAM.

' There are now five steam navvies at work in the second lift at Eastham. The noise and smoke from ten steam navvies, on this section, and a score of locomotives run- ning about with 200 or 300 wagons, is very great, and gives the place the appearance and sound of some great foundry. On this section, and mostly in the yard at Eastham, are engine sheds, joiners' shops, brickyard,

blacksmith's shop, with four fires and steam hammer working night and day, large cement shed, pumping machinery, fitting shop, containing drilling and planing machines, which will be shortly augmented by other machinery, offices, storerooms, mission-room to hold 200 to 300, and 72 huts, each hut large enough for a family and some eight to twelve lodgers in additio%. Altogether there are now on this section alone upwardsof 1,800 men. I larger and more permanent mission-room is to be built. Great progress has been made with the embank- ment across the estuary, which will be upwards of a mile and a half in length. The bottom part of the outer side of the embankment has been laid, with the ex- ception of about 250 yards in the deepest part, and the foundation of the inner or land-side embankment has been put in for half a mile or so. ELLESMERE PORT, Sm. _

At Ellesmere Port the number of buildings are being rapidly increased, in order to find convenience for the men, some of whom have to walk as much as five miles to lodgings. Two steam navvies are at work at Stanlow Point, and a large number of huts have been built. Upwards of 800 men are employed here, and 400 are at work between Ince and Weston Point. A German navvy has arrived and will be put in a cuttini; to be made on the Ince side of the river Weaver. LANDSLIP AT INCE.

A landslip, the second that has -oc.curred on this section, took place on Saturday at the Manchester Ship Canal Works at Ice. The slip happened while the men were at work, but fortunately none of them were injured. The earth, hoover, fell upon and displaced a line of rail on an important part of the sec- tion, over which large quantities of earth were drawn. A gang of men had at once to be sot to work, but it was some considerable time before the rails were replaced to enable the traffic to be resumed. Some hundreds of tons of earth were displaced.

- SALFORD DOCK. The works in Salford are being vigorously proceeded with. There are now 400 men at work in three large cuttings in connection with the Salford Dock, at Traf- ford-road, with three steam navvies, seven locomotives, and seven steam cranes. The dock will contain 26ft. of water, and already the full depth has been excavated in some places. A line of railway is being laid for the pur- pose of connecting the Salford works with Barton, and there will shortly be railway communication throughout the entire length of the canal. There are 1,000 men em- ployed on the Mode Wheel, Barton, and Eccles section.

div.head: NEW BILL.
div.p: THE NEW BILL.

The bill promoted by the Manchester Ship Canal Com- pany for the purpose of enabling them to make certain alterations in the works will be considered by a Select Committee of the House of Commons on Tuesday next. The Committee will consist of Mr. Maram (chairman), Sir T. Lawrence, Mr. J. Stuart, and Mr. Joseph Howard.

DISCOVERY OF A ROMAN PATHVVAY. What is supposed to have been a Roman pathway has been discovered during the cutting operations at Nether- pool, between Ince and Eastham. An antiquarian writer who has visited the place states that there is no doubt that the road dates back to a very remote age. He pro- ceeds—' It consists of 4,5, and 8 inch boulders, edged with rough hewn ashlers 6 inches thick, and 10 to 12 inches deep, varying in length. The stones are im- bedded on a bank of clay of about 12 to 18 inches deep; this would seem to indicate that it was thus raised up by the side of the stream, as it lies on the old Lias clay, and the debris caused by the overflow of the stream. To fix the :period of its- formation must, we fear, ever re- main a mystery. MANCHESTER GEOGRAPHICAL SOCIETY.

As the result of a special invitation, about 180 members of this society paid a visit to Eastham on Saturday for the purpose of inspecting the progress of the canal works in the immediate neighbourhood. A special steamer conveyed the members to Ellesmere Port, where they were met by guides who conducted them over the works between that place and Eastham. Great interest was shown by the visitors in the gigantic undertaking, and the visit was evidently a source of general interest to all who were present. Mr. T. W. Thompson, proprietor of the Eastham Ferry, was entrusted with the catering, and his efforts gave the greatest satisfaction. The passenger traffic to the "Richmond of the Mersey" during the season beats the record of any previous year, the Man- chester Ship Canal operations adding greatly to the at- tractiveness of this delightful trip. A HAWKERS NARROW ESCAPE. The other day a hawker, named Mary Murphy, was going from hut to hut, on the Eastham section of the canal, selling drapery, when her business took her for a short distance along the route. She had not proceeded far when an engine running for water overtook her. She was walking along the side of the route where, if the had remained, she would have been in perfect safety. In- stead of so doing, however, when the engine was close to her she stepped into the four-foot and was instantly knocked down, the machinery of the engine pushing her along the sleepers. When the engine stopped she was half-way under it, and everyone thought she would be completely mangled, but when she was taken out it was found that her toes only were injured. She was run on an engine to the Ellesmere Port Hospital and put to bed, but it was not found necessary to detain her, so she was sent to her home in Liverpool on Tuesday morning. Her injuries consisted of a crushed too and rather a severe bruise on the back. A PROMISING FORECAST. The" Ship Canal News "says :—We have pleasure in again reporting an increase in the Manchester Ship Canal shares. A rise of six shillings in a fortnight speaks well for the undertaking, and shows the increased favour with which it is being received by the public. The threatened opposition which has sprung up from several parties, to the Bill now before Parliament for altering the boundaries of Stretford and Salford, and for re- arranging the Manchester and Salford Docks, is not of any vital importance, and the differences will, it is be- lieved, be easily arranged to the satisfaction of all par- ties, and without the company havingseriously to depart from their proposed plans. Respecting the progress of the works, there is everything favourable to report. The fine weather which we have had for the last two months has enabled the contractor to make great progress, and we believe we shall be within the mark in stating that the displacement of earth, rock, ,kc., for the month of June will show half as much again as the month of May, or a total of 1,500,000 cubic yards. This will compare very favourably with the cutting on what is supposed to be a much greater undertaking—the Panama Canal. From figures before us we find that the total displace- ment for May on this work is 1,655,810 cubic yards, or only about 10 per ceat. more than on the Manchester Ship Canal. This amount, large as it is for our canal, will, before the summer ends be increased up to 2,000,000 cubic yards per month. At this rate, after allowing for the drawback of wintry weather, the cut- ting of the canal will be complete in about three years' time, anel the contractor will in the meantime have suf- ficient help to make the locks, docks quays, and rail- way deviations, so as to have the canal ready for traffic by the required time."

TRUTH STRANGER THAN FICTION. The -a- "Captain's African Bride" over and over again has what appeared to be the most preposterous flights of a novel- ist's imagination, proved to be either founded upon or subse- quently'justified by actual facts. James Payne's story of "Lost Sir Massingberd "Is a well-known case in point; the circumstances delineated in the chief incident in the tale ac- tually occurring some time after the publication of the story. The strange story of Commander Bethel's dusky bride and her claims to an important estate in England, would, if it had first appeared in ao novel, have beeii pooh-poohed as out of reason. Other no less well-established facts are every day pooh- poohed. For instance, some people are yet foolish enough to look upon the virtues claimed for Gwilym Evans Quinine ' Bitters as fiction, whereas they are really only the sober truth. ' That Affections of the Chest, Indigestion in every form, Liver Complaint, and Nervous Disorders have been cured by this unequalled medicine is every day proved in the experi- ence of hundreds. Read the following testimony, authenti- cated names and addresses, of well-known persons :—Sir Thomas Williams, 6, Wayne-street, Gadlys, Aberdare, under date August 27th, 1887, writes:—" Dear sir,—My son has been suffering from debility these last two years, and could not find any benefit until he tried your wonderful medicine. We tried all doctors, but of no avail." Mr. Isaac Davies, 10, Church-street, Pendarew, March 4th, len, says Dear sir,—l have been suffering for years from bronchitis, and I have tried ati kinds of medicine without relief, until I was Induced to try your Quinine Bitters. I find your medicine agrees with me splendidly, and I sincerely thank you for your great discovery."
