POLICE INTELLIGENCE.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT-.

SATURDAY.—Before Aldermen Chandley and Burgess. DESERTION BY A FATHER.—Thomas Ridia,rd, Sankey Bridges, was charged with having on thel6th November. 1887. deserted his child, leaving it chargeable to the Warrington Union. The Bench committed him to gaol for one month with hard labour.

HER HEAD WAS AFFECTED.—SeIina Rowbottom, (19), Who lives at 303, Winwick-road. was charged on remand with stealing from the stall of James West, Market Place, at midnight, on Thursday, a pair of gloves, value Is, and from the stall of Joseph Frisby, on the same evening, a pair of shoes, value 3s 6d. Thecase having been proved. it was urged for the defence that the girl's head was affected, and that she was unaccountable for her actions. The prisoner's conduct in court appearing to bear out this statement, the Chairman said that the Bench had de- cided not to send the prisoner to gaol, but he reminded her mother of the serious responsibility resting upon her- self, warning her that the next time her daughter would be committed to prison. MONDAY.—Before Aldermen Davies and:Holmes. DRUNKENNESS. The following persons were dealt with for this offence : Sarah Massey, Michael Kelly, Thomas Oates, and James Curley, in Bridge-st., on Sat- urday night, fined 5s and costs each; James Rostock and James Mochin, in Dial-st., on Sunday morning, fined 5s and costs each; Michael Craghan, in Horsemarket-st., on the 11th June, fined 10s, including costs; Hannah Cooke, in Wilderspool-road, on the 16th mat, fined 5s and costs; Sarah Percival alias Riley,. in Turner-st., on the 19th, dis- charged; John Potts, in Orford-st., on the 19th, fined 3.3 6d, including costs. HIS EIGHTY-SEVENTII APPEARANCE.—John Rohan was charged with having been drunk and disorderly at the Police Station, on Saturday night. The Chief Constable stated that it was the defendant's 87th appearance. The magistrates, however, as he had been teetotal for some weeks, decided to dismiss the case in order to give defen- dant another chance.

SAVING UP FOR A SPREB.—Sarah Burke, for having been drunk in Hill-st., on the 14th and 15th of June respec- tively, was ned 5s and costs in each case. The Chief Constable stated that defendant and her husband worked nard for some time and then with the money carted they had a spree. The husband corroborated the statement, explaining to the Bench that they were teetotal but when one " broke " the other "broke." WEDDED MISERY.—Moses Guise was charged with having assaulted Emily Guise, his wife. Mr. Hunt (Chief Constable) said that the pair had only been married twelve months, and disagreed continually. Both had hot tempers, and complainant was very unforgiving. The defendant bore an excellent character from the place where he was employed. Complainant was defendant's third wife.—Alderman Davies (to the defendant) : Well, you can't expect to have three good ones,—Defendant was bound over in his own recog,nisances of £5 to keep the peace for 6 months.

PUGILISTS.—John Shaughnessy, Patrick Shaughnessy, and Thomas Hogherty were fined ss, 10s, and 5s respec- tively, for fighting in Dial-st., on the 27th inst. William Connor was fined 3s 8d for fighting in the Swan entry on the 18th. Defendant pleaded in extenuation that it was "holiday time."

A Loo LlST.—Timothy Costello was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Ship Yard, on Sun- day.—Alderman Davies : I see that you have been fud- dling, fighting, and otherwise getting into trouble for twenty-one years. We shall fige you lOs aid costs, or, in default, 14 days' imprisonm6ht. ASSAULTING A FATHER.—Winifred McGuire was charged with having assaulted Michael Tully, her father, on the 11th of June. She was bound over to keep the peace for six months in her own recognisances of £5. CIIIMNEYONFIRE.—James Hodgkinson was fined 2s 6d for having allowed the chimney of his premises, in Bridge- st., to be on fire on the 18th inst.

6217ELTY TO A HOESE.—John Owen was charged with having illtreated and tortured a horse by working it when in an unfit state. Inspector Aplin R.S.P.C.A., who pro- secuted, said that defendant had promised he would not work the horse again and he would be satisfied if the defendant paid the costs. This having been done, the case was dismissed.

Wl',rut TRESPASS.—Edward Howard, a youth aged about 18, was charged with wilfully damaging, to the amount of Bd, growing grass belonging to Mr. James Lunt. The Chief Constable said that he had received numerous complaints about trespassing on the field in question, which was situated off Salisbury-st. A great number of young men went there to play cards, and pitch and toss, getting into the field by jumping the ad- joining wall, which was quite seven feet high. Defen- dant was fined lOs and costs.

Tuesday.—Before Alderman Pickmere. Drarysit AND DISORDERLY.—Francis Riley was brought up in custody charged with this offence, in Winwick-st., on the previous night. She was discharged on promising to take the pledge. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. John Fairclough. DiuncKENNEss.—James Toole, Foundry-st., was fined 108 and costs for having been drunk and disorderly in Scotland-road, on the previous day, and Michael Griffin, of no settled abode, was fined ss, including casts, for a similar offence in Buttermarket-st. Eliza Smith, for having been drunk and disorderly in Dallam-lane on the night previous, was fined lOs and costs _ .
, 'THURSDAY.—Before Major Litton and Alderman Webster.

ASSAULT ON A FATHER.—DanieI O'Loughlin, a young man, was summoned for having assaulted his father on the 23rd June. Complainant stated that his son hit him on the eye and knocked him down, but defendant asser- ted that he only interfered to prevent his mother being assaulted by complainant. The magistrates ordered de- fendant to find a surety in the sum of £5 for his good be- haviour for six months, and to pay I2s 6d costs, or in default, to be imprisoned for fourteen days. PRIINECENNESS.—DanieI Crosby made his 59th appear- anbe for this offence, and was sent to prison for a month. William Cuff was fined 5s and costs for having been drunk whilst in charge of a horse and trap, on the previous day, in Buttermarket-st. •

• FuznAy.liefore Alderman Harrison and Dr. Gornall. , DRINK AND VIDLENCE.—George Tones was brought up in custody on a charge of having been drunk and dis- orderly in Mersey-st., on the previous night, and of hay • ing assaulted P.C. Chantler, by whom he was arrested. A fine of lOs and costs, or 14 days' imprisonment was imposed.

ASSAULT CASES.—Michael Butler was summoned for having assaulted Patrick Ganley, a pensioner, on the 22nd instant. He was ordered to be bound over to be of good behaviour for six mgnths, himself in £lO, and one surety of £lO, and to payl.2s 6d costs. In default of so doing, he was to go to prison for 14 days.—Ed. Webster was summoned by his wife Ellen for having assaulted her on the 22nd inst. He was bound over to keep the peace for six mohths, himself in £lO, and one surety in £lO, or, in default, fourteen days' imprisonment. He had also to pay costs.—Annie Chrimes was summoned for having assaulted Annie Littlewood on the 25th inst. Defendant said that the affair arose in regard to a quar- rel about the children of the respective parties. She alleged that complainant struck her first. The case was dismissed, each party to pay 2s each, court costs.—John iLongshaw was summoned for having assaulted Eliza- beth Longshaw, a relative by marriage, on the 24th inst. He was also summoned for having assaulted ,James Hunt on the 26th instant. For the first offence he was ordered to be bound over to keep the peace for six months, himself in £lO, and one surety of £lO, or go to prison for fourteen days. He had also to pay 13s 6d costs. For the second offence he was fined 40s and costs, or, in default, another fourteen days' imprisonment.— I A lad named George Bloomfield was summoned for hav- ing assaithed another lad named James Buckley Mellor, ,on the 25th instant. It was alleged that defendant threw a piece of glass at the other boy, which cut his foot. The case was settled on Mrs. Bloomfield paying £1 as compensation, and 3s 6d, the costs. In connection with the same case James Buckley was summoned for having used threatening languageto Mrs. Blobmfield. He was bound over in his own recognisances of £lO, to keep the peace for six months, and ordered to pay the costs. —Thomas Robinson, summoned for having, on the 25th inst., assaulted his daughter-in-law, Catherine Robinson, was dismissed.

THREATS.—WiIIiam and Catherine Cunningham were summoned for having used threats towards Michael Jeffries on the 25th inst. The case was dismissed.—Alice Henshaw was summoned by Rebecca Chadwick for hav- ing used threats to her. She was ordered to be bound over to keep the peace for six months, in her own recog- nisances of £lO, and pay 12s costs DAMAGE.—Thomas Locker was summoned for having damaged a spring cart belonging to Richard Burrows on the 22nd inst. He was ordered to pay is costs, and 2s damage.

div.head: DARESBURY PETTY SESSIONS.
div.p: DARESBURY PETTY SESSIONS.
TUESDAY.—Before Messrs. E. Greenall, H. Marion, and H. Neild.

Don CASES.—John Sutciff,2, White-st., Warrington, was charged with having a dog at large on the North- wich-road, on the 28th May, and was fined is and costs. —John Joyce, for a similar offence, at Appleton, on the Ist June. is, and 8s 6d costs ; Charles Williamson, Whit- ley Inferior, Ist June Is and costs ; John Smith, 46, Ashton-st. Warrington, at Stretton, 3rd June, is and costs; Jolin Bate, of Latchford, at Walton Superior, 10th June, is and costs; John Richards, at Moore, 11th June, Is and costs.

DRUNKENNESS .—John Cliffe, labourer, was charged with two offences for drunkenness, on the first occasion at Appleton, on the 26th May, and on the second on the 11th June, on the Tarporley highway, 2s 6d and costs in each case.—John Clayton, labourer, for having been drunk at Appleton, on the 17th June, 5s and costs. Pin CASES—John Ashley was charged with having re- moved a pig from Thelwall to Warrington without a license. He was ordered to pay costs, 3s 6d ; Thomas 'Roberts, for removing a pig from Granpenhall, without a license, fined is, and 12s 6d costs ; Enoch Jackson, re- moving a pig without a license, at Bartington, on the 24th May, is and costs; John Barker, for removing three pigs, at Appleton, without a license, on the 14th June, is and costs; Joseph Boardman, for causing the same to be removed, is and costs. CARELESS DRIVING.—SamueI Houghton, for not hav- ing been in proper control of the horses of a dray, at Whitloy Inferior, was fined 5s and costs; William Hunt, for a similar offence at Stretton, on 11th June, 108 and costs, this being the second offence; John Toole, asleep
WARRINGTON RATEPAYERS' ASSOCIA- TION AND THE GAS QUESTION.

On Tuesday evening a meeting of the members of the Warrington Ratepayers' Association was held in the Workmen's Club Room, "to consider the pro- posals of the Corporation Gas Committee respeting changes consequent on Mr. Paterson's retirement." Mr. James Smethurst presided; there was not a very large attendance. Amongst others present were Councillors W. Pierpoint and F. Dixon; Messrs. G. Woods, J. McCollom; J. Walker, T. Jones, W. Roberts, R. Isherwood, S Davies, H. J. Langton, H. Thornton, J. Toft, W. Diggle, A. Woods, R. Twiss, Dr. Mackie, W. Walker (sec.), &c. The CHAIRMAN said it did not seem to him that the ratepayers of Warrington thought sufficient about the outgoings of their hard-earned money, or they would have had that meeting crowded. It was for that meeting to consider whether it was advisable to request the Mayor to call a public meeting of the inhabitants to consider the gas question. (Hear, hear.) After some conversation as to the advisability of calling a public meeting, MrI<IiLFRED WOODS said several gentlemen had been sent to the Town Council by the Ratepayers'Association to look aft& the interests of the ratepayers ; they had been put into that position at very little expense to them- selves, but at great expense to the association, and he considered they ought to be cailed upon to tell them what i they had done n the .7. Town Council and what they intended to to. (Hear, hear.) Mr. WILLIAM ROBERTS asked if any membes. of the Town Council had attended any of the meetings of the Ratepayers' Association since his election. (Hear, hear.) The CHAIRMAN said that some of the members of the Town Council had been most regular in their attendance. The gas question had been discussed several times. The committee of the association hadnot been idle, he assured them.

Mr. Jo rm WALKER asked if the rumour he had heard was true, that some of the members of the Town Council who were on the committee of the association had retired ? If so, how many, and why had they re- tired ?

The CHAIRMAN said Mr. J. E. Wright had retired, because, he supposed, the committee said something at their last meeting that he did not agree with. Thdy seemed to be treading on Mr. Wright's toes. He said he was not exactly a Ratepayers', Association candidate, but that -he went to the Council for the benefit of the whole of the ratepayers. Mr. WILLIAM ROBERTS said he was assured .by a mem- ber of the committee that one or two town councillors had not attended a single meeting since they were elected. If their secretary had a register of the atten- danee it would be very interesting to have it read. (Hear, hear.) Mr. W. WALKER (secretary) said be had not a tabula- ted statement of the attenclancesobut he must say that there were one or two rnbmbers of the Town Council who had not attended the meetings. With one or two exceptions, the others 'ad attended, as the Chairman had said.

The CHAIRMAN: Mr. Shaw Green has attended very regularly, Mr. Blackhurst has been to several meetings, and Mr. Percival had attended regularly. Mr. H. J. LONGTON moved the following resolu- tion, for presentation to the Mayor :—" We, the un- dersigned ratepayers of the Borough of Warrington, hereby respectfully request your Worship to con- vene a meeting of ratepayers to take into con- sideration the recommendations of the Gas Committee with reference to the future management of the Gas Works, and also to consider the position of the Sanita7 Committee." At the request of several gentlemen, it was, however, agreed to withdraw that part of the reso- lution referring to the Sanitary Committee. Mr. H. THoaraox seconded the motion. Mr. GEORGE WOODS said that the speeches made last week at the. meeting of the Ratepayers' Association Committee were nothing more or less than a series of mistakes—he did not say intentional mistakes, but they were certainly calculated to mislead the public generally. When the Corporation of Warrington took over the gas works the amount of gas consumed in the town was 125,000,000 of cubic feet • in the year 1886 the amount had increased to 185,000,000; and he was told on good authority that this year the consumption would not amount to far off 21:5,000,000 of cubic feet. If the Cor-

_ whilst in charge of a lorry, on the 12th June, at Stret- ton, Is and costs ; Richard Has4all, for a similar offence at Appleton, 13th June, 5s and costs. A LOCOMOTIVE DRIVER FINED. Edward Stoddart was charged with having driven a locomotive on two occasions between the hours of 7 p.m. and 3 a.m, in con- travention of the orders of the county authorities. The first offence was committed at 11-40 p.m. on the 16th inst, and the second at 8 p.m. on the 19th inst. It was stated that the defendant was employed by Mr. Walker, the Ship Canal contractor, and that the first offence was owing to the locomotive having stuck fast on the road at Moore; the second being due to a misunderstanding of the byelaws. In reply to the Bench, it was stated that Isuch an offence should not again be committed if it were possible to avoid it. A fine of 5s and costs was im- posed in each case.

- STRAYING Co—Wi.—Williarn Burgess was charged with having allowed cows to stray on the highway at Antro- bus, on the 19th June, and fined la and costs. LEAVING WORK WITHOUT NOTICE. A young man named Guest was charged by Mr. Dallow, cartwright, of London Bridge, for having left his employ without the requisite seven days' notice on the 25th May ; dam- ages were laid at ss. Mr. Browne appeared on behalf of the complainant. Defendant was ordered to pay the 5s and Costs. CLAIM AGAINST A DOMESTIC SERVANT.—William Whit- low, farmer, Preston Brook, claimed a sum of lOs 6d as damages from Alice Ann Speed, a general servant lately in his employ, for having left his service on the 11th June before the expiry of her term. Mr. W. Ht J. Jenkins appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Arthur Browne for defendant. The defence was that the girl had been obliged to leave in consequence of illness. After the case had been partly heard a suggestion, thrown out by the Chairman, was acted upon, and the case settled; each party to pay their own costs, and the girl to have her clothes returned and the balance of wages, less a slight reduction agreed upon, due to her.

WIDNES POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before Mr. G. Pilkington and Mr. J. Brock. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY .—For this offence the follo- wing were each fined 5s and costs :—Patrick Tivnan, 20, Iloward-st. ; Thomas Baguley, Alick-st. ; Marcilla Kelly, Sutton's-lane, and Elizaprennan, Sutton's-lane.—Patrick Killalea, a youth, of Sankey-st., Edward Jackson, of 37, Alforde-st, and Catherine Hynes, a well-known charac- ter, were charged with committing breaches of the peaCe at different times and places. Each defendant was bound over to be of good behaviour for three months, or go to gaol for 14 days. TICKET OF LEAVE.—Ellen Whaling, a convict at liberty on ticket-of-leave, was charged with failing to report herself, and she was committed to gaol to serve the re- mainder of her term.

RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS: MONDAY.—Before Mr. C. Reynolds and Major Hazlehurst. DRUNKENNESS.—John Ellis, John Brannon, and Patrick Kernon, were each fined 5s and costs for the offence. BREAca OF THE HIGHWAY ACT.—A fine of Is and costs, Eis 6d, was imposed upon Thomas Stevens, coal dealer, for using a cart without having his name painted on. WATER RATES.—At the instance of Mr. W. Wright, col- lector to the Runcorn, Weston, and Halton Waterworks Co., 43 persons were summoned for non-payment of the water rate. The rates had been since paid in 39, and orders to enfore payment in the remaining four cases were granted._ _ _

THi Does Wpm-L.—John Bebbington, of the Bridge Hotel, Ashridge-st., was fined 2s ed and costs for allow- ing his dog to be at large insecurely muzzled.—Edward Woodward, farmer, Norton, was summoned for a like offence. The muzzle was placed upon the dog in court, and Stephen Gibson swore that it was in exactly the same position as on the date for which the summons was issued. After the magistrates had examined the dog Mr. Reynolds said : I think we will dismiss this case.

WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. THURSDAY.—Before Mr. H. Wade Deacon. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—For ttlis offence the follow- ing persons were fined 55 and costs :—Daniel Lamb. Beamont-st. ; John Murty, 30, Major Cross-st. ; Patrick Garrity, Harrison's-row, Ditton. The following were each fined 7s 6d and costs :—John Roscoe, Church-st., Farnworth ; Bridget White, Caroline-st. ; and Albert Young, Charlotte-st.

BEACHES Or THE PEACE.—Peter Jones. of Vine-st.,and Patrick McCrush, of Midwood-st., were charged with creating a breach of the peace in Widnes-road on the 16th inst.—The defendant Jones said McCrush attacked him with a belt, and a gang that was with him set upon him. Evidence was given of this, and the charge was dis- missed against Jones. A warrant was issued for the ap- prehension of McCrash, who did not appear.—Ann Lawton, of 30, Water-st., and Mary Ann Wood, of 6, Sankey-st.' were charged with fighting together and creating a disturbance in Sankey-st. Lawton did not appear and a warrant was granted for her apprehension. Wood was bound over to 'keep the peace for three months. CHIMNEY ON FlRE.—James White, of Widnes-road, was fined is, and costs 4s, for allowing the chimney of his dwelling to be on fire. ABSENT MILITIAMEN.—John Burns and Michael Burke pleaded guilty to being absent without leave from the Liverpool Regiment 4th Battalion of Militia, stationed at Warrington. P.C. 700 said he met the prisoners walk- ing in the direction of Liverpool at two o'clock that • morning. The prisoners were remanded to Walton Gaol to await an escort.

ALLEGED DEFAMATION OF CHARACTER.—Mary Meaden, of 15, Eleanor-st., was summoned for using defamatory language to Elizabeth McCormick. The defendant said she knew nothing whatever against the character of Mrs McCormick and the case was dismissed.

" CADMUS " AGAIN. Sir,—ln my last letter I said that what " Cadmus " had previously written was too pitiful to waste much time upon • and I have "confirmation dire" in his re- ply. But I made no excuse, far from it, for any- thing I had said. And if I ant ashamed of anything, it is because I have been tempted to reply to his absurd puerilities. I have however, explained, without using say quotation, what I think of the man, or men, who would rob another of his living; and I have not seen any reply worth the name "A thief is a thief," no matter what else he may be called. That I have "a keen and infallible scent for literary offal" is "true as death," when carrion like "Cadmus" scatter it under my very nose; the malodorous (literary) fluid is skunk-like, and I thank him for that peculiarly applicable word! It's so appropriate to his case. lam accused of using muddy quotations. This sounds well, coming from a scribe whose reading has been so cruelly circumscribed, that the best known poets are a dead blank, and their choice sayings as completely lost to him as if they had never been written. Verily, I have been "casting pearls to swine" with a vengeance! BELLEROPHON.
Warrington. 25, 6, 1888. [With this letter we close the correspondence ori this question.—En., Ely.]

MR. GEORGE WOODS' DEFENCE OF THE GAS COMMITTEE. Sir,—Surely Mr. George Woods took up very shaky ground when he set up as a defence of the Gas Ccm- mittee at the ratepayers' meeting on Tuesday night that more gas was being made every year at the gas works. If he had shown that more gas was being sold and paid for it would have been more to the point. But what do we find? Taking the last twe years—ending March 1888 and March 1887—for which we have the gas works returns, it is true we find that some 8,000.000 more cubic feet of gas was made in 1887 than in 1886, but at the same time some 13,000,000 feet less was sold and _paid for. That is to say, all the increase in the manufaCture of gas, together with a lot more, has, to all appearances. been made simply for the purpose of sending to waste through the pipes. At this rate of " progress " I think the gas works would not be long in reaching a condition which even Mr. George Woods would find it hard to defend. Mr. Woods made a violent attack on Coun- cillor Dixon for saying that no accounts had been pre- sented to the Council for some years back by the Gas Committee, but I believe even here Councillor Dixon is right and Mr. Woods all wrong. The accounts are not presented to:the Council by the Gas Committee they are simply included in the annual compilation known as The Borough Treasurer's report a the receipts and expenditure of the Corporation of Warrington."— Yours, &c., Warrington, June 29, 1888.
VERAX.

Sir,—lt has come to my' knowledge that some mem- bers of the Ratepayers' Association have stated that the chairman of the Gas Committee supplied me with the data upon which I based my remarks at the meeting of Tuesday last. I was not unprepared to hear such a re- port. Kindly allow me, through the columns of your esteemed journal, to give that report the most unquali- fied denial. My sources of information were the reports which have been issued annually to the Corporation, compiled by the official heads of the several depart- ments. The graduated increase in the consump- tion of gas from the year 1877 to 1887 may be found at the end of the report ending March 25th, 1887. It is in the form of a chart carefully executed by Mr. Paterson. The facts and figures in reference to the gas accounts may be found at the end of the report ending March, 1888. They occupy about 25 pages, and five pages are given of a special report by the committee. Mr. Walker, who spoke after me, obtained his information from .the same source. These reports I held in my hand at the meeting. The data respecting salaries may be found in a report presented to the Corporation only a few weeks ago. The question which prefaced the remarks of Mr. Toft did not reach me at the time it was asked. It was, "whether I was an annuitant or bondholder of the Cor- poration ?" The question is suggestive, but one which no gentleman would have asked, and only a person a stranger to good manners could have done so.—Yours truly,
GEORGE WOODS.
THE COMPENSATION QUESTION.

Sir,—" Ile-11-ere-p-ho-n-,7'-t-O my mina, is not an honest debater. He fails to deal with the arguments that have been adduced, and introduces irrelevant remarks that have no bearing on the question at all. In affected horror, he says that I called him a thief. He affirmed that those who sought to deprive a man of his license were dishonest. I met his argument by saying that those like he who would make the nation pay for the withdrawal of licenses are the thieves; and I repeat it. He boils over with accusations that " Cadmus ' and I are full of "cant," and fail to keep in mind the com- mandment, "Thou shalt not steal." His assertions,how- ever, are worthless,not being backed up by a single argu- ment in his last letter to show how he brings us under the category of thieves. It has been pointed out to him that licenses are granted only for a year, and that those who hold them possess great advantages over those who do not. If by the wish of the nation the licenses are not renewed, is there anything dishonest in placing the publicans on the same level with other tradesmen? Let "Bellerophon" answer this question, instead of wasting his time in hurling false accusations at his neighbours. Let him argue, and not indulge in unmeaning declama- tion. The publicans pay for their license for one year and no longer. If the license was withdrawn without cause before the expiry of the license then, and only then, could compensation be justly demanded. It is argued that large sums of money are invested in licensed properties, and that this would be, to a great extent, lost. The publican, however, entered the business knowing the power of the Justices to withhold the re- newal of licenses at the end of the year, and if he loses by the transaction be has no one but himself to blame, for he was not compelled to take the license; instead, he used every effort in his power to obtain it. More than that, if the publican was not blind he would haveseenthe rising tide of temperance sentiment, and if he does not set himself to cope with it, then he must take the conse- quences. The fate of the compensation clauses should be ample warning to the man who is not fond of specu- lation. "Bellerophon" is strong in his indignation at such as I, who would take away licenses without com- pensation. He blabs loudly of honesty, and commiser- ates the publican; yet honesty to, and sympathy for, , the people is not part of his creed. Yes, we would keep the nation sober by Act of Parlia- ment. " petifogging " though " Bellerophon" may think our notions to he. Better this than that 600,000 of our fellow-countrymen should go every year to a . drunkard's grave, sent there by the liquid that " Bellero- phon's " friends readily supply them with. Better this than to hear the cry of the widow and orphan, calling for , judgment on those who denied that they were their brother's keeper, and gave drink to men when their hearts told them that they should have warned them at d refused it. Interest and custom have made us callous I to the havoc wrought by drink. Let " Bellerophon "be I a man, and use his influence to crush a traffic that` is ruining body and soul. Let him think of the stimulus that would be given to trade were the money spent in drink judiciously expended. For 20s worth of drink, the purchaser gets about Is worth of labour; for 20s worth of cloth he would get 133 to 15s.—Faithfully, G. H. Buckie, N. 8., 25th June, 1888.

WESLEYANISI.II AT GOLBORNE. Sir,—With respect to the excellent letter in yours of 16th inst., allow me to say a word. Mr. Baine cannot pass it over in silence without making a complete ad- mission (none the less cogent, because tacit) of his great and fatal error in the affair. I hope, therefore, he will reply, and reply satisfactorily; if he ea, I.—Y ours, &c., PROTEUS.

Sir,—Mr. Kent's letter in (attemped) reply to "Wes- leyan" in your issue of June 16th, may be critically summed up in one word—" weak." First he objects to the anonymity of the writer; forgetting that, in these days, it is obviously impossible—for any public person— to write other than anonymously. Then Mr. Kent says "Wesleyan" " ruphed into print !" which is very weak, considering that the affairs under consideration occurred in November and December, 1887; and "Wesleyan" never " rushed " till June, 1888! "Wesleyan" is so very well informed, in nearly every detail of this matter, that Mr. Kent's sentence (containing the words "careful to make himself thoroughly acquainted, with a mind free from prejudice, escaped mistakes (?) into which he has fallen," "avoided the misconceptions, misrepresenta- tationa, misjudgments, and unfair conclusioas ") is simply delicious, and warthy the pen of some fledgling sprig of divinity "fresh from college;" andeagerto airhispowers of verbosity, irrespective of direct relevance to facts. It is very hard to choose nice words in dealing with a " Rev." ; but it is scarcely possible to criticise the next sentence (In which Mr. Kent accuses " Wesleyan" of having "-spun a misleading letter"), without using the the strongest possible words. Suffice it to say again that "Wesleyan" spun" nothing, as Mr. Kent must well know; and, in his own interests and the interest of the Christian Gospel, of which he is one of the accredited messengers, he had much better have omitted this—well, I will only call it—attempted denial of facts! Next Mr. Kent goes in for a weak attempt at " Tup- perian " proverbs, which are amusing, if not very in- structive, but require no further comment. Now to take his heads in detail. As regards No. 1, the "unpleasantness" does certainly "involve a settle- ment with a minister; and it is a weak quibble for Mr. Kent to deny it in the way he does. Mr. Kent knows this well. No. 2: This it was wasted time, paper and ink for Mr. Kent to write. No. 3: This Herculean effort (I use the word effort advisedly) at wit needs neither denial nor affirmation. No. 4: In regard to this head, I am distinctly of opinion that Mr. Kent's " proposal " was to " increase the number of trustees," so as to be "able to outvote" those whose action had caused the disruption. The are Mr. Kent's own words, in reply to the question "what good would that do ? " Will Mr. Kent say that I have "spun" this out of my imperfect

knowledge ? " I trow riot. I said at the time that the proposal meant simply "diamond cut diamond," and was utterly unworthy of men professing Christianity. No. 5: So far as I could learn nothing salient was aver tried (or even suggested) to heal the breach. Attempts to gloze the matter over were made again and again; but the dissentients most justly demanded (and still de- mand) that the main cause of offence should be acknow- leged and rendered impossible fer the future. As regards No. 6. Mr. Kent is right in connecting" Wesleyan." .so far as the Dissentients were only a part of those who erected the schools, but they were so important a part, that it would have been just graceful for Mr. Kent to , have left this unsaid, pace, the "sop to coarberus," im- plied in his finishing touch," could cheerfully write in their praise." Really! How distinctly precious and sweet! No. 7. This is beautiful in its simple weakness! As, so far, not a resource of " Weslevanism," with the name, has been tried. Nos. 8 and. 9 may, for the sake of brevity, be passed over; requiring no com- ment. And now, let me just allude to one important matter in Mr. Kent's letter. " Wesleyan " says Mr. Kent styled the cause of the disruption as "a piece of work he (Mr. Kent) would not have touched with his finger- ends." This may may not be an exact reproduction of Mr. Kent's protest against the affair, but, so far as I can remember, it is, to all intents and purposes, the echo of Mr. Kent's views as stated at the time. To this point Mr. Ken 4 makes no allusion whatever, and this silence— so complete and astounding—cries most loudly to Mr. Kent to adhere to his intention to take no notice of fur- ther press correspondence upon this matter. Before I conclude, I had perhaps better state briefly— divested of all side issues—the cause of this sad disrup- tion. Money was paid irregularly to the contractor for the Golborne schools, the building committee and the trustees not having sanctioned it. That is— a gentleman (a non-resident trustee, and a personal friend of the contractor) saw fit to pay it. Then, instead of appeal- ing to the trustees and building committee for re-imburse- ment, this gentleman went to St. Helens to Mr Baine,and through him privately obtained the money without any further meetinge or discussion. These are the facts, and contain the main cause of all the trouble. And now, Mr. Editor, lest you begin to think me afflicted with the cacoethes scribentli, I will conclude, thanking you for giving me so much of your valuable space, and trusting my object in writing may be my sufficient excuse.— Your critical friend, SAINT HELEN. June 25th, 1888.

div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. (Continued from page 6.) WESTON.
div.p: THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. (Continued from page 6.) WESTON.

There is nothing of special interest to report on this section. The construction of the stage at the entrance to the Weaver is being proceeded with with all despatch, and will be completed in a few days. When that time arrives the machinery necessaiy for cutting out the canal on the Frodsham Marsh will be landed from barges, and about a thousand men employed ix removing soil. The men engaged by the firm of Messrs. Thomas Kirkham and Co. have commenced the erection of workmen's huts on the marsh, Thirty-six of these spacious dwel- lings are being constructed in the form of a square, the centre of which will be occupied by a mission-room. A smithy, joiner's shop, and other buildings are to be con- structed.

div.head: RUNCORN.
div.p: RUNCORN.

Work on this section has been partially suspended during the past week. An enormous amount of soil and clay has been deposited on the marsh at Norton, as a spoil bank, and the receptive capacity of the marsh is not yet exhausted. A vast quantity of clay will, how- ever, be needed to form the banks of the canal in the river bed, and it is considered to be inadvisable to con- vey more to the marsh when the trouble and expense of again removing it to the river will have to be afterwards undertaken. But operations in the river have not yet been commenced, and in consequence three of the Ameri- can steam navvies have been stopped from working. The fourth digger is still actively engaged in lengthening the cutting, and has now got to a point west of the works of Wigg Brothers and Steele . We understand that a bridge will be constructed over the Old Quay canal near the works named, and when that structure is made the diggers will be again started, and the clay removed to the banks of the river. Until then a considerable number of men will be thrown out of employment. MOORE, &c. There is nothing fresh to report this week in connec- tion with the works at Moore and Walton. At the latter place the two steam navvies continue to make headway in the cutting leading towards lh'ilderspool, and considerable activity is displayed both here and at Moore. THELWALL AND.STATHAM.

In consequence of the rain work was partially sus- pended in this neighbourhood yesterday. It may be mentioned that operations continue to be carried on at a very rapid rate, and that during the week a fresh steam navvy has been brought on the ground at Thelwall, and is awaiting the necessary fitting up preparations. Nearer Statham a German navvy is also waiting to be put in readiness for work, ftcl-Ib4vo I..)cen, erected on the new brickfields at Statham to protect the newly-hiOuidea brick from the weathers and flues are being constructed for drying purposes. The steam navvy has cleared away an immense quantity of material, and in doing so, has torn through the strata of clay, which is not so deep as it recedes from the river, crossing to Rixton ley, into a bed of gravel. Water is now being met with in considerable quantities, and a large ditch has been cut. From it a pulsometer is drawing a steady stream. Another pulsometer driven by a powerful engine is at work about 50 yards ahead of the navvy, drawing the water from the subsoil at a depth of 40 feet or thereabouts. A heavy fall of rain took place on Wednesday night and Thursday morning, which stopped all manual work. An additional steam navvy of a most powerful type arrived this7week at the junction of Thelwall and Statham, and is being fitted up ready to begin work. CADISHEAD.

The deepest cutting which-11-a—s -yet been made on the Lancashire side of the Irwell is at Skeer Rock, Cadis- head, where a depth of 40 feet has been reached, and two more "grafts" (15 feet each) remain tu be cut. Mr. Trevor is engineer for the Cadishead section.

div.head: FTIODSHAM.
div.p: FTIODSHAM.

A SAVAGE IRISHMAN AT FRODSHAM.—At the Eddisbury Petty Sessions, on Monday, Thomas Henry, an Irishman, was charged with having been drunk, and refusing to quit the Bear's Paw, Frodsham, on the 23rd inst. It ap- peared from the evidence of P.C. Brewster and Mr. Youd, the landlord, that the defendant was very drunk, and when being put out bit Mr. Youd on one of his hands, which had since caused hint considerable pain and expense. It wa4 thought the blood was poisoned. Defendant was fined lOs and costs.

PARISH CHURCH SUNDAY SCHOC TREAT.—The annual treat in connection with the abov e school took place on Tuesday. The scholars and teachers, numbering about 230, assembled at the Grammar School, Overton, at half- past ten o'clock, and quickly took possession of the decorated hurries, &c., which had been kindly lent for the ocoasion. Leaving the school, they proceeded to the house of Mr. Jeffrey Wright, of Manley, who had placed at the disposal of the scholars a suitable field, and they thoroughly enjoyed themselves with races and several well-known sports and games. Tea was served to the children on the grass, and the teachers dined together afterwards in one of the barns. Previous to the return journey the children gathered together, and vociferous cheers were given for Mr. Wright and the members of his family. TRINITY WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL.-011 Tuesday afternoon the annual treat of this school was held. The scholars, together with their teachers and friends, alto- gether numbering nearly 300, mustered at the school-room Chapel-lane, where hurries and carts, with the horses decorated with flowers, Sic' were in readiness to convey them to their destination. Seats having been procured for all, they proceeded to Riley Rank, the residence of Mr. William Andrews, via Woodhouses, headed by the Drum and Fife Band. Tea was served out to the chil- dren shortly after the arival at Mr. Andrews's, in a field opposite the house, whilst the teachers and friends par- took of tea in the granary. Subsequently all adjourned ! to a large field, in which many games were indulged in and heartily enjoyed. On re-assembling for the return journey, a hearty vote of thanks was given to Mr. and ! Mrs. Andrews and family for their kind reception. FURIOUS DRIVING AT HELSBY. At Eddisbury Petty Sessions, on Monday, George Spruce, of Kingsley, was summoned for furiously driving a horse at ilelsby, on the 7th June, and also for cruelly illtreating a horse at the same time and place; and John Carter, of Sutton Weaver, was summoned for causing the horse to be ! cruelly illtreated. The horse and trap, it appeared from the evidence of Sergeant Whalley and P.C. Pearson, be- I longed to Carter, and on the day named, about three o'clock in the afternoon, both defendants, who were very drunk, were in the trap, driving along Chester-road near Helsby. Spruce was driving and " "the horse with an ashplant, and Carter I was sitting on the trap urging it on. The horse was go- ing at a furious rate, and perspiration was not only dropping, but running trorq it. In the opinion of the officers, if it had gone mach farther it would have dropped.—Spruce, who was the only one who ap- peared, said that he was taking Carter, who was the worse for drink, and flush of money, home.— Spruce was fined 20s and costs for furious driving, and the costs in the other case, and Carter was fined 20s and costs.

THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY JUNE 30, 1888 ACTION AGAINST AN INSURANCE SOCIETY AT WIDNES. Before His Honour Judge Thompson and a com- mon jury, at Widnes County Court, yesterday, Ann O'Neil, of '2l, Lacc,y-st., Widnes, administratrix of Owen O'Neil, sued the Wesleyan and General As- surance for .glOO on a policy on her husband's life. —Mr. Segar (instructed by Mr. P. A. Lake, of Run- corn) was for the plaintiff, and Mr. Swift (instruc- ted by Mr. J. 0. Swift) was for the defence.—Mr. Segar said the policy upon which the action was brought was dated 20th April,.lBB7, and the insurer, Owen O'Neil, died on the 30th December of the same ybar, after suffering from bronchitis for four weeks. By a will the deceased bequeathed the whole benefit of this policy to a man named Horan, on the latter paying £3 towards the expenses.—The plaintiff said her husband was 55 or 56 years of age when lie died. She had been married to him 34 years. His general health was good.—By Mr. Swift : Her husband told her that Horan was putting him in the Assurance Society, and that he was paying the, first pre- mium. Her husband had been several times in • the workhouse. He was not suffering then from bronchitis or rheumatism. She did not know that at the time of her husband's death there were four policies on his life in the Prudential. There were twt.). She did not know why her two sons had no benefit Under the will.—Mr. Swift- characterised Horan as a speculator in policies.—His Honour pointed out that under an Act passed in the reign of George 111., when a policy was taken out for the benefit of a person other than the insurer, it must be so stated across the face of the policy. There was no doubt that this policy was taken out for the benefit of Horan, and this legality had not been car- ried out.—Mr. Segar said he could not deny that this policy was for the benefit of Horan.—A verdict was then entered for the defendant company, each side to pay their own costs.
CUT TO PIECES BY AN EXPRESS AT RUNCORN.

A shocking fatality occurred at Runcorn Railway Station on Wednesday night. When the II o'clock p.m. train from Lyme-st. arrived at Runcorn, a man, having the appearance of a sailorAwent to the guard, named John Corrin, and said he had come to Run- corn by mistake; he ought to have gone to Garston. Corrin told the man to cross over the bridge to the other platform, and he could return to Liverpool by a train that would start in a few minutes. The stranger then walked away, and shortly afterwards the London express passed through the station at a speed of 45 miles an hour. I.hym crossing to the other platform Corrin found the billycock hat of the than who had accosted him, and Mr. Howard, the foreman porter, upon making a search found a mutilated human foot, and a hand. Inspector O'Donnell and several constables appeared on the scene, and they also engaged in the search, with tke result that other portions of the body were found, and also some loose clothing. On the arri- val of the express at Liverpool the carriage exami- ner found the face and body of a man under the second carriage from the engine. The driver, Wm. Coppock, said he felt the engine give a jerk when passing through Runcorn Station, but it was not of so serious a nature as to cause him to stop the train. On the following day the scattered portions of the body were taken to the mortuary at Runcorn Cemetery, In the clothing or near to the remains on the line were found the return half of a ticket Liverpool to Garston, a boarding-house bill, and a knife, together with Is 2d in money. Yesterday Mr. H. B. White, the deputy coroner, held an inquest upon the body at the Burial Board Office. Evidence bearing out the above narrative was given. The body had not been identified.—ln answer to Mr. Ferrand, the railway company's re- presentative, James Robert Dustin, a shipping agent ' for the Cunard Company, said that had he had the boarding-house bill he could have traced the de- ceased.--Inspec.ter O'Donnell said no application was made for the paper.—The Coroner said identifi- cation formed no part of that inquiry, but no doubt the railway company would endeavour to trace the man and let his friends know his fate.—A verdict of accidental death was retuiPned.

div.head: ST. PATRICK'S ROMAN CATHOLIC CHURCH, WIDNES. OPENING CEREMONY.
div.p: ST. PATRICK'S ROMAN CATHOLIC CHURCH, WIDNES. OPENING CEREMONY.

To meet the needs of the large Catholic popula- tion, the Church of St. Patrick has just been erected in West Bank-st., off Waterloo-road, and on Sunday morning the ceremony of consecration was per- formed by the Right Rev. Dr. O'Reilly, the Roman Catholic Bishop of Liverpool. At eleven o'clock High Mass was celebrated before ' a crowded cm- gregaiion. There was a large attendance of clergy. The Rev. Patrick Clarke, King's Cross, London, wasthe cele- brant for the occasion, and he was assisted by the Rev. Fathers John Oldham, W. Shehy (professor of St. John's College, Waterford), Canon Carr, V.G.9 the Very Rev. Dean Finegan, the Sub-Dean, the Very Rev. M. Beggan, and the Rev. Father Clarke, rector of the mission. Amongst the visitors were Fathers O'Connor, P. L. Kelly (Bootle), E. Caffrey, E Brannan, Spencer, and M. Quirk°. A sermon appropriate to the occasion was preached by the Rev. Father John Kelly, of Gillrnoss, on the life and virtues of St. Patrick. In the course of an eloquent discourse, the prsacher described the labours of St. Patrick, and the marfellous effect produced by him on the Irish people. Within a single lifetime he changed Ireland from the Isle of Druids into the Isle of Saints. I Was it therefore any wonder that the Irish race should cling to the memory of St. Patrick with such tenacity and affection? The sacred edifice was again crowded in the evening, when the Rev. Father Chrysostom preached a sermon. We are indebted to the architects for the fol- lowing description of the church The style of the building is that of the early English period, a style that may justly claim to have no parallel for magnificence and grandeur of effect, but here it is of the simplest treatment in order to render it suitable to a locally where elaborate detail and broken surfaces would be quite out of place. The walls and piers are of mas- sive proportions for a church of its dimensions, impart- ing an effect of solidity which, with its simple lints and [details, forms its chief characteristic. Externally, the lwalls are faced with red pressed brickwork freely dressed with Rainhill stone. The west gable is surmounted by a bell turret, which rises nearly 100 feet from the street. The principal entrance is through the wes- tern porch, which extends across the full width of the nave, having a doorway at each end and an arcade of windows in front, facing West Bank- st. The baptistry, with its high-pitched roof, stands at the north-west corner, and has a second porch in connec- tion with it; the remainder of this side being flanked by the confessionals and sacristies. The choir and organ chamber, measuring 35 feet in length by 18 feet in width, is over the sacristies, opening into the church by an arcade 30 feet long, and affords accom- modation for a large choir. The church measures inter- nally 117 feet in length. by 52 feet in width across nave and aisles, and 50 feet in height. The nave arcade con- sists of six wide bays having octagonal columns with moulded bases and capitals and arches in Rainhill stone; with a clerestory above of long single deeply-splayed lancet windows. The west gable has a large traceried window, and the east a triplet of long lancet windows; the aisles, which are wide and lofty, have a double lancet window in each bay, and larger r ones of different design in the ends. The roofs are in pitchpine, boarded and panelled with moulded ribs. The nave roof is unbroken in its length of 108 feet by any chancel arch or division. The easternmost bays form the chancel and side chapels, which are separated and raised from the body of the church by two wide steps, on which stand the altar rails. The flooring of the chancel and chapels is in solid oak and wal- nut parquetry; the passages of the church are laid with large polished flags, and * the spaces occupied by the benches with wood blocks. The glazing throughout is with cathedral lead lights ci extra strength, of simple yet effective design. The high altar and reredos, which have been executed from the designs of the architects by Messrs. Norbury, Paterson, and Co., of Liverpool, at a cost of £250, are in alabaster and a combination of coloured marble. The church I throughout is heated with hot water. Seat accommoda- ' tion is provided in the nave and aisles for 684 persons,' and the contract, exclusive of benches and high altar, was for £3,269 5s id. The architects of the building were Messrs. James and Bernard Sinnott, of 13, Herring- ton-st., Liverpool, and the contractors wgre Messrs. J. and T. Yearsley, of St. Helens. Mr. Tilley acted as clerk of the works. The boundary walls are now in course of erection, and a presbytery remains to be built.

div.head: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD INSPECTION.
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD INSPECTION.

In accordance with their annual custom the mem- -I,9rtt Qf thQ Widno Local I3oard en Tuesday inspec- ted the valuable property which they have managed so successfully in the interests of the ratepayers. The members who took part were Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. E. Carey, B. Brown, R. Cook, S. Sadler, D. Wright, F. Liddell, W. W. Gossage, J. Taylor, and T. Handley, and they were accompanied by the officials, J. T. Allen (clerk), I. Carr (engineer), Dr. Cooper (medical officer), T. Higginson (surveyor), and J. Dickson (nuisance inspector.) The party met at the gas works at eleven o'clock, and made the tour of the various buildings and examined the apparatus. Everything was found in the most complete order, and the arrangements in the usual state of efficiency. For the benefit of the members who had liot pre- viously attended the inspection, Mr. Carr gave a short, but lucid, description of the process of mak- ing gla, and illustrated the method by which its il- luminating power is tested. The chief interest of the members was, however, centred in the apparatus which is in course of construction for making gas by the Dinsmore process—a patent method which the Board has recently adopted. It is claimed that by this method a much greater quantity of gas can be manufactured from the amount ot coal con- sumed than is at present obtained, because the chemical compounds now deposited as a bye-product in the shape of tar, will be converted into illuminating gas. Although gas is Row sold in Widnes at a cheaper rate than in any other town in Lancashire, it is quite possible that if the patent is a success that a still further reduction may be made in the price of gas. Thence in a brake, supplied by Mr. Lee, and drawn by four horses, the party were rapidly taken to the Infec- tious Diseases Hospital at Halton View. Everything was fonnd in the most orderly and spotlessly clean condition, and it was satisfactory to notice that there was only one patient—a boy suffering from typhoid fever. A short drive brought the party to Pex Hill, where are situated the two reservoirs that supply the town with water, and here the party were treated to a unique sight. For the first time since it was opened by Miss Gossage ten years ago, the largest reservoir, .which, indeed, up to a few years ago was the largest covered reservoir in the world, had been allowed to empty itself, and in order that the members could inspect it Mr. Carr, had the huge caneon illuminated with 600 wax candles. Cut into the solid rock the reservoir is 330 feet long, 240 feet wide, and 23 feet high, the ponderous roof being supported by 360 massive stone pillars. The storage capacity is Ili mil- lion gallons, a sufficient quantity of water to just supply the town of Widnes one week only. Armed with lights, the party made a complete tour of what had the appearance of a subterranean cave, and expressed great satisfaction that the reservoir was in as good condition as when it was opened. Not the least gratified of the party was Mr. John Taylor, who was the successful contractor for the work, and who is now a member of the Board. For the edification of his fellow members Mr. W. W. Gossage blew some notes upon a horn that had been brought from the coach, and the sound as it echoed from a hundred points produced a tone like the prolonged note of the key of a pOwerful organ. On the spot the members decided that the reservoir should be kept dry until Thursday, and on that afternoon, despite the somewhat. unfavourable atmos- phere, considerable numbers went to view the strange sight. The reservoir was illuminated with 2,000 can- dles. The pumping stations at Stock's Well and Netherley were next visited, and the valuable and extensive machinery was in capital working order. The improve- ments introduced into the engines at Stock's Well last year, which have been fully described, have resulted in a much greater yield of water, and daily 1,750,000 gallons of water is pumped from the bowels of the earth. At Netherly the daily yield is abo-it 1,400,000 per day. At Stock's Well a new economiser has been introduced, and a saving in fuel is the result that it will amply repay the Local Board for the outlay of £3OO. It will be gratifying to the rate- payers to learn that the Board have sueh an abundance of water that they can with complete safety dispose of a million gallons per day, and a few months ago they were , approached by the Liverpool Corporation with a view toal- lowing that body a supply. On reasonable terms the Board offered the Corporation the quantity named, and also the use of their Belle Vale site, from which another mil- lion and a half gallons per day could easily be obtained. However the negotiations fell through, and pow Mr. E. Timmins, engineer, of Runcorn, is engaged boring for water at Naylor's Bridge on land belonging to Sir A. B. Walker. The members of the Board made a brief stop- page at the works on their journey. Although a depth of 348 feet has been pierced, the yield of water has fal- len far below expectations, and the fact that a bed of marl was met with at a depth of 330 feet is nOt encoura- ging. The horses' heads were now turned towards Gate- acre, and after passing through that picturesque village to Woolton, a stoppage was made at the Hunt's Cross Hotel, where the party sat down to an excellent dinner provided by Mr. H. Hilditch, the landlord. Afterwards the members paid a visit to Mr. F. H. Gossage, the chairman of the Board, at his residence, and this ended a successful inspection, the weather having fortunately , been fine.

div.head: ALLEGED ILLEGAL DISTRESS AT EARL ESTOWN.
div.p: ALLEGED ILLEGAL DISTRESS AT EARL ESTOWN.

At Warrington County Court, on Monday, before his Honour Judge Ffoulkes and a jury, a case was heard in which Derby Dowd, 3, Grant-st., Earles- town, formerly a green-grocer but now a labourer, claimed damages from Benjamin Corlett, timber merchant, Sze., Market-st., Earlestown, for an alleged illegal distress. Mr. H. L. Riley appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. 11. J. Longton for the defendant. In opening his case Mr. Riley told the jury that the defendant, besides being a grocer, was an agent for the collection of rents of small properties. It was alleged that, in December last, the defendant illegal- ly distrained on a shandry tl.at belonged to the plaintiff, who now demanded the return of the trap and damages for its detention. It appeared that the plaintiff was tenant of a house, for the landlord of which Mr. Corlett was agent. He became tenant in February, 1887, and seemed to have continued in occupation until November. On the 28th of that month Mr. Corlett called on Dowd and said that he thought he should have to give him a week's notice. Dowd replied that he had been thinking of doing the same thing, and would leave the premises on the following Monday—the fifth of December. On that day, however, Mr. Corlett refused to take the key. Between the sth and 12th of December Mr. Dowd was removing his furniture, when Mr. Corlett came upon the scene, and said-" What about my rent?" Dowd replied that if he would wait a little while he would pay him; meanwhile, he said, there was plenty of security on the premises in the shape of fixtures that might be purchased by the incoming tenant. Defendant, without producing any warrant of distress, and without any show of authority except the power of his own right hand, seized the shandry, took it away, and it yet re- mained in his possession. Plaintiff was in the habit of using the shandry in the course of his business, he was too poor to buy another, and soon afterwards his horse died, since which time he had not been in business. The value of the shandry was £4 10s, and plaintiff was en- titled to be recompensed for any damage that was im- mediately caused to him by reason of its detention. On the defendant being applied to for the shandry he wrote a letter in reply, in which he said that he held the trap, with the consent of Dowd, for rent owing. He alleged, in the letter, that it had been an understood thing for some time that he sisould keep the trap until Dowd paid the rent. It would be a question for the jury, after hear-' ling the evidence, to say whether or not on the occasion in question the plaintiff did consent that Corlett should take away the trap. Defendant had put in a counter- claim for 30s due for arrears of rent.—Plaintiff then gave evidence bearing out his advocate's statement, and Frederick Dunstan Grimshaw, tripe dresser, Earlestown, said that on the day in question he assisted Dowd to re- move his furniture. Mr. Corlett came up, and said "What about the rent, Derby?" Plaintiff replied "Wait a little while, and I'll pay you." Corlett then took the trap, and witness told him that it was wrong for him to do so without a warrant of distress. Corlett replied that Dowd could have the trap when he paid the 30s owing. —At this point his Honour said that there was evidence of irregularity, but not of illegality, as it seemed to be admitted thai some rent was owing. Plaintiff went to demand the return of the trap, but did not tender the rent owing. After argument between his Honour and Mr. Riley had followed, his Honour amended the claim from "illegal" to "irregular" distress.—For the defence Mr, Longton said that he should prove that there had been nothing irregular in the matter, because the trap was detained with the consent of the plaintiff.—ln sup- port of his contention he called the defendant, who said that he detained the trap with the consent of the plain- tiff, and who also gave evidence regarding the rent ow- ing.—Corroborative evidence was given by Charles Cor- lett, the son of the defendant, and evidence was also given by Jane Corlett, wife of the defendant; Thomas Scott, builder, Earlestown ; and Richard Sides, joiner, Earlestown ; the two latter being called to speak to the value of the trap, which they placed at from 20s to 30s. His Honour haying summed up. the jury found for the defendant on the original claim, and on the counter-claim for 18s.

LYMM BIBLE SOCIETY.—A service of song in connec- tion with this society was held in the Drill Hall, Lymm, on Sunday evening, conducted by Mrs. Mac Gill. STATHAM INFANT SCHOOL.—On Wednesday afternoon Mr. Parkes, assistant to the Rev. Mr. Lomax, inspected the Statham Infant School. Miss Moore, the mistress, presented 45 children. ALLEGED SHOPLIFTING AT LYM3l.—Thomas Brown, navvy, was brought up on remand at the Sale Petty' Sessions, on Monday, before Mr. R. H. Joynson and other magistrates, charged with stealing a pair of boots, value 15s, last week, the property Mr. of William Derbyshire, Lymm. It appeared that, on the 21st inst. the prisoner entered the shop of Mr. Derbyshire, and helping himself to a pair of boots, put them under his jacket and ran out of the shop, pursued by the prosecutor. He was found after a while and handed over to the custody of P.S. Harrington, to whom he admitted having taken the boots.—The prisoner was sent to gaol for one calen- dar month, with hard labour. SCAFFOLD ACCIDENT.—On Monday afternoon a scaffold accident took place at the new stable which is being erected for Mr. Tetlew at the back of his residence. Mr. T. Readitt, plumber; in the employ of Mr. Frangleton, together with the son of the latter, were on a plank which was supported by a pole and resting on a pad- lock. As Mr. Readitt was screwing spouting against the end of the rafters, the pressure which he applied in his work was sufficient to press bade the pole and allow the padlock to fallout. There were a few slates on the Plank at the time, and these also fell and reached the ground first, and on one of these Mr. Readitt fell with his foot, receiving a gash prom which blood flowed copiously. THE FUSTIAN CUTTING THADE.—On Monday evening a meeting of fustian cutters was held in the large club- room belonging to the Mill Stone Inn. Mr. Thomas Gatley presided. Thirty years ago, he said, the price of velvets was 7s per 100 yards, and in a short time after the prices advanced from 7s to us per piece. This was maintained in 1862, although the cotton panic began in 1860, but the outside districts were not in harmony with them. By the power of combination in this neighbour- hood they at that time met all opposition for 12 months ' during the most severe depression in their business. He might say that Lymm had always taken the first step for an advance in prices, and he hoped that that night they would be unanimous in trying one more attempt to in- crease the well-being of their class. If they could only get an increase of 20 per cent, it would be a considera- tion worth striving for. They must, be firm on that point, for the masters looked upon any attempt on their 1 part to better themselves as antagonistic to the em- ployer's interest, although there was no reason why that should be so. He suggested that Lymm and Warnngton should join with Cadishead and other districts, and have a central meeting at Manchester, when some good might be done. Isolated action would be of little avail. Ultimately it was decided to form a society of fustian cutters, and a committee pro. tem, was elected.

LATEST NEWS.
The Queen held a Privy Council at Windsor on Friday,. a .
The King of the Belgians left London on Friday for Brussels.

The Duke of Westminster has joined the :Liberty and Property Defence League. Lord Hartington has promised to preside at the annual meeting of the National Association for the Promotion of Technical Education which will be held in London held Saturday afternoon. A MEETING of Conservative agents from all parts of the country was held yesterday afternoon at the Constitu- tional Club, London, to consider a new scheme of party organisation for election purposes. The proceedings were private.

FATAL ACCIDENT TO AN OCTOGENARIAN.—On Thursday night, a man named William Harper, an octogenarian, who was by permission hawking temperance drinks to the night-shift men at the chemical works, Northwich, was run over by a railway waggon. He was removed to the Victoria Infirmary, and died during the night. THE SMALLPDX EPIDEMIC AT PRESTON.—Three fresh cams were on Friday morning added to the books of the sanitary department, making, with thirteen on Thurs- day, sixtreen in the two days. There has been another death at the Workhouse Hospital. This makes a total of twenty-two deaths since the epidemic began. The total cases registered during the epidemic have been over 340.

THE OTIONNEL LIBEL CAsp.—Mr. T. Harrington has been subpcenaed to produce in the "Times "action all the books and documents relating to the Land League, the Ladies' Land League, and the National League. Earl Spencer and Lord Aberdeen, -ex-Lords Lieutenants of Ireland, and Sir George Trevelyan and Mr. Campbell- Bannerman, former secretaries to the Lord Lieutenant, have been subpcenaed to appear in the case, which will come on next Monday. Tlng LIBEL ACTION BY A JOCICEY.—The hearing of the case of Wood v. Cox was resumed on Friday morning, in the Queen's Bench Division of the High Court of Jus- tice, before the Lord Chief Justice (Lord Coleridge) and a special jury. The Lord Chief Justice continued his summing up to the jury, The jury retired at two minutes past one, and on,their return the foreman an- nounced that they had found a verdict for the plaintiff, damages one farthing. Drnsion on MB SUNDAY CLOSING CLAUSE te Lo division on clause 9of the cal Government Bill, the minority which supported the clause consisted of 147 Gladstonian Liberals (including Mr. Childers, Sir Wm. Harcourt, Mr. Morley, Mr. Mundella., Mr. Stansfeld, Sir George Trevelyan), 67 Parnellites, and 1 Conservative (Captain E. Heathcote.) The majority -which rejected it consisted of 222 Conservatives, 53 Liberal Unionists (including all the leaders, but not including Mr. T. W. Russell), and 2 Gladstonian Liberals (Dr. Clark and Mr. Evershed.) SWINDLING THE SHIP CANAL CONTRACTOR.—At Altrin- cham, yesterday, James Hodnett, butler, late in the em- ploy of Mr. Walker, contractor of the Manchester Ship Canal, was committed for trial for stealing silver and table linen, value £7. The prisoner told Mr. Walker he was a teetotaller, but he was discharged for intemper- ance, and on his boxes being searched the articles in question were found, and also a quantity ef silver ready packed for removal. Mr. Walker stated that he did not know the extent of the depredations until an inventory was made.

ISLE OF TIIANET ELECTION.—The polling for the Isle of Thanet Division of Kent commenced on Friday morn- ing, the candidates being the Hon. E. Knatchbull- Hugessen (G.L.), and the Right Hon. JamesLowther (C.) The weather was beautifully fine and the polling com- menced briskly at Ramsgate, but slowly at Margate. The result will be declared about noon to-day (Saturday.) Mr. Hugessen drove through the streets in the morning with the Countess Tolstoi, the Hon. Philip Stanhope, M.P., and others, and was received with cheers, mingled with groans. Mr. Lowther, who left Ramsgate for Mar- gate at eleven o'clock, received cheers and some hoot- ing.

MARRIAGE OF THE DUKE OF MARLBOROUGH. NEW YORK, FRIDAY AFTERNOON.—The Duke of Marl- borough was married to-day, at the City Hall, before the Mayor, to Mrs. Hammersley, a wealthy, middle-aged American widow.
YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.
The House met at 4 o'clock.

A Bill to amend and consolidate the law, relating to patents and inventions, and the registration of designs and trade marks, was read a first time. REFORMATORY SCROOL9.—Lord NORTON called atten- tion to a report of the Select Committee on Reformatory and Industrial Schools, and introduced a Bill to consoli- date and amend the enactments relating to them. The Bill was read a first time. THE SAFETY OF THE COUNTRY. _

Lord WEMYSS drew attention to defective armaments, and moved a resolution approving of the proposals to increase our defensive means.—Lord WOLSELEY challen- ged Lord George Hamilton's statement as to the enor- mous transport required to convey the one hundred thousand men across the Channel wanted to capture London.—Lord Henws said that the Government had made important changes at the War Office in the public interest.—The DUKE OF CAMBRIDGE believed that there was no immediate danger to the country, but—" We must be prepared." Lord SALMI:GM rebuked Lord Wolseley for raising unfounded alarms of a sudden in- vasion.—The motiorrwas agreed to. HOUSE OF COMMONS. The House met at 2 o'clock.

POLICE SurmaAwEHATioN.—Mr. RITCHIE, replying to Mr. S. Leighton, said the conditions as to superannua- tions and pensions of the police, including chief con-. stables, would not be in any way affected or modified b 3/ the provisions of the Local Government Bill. THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT BILL.—The House went into committee on the Local Government Bill, and resumed the consideration of clause 15, which provided for the maintenance of main roads.—Mr. WOODWLLL moved the first of a series of amendments, with t. 4 view of pro- viding that any part of a main road which waH situated in a borough, should be repaired and maintained at the expense of such borough, and that every borough should be exempt from contributing towards the ex- pense of maintaining any other main road, or portion of main road, without the county.—Mr. RITCHIE pointed out that under the clause the county authorities would be ob- liged to devolveupon boroughs the maintenance of a road within a borough, if applied to for the purpose, so that boroughs would have a perfect right to main- tain their roads in their own way and area.—After a dis- cussion the amendmesit was withdrawn.—Mr. J. T. BRUNNER proposed an amendment to the effect that con- tributioas should be fixed by the Local Government Board, instead of by arbitration.—Mr. RITCHIE said that the Local Government Board would not shrink from that duty, but if so decided the staff of the Board would have to be increased.—The amendment was agreed to.—An amendment, moved by Mr. BRUNNER, giving County Councils a permissive right to contribute to the main- tenance of public footpaths, as well as highways, was agreed to.—On the consideration of Clause 16, which authorized County Councils to enforce the provisions of the Rivers Pollution Act, Mr. BRUNNER moved an amend- ment to the clause —Mr. RITCHIE promised to reconsider the clause, with a view to strengthening the powers of County Councils on the subject.—The amendment was then withdrawn, and the clause was agreed to. and pro- gress reported. The House resumed at nine.—Mr. THOMAS ELLis called attention to the serious condition of the agricultural tenantry in Wales, and moved a resolution stating that owing to the prevailing agricultural depression, the Government should take steps to provide a measure of relief which should secure fairer conditions of tenure and re-adjustment of rent more equitably corresponding to the fall in prices, and make such other provisions as would enable the cultivators of the soil in Wales to meet the trying circumstances in which they were placed. [LEFT SITTING.]

div.head: TECHNICAL INSTRUCTION.
div.p: TECHNICAL INSTRUCTION.

The following communication from the Vice- President of the Council has been received in reply to the memorial of the Warrington Association for the promotion of Technical Instruction, which ap- peared in our columns last week : Education Department, June 22nd, 1888. Sir,—l am desired by Sir William Hart Dyke to ac- knowledge the receipt of your letter of the t Oth inst., and the memorial that accompanied it, from the War- rington Association for the Promotion of Technical Instruction. _ _

I am to state in reply for the information of that body that clause 3 of the Technical Instruction Bill is designed to give to Local Authorities, where no School Boards exist, all the powers which School Boards may exercise under clause 1, including, of coursp, the right to collect the seventh standard children in central classes for the purpose of technical instruction. The question as to the rate permissible in such cases will receive careful consilleration. I have the honour to be, sir, Your Obedient Servant, ALMER/C FITZROY.

/ CHARLES MADELEY, ESQ. ' The final report of the Royal Commission on Elementary Education, which was appointed two years ago, has at last been issued in a volume of some 300 folio pages. Some of its suggestions in regard to manual and technical instruction have been anticipated in the Government Bill. In regard to drawing, the repert recommends that it be made Compulsory in all boys' schools. Manual instruc- tion should not be given in the elementary schools, but in separate workshops to which should be admitted only those boys of ten years old and upwards who show ability. Though boys at school should not be taught trades, some elementary instruction in science is only second in importance to reading, writing, and arithmetic. "By technical instruction, we mean instruction in the scientific or artistic principles
